papers.title: Decision Attacks on Known-Covariance Ring-LWE via Public Gram Determinants
papers.abstract: Known-Covariance Ring-LWE (KCov-RLWE) was introduced by Micciancio and Suhl to support simulation-secure threshold encryption. It strengthens ordinary Ring-LWE by revealing an exact quadratic summary of the hidden secret and errors, and its decisional hardness was left open. We give explicit polynomial-time decision attacks for broad families of prime moduli at ring rank one. Our key observation is that the public sample and the covariance hint together determine a bordered Gram matrix whose determinant exposes a hidden residual with a different distribution for genuine and uniform samples. After reducing the ring into finite-field components, this residual has one of two forms: a product across reciprocal components, or a Hermitian norm when a component is preserved by conjugation. The latter case yields a particularly strong distinguishing signal. Moreover, reduction modulo any divisor preserves the KCov real and random experiments exactly, so every attackable odd prime divisor of a composite modulus transfers the corresponding distinguisher with no loss of advantage. The attack covers the one-sample setting globally in the self-reciprocal regime and, under the coefficient-product Gaussian specialization, locally in the completely split regime. More generally, we obtain a complete classification of how this residual-based attack behaves for odd prime moduli when $m\ge2$, and extend these guarantees to arbitrary moduli possessing a suitable odd prime divisor. The classification does not imply insecurity for every parameter family: when the relevant residue fields are sufficiently large, the guaranteed distinguishing advantage in the reciprocal case can become negligible, and pure power-of-two moduli remain outside the divisor-reduction extension. Accordingly, our results invalidate the KCov pseudorandomness assumption in the quantified families; they do not show that every parameter choice permitted by the motivating Ring-PKE sketch is insecure, nor do they give a direct IND-CPA break of the complete threshold-encryption construction.
papers.authors: Anis Bkakria

papers.title: On Robust Combiners for Pseudorandom Codes and PKE with Pseudorandom Ciphertexts
papers.abstract: Robust combiners are a standard way to hedge cryptographic assumptions: given several candidate constructions, they produce one construction that remains secure as long as one candidate is secure. In favorable cases, such combiners also yield universal constructions. We ask whether this paradigm applies to cryptographic primitives whose public outputs must be both pseudorandom and sparse. Our first result gives a negative answer for pseudorandom codes (PRCs), i.e., error-correcting codes whose codewords are computationally indistinguishable from uniform strings. We prove that secret-key PRCs admit no black-box robust combiner. The impossibility holds even for the weakest meaningful guarantee, where the combined scheme is required to be secure when all but one candidate PRC are secure. We then show that the obstruction is not specific to error correction. In the sparse ciphertext regime, public-key encryption with pseudorandom ciphertexts also admits no black-box robust combiner. This stands in contrast to ordinary IND-CPA encryption, for which robust combiners are easy to obtain. Thus the requirement that public outputs look uniformly random introduces a genuine barrier to black-box assumption hedging, and rules out the standard combiner route to universal constructions for these primitives.
papers.authors: Nico Döttling, Venkata Koppula, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree, Felix Rohrbach

papers.title: Subexponential Algorithms for LWE via Rejection Sampling on Superlattices
papers.abstract: Recent superlattice algorithms have improved the provable complexity of lattice problems. Ducas, Engelberts, and Loyer used this framework to obtain a subexponential algorithm for infinity-norm short integer solution, while also identifying a key obstacle to extending it to learning with errors (LWE). A similar difficulty arose in the analysis of Kirchner and Fouque, whose claimed subexponential running time with only linearly many LWE samples was not rigorously established. Building on the framework of Ducas, Engelberts, and Loyer, we develop two refinements based on rejection sampling that solve this open problem. First, we use rejection sampling to cancel the shift-dependent normalization factor that arises when sampling from a shifted, scaled integer lattice. This factor is a product of one-dimensional Gaussian masses and can be evaluated efficiently. This yields a provably subexponential classical search-LWE algorithm for prime $q\in[n^2,2n^2]$ and constant Gaussian error width. It uses only $m=4n$ independent samples and runs in time and space $\exp(O(n/\ln\ln n))$. Second, we use random auxiliary superlattices and apply rejection sampling to the difference of two Gaussian lattice samples, ensuring that the accepted output follows the desired discrete Gaussian distribution up to a small statistical error. For $q=n^{\kappa+o(1)}$, $m=n+h=O(n)$, and $R=h\ln q/[m\ln(2+\sigma)]\to\infty$, the resulting algorithm uses time and space $2^{(1/2+o(1))n/\ln R}$, where $\sigma$ is the Gaussian error width. In particular, for $\sigma=n^{o(1)}$ and any fixed $m/n>1$, our algorithm achieves provable subexponential classical running time, whereas the primal and dual baselines have exponential-time bounds and earlier provable subexponential BKW analyses require $\Omega(n\ln n)$ samples.
papers.authors: Ligeng Fan, Changpeng Shao, Hongbo Li, Dingkang Wang

papers.title: Strongly Adaptive Asynchronous Byzantine Agreement with Linear Communication and Almost-Everywhere Termination
papers.abstract: It is well known that Byzantine agreement requires $\Omega(t^2)$ messages against a strongly adaptive adversary that may corrupt $t=\Theta(n)$ parties and suppress a party's undelivered messages upon corruption. We circumvent this lower bound by relaxing termination: for any constant $0 0$ and every $t\leq(1-\delta)n/3$, we construct binary agreement with this guarantee in authenticated asynchronous networks against strongly adaptive corruptions with message takebacks. Except with negligible probability, these guarantees hold and every honest decision carries a transferable justifier. The protocol achieves almost-everywhere termination in expected $O(1)$ rounds, expected total communication $O(n\kappa^2)$ bits, and expected maximum communication $\widetilde O(\kappa^2)$ bits over honest parties before corruption, where $\kappa$ is the computational security parameter. Our construction combines a recursively shared BLS signing key with certificate dissemination over a sparse graph. The recursive sharing is used to implement threshold signing with distinct safety and liveness thresholds. Dissemination propagates existing certificates to almost all honest parties. The construction uses a trusted setup and is secure in the random oracle model under the algebraic one-more computational Diffie--Hellman assumption. We further obtain full binary agreement with the same asymptotic communication and round complexity against adaptive corruptions without message takebacks. The extension requires neither atomic multi-send nor private communication channels.
papers.authors: Renas Bacho, Simon Holmgaard Kamp, Julian Loss, Jesper Buus Nielsen, Maciej Obremski

papers.title: Provable Security of SHA-256-Based LMS Revisited in the Ideal-Cipher Model
papers.abstract: The hash-based Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) has been standardized by IETF, NIST and ISO. State-of-the-art non-quantum security proofs for LMS have been given by Katz (SSR 2016) and Fluhrer (Eprint 2017/553). However, the actual structure of SHA-256(/192) is the (chopped) Merkle-Damg{\aa}rd construction using a blockcipher-based Davies-Meyer function, and precise security bounds of SHA-256-based LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and SHA-256/192-based LMS\_SHA256\_M24 should be derived in the {\it ideal-cipher model (ICM)}. This was {\it not} considered in Katz and Fluhrer's proofs. In fact, by leveraging structural properties of (chopped) Merkle-Damg{\aa}rd, we exhibit forgery attacks against LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and LMS\_SHA256\_M24 that expose the inapplicability of Katz's and Fluhrer's random-oracle bounds to the concrete SHA-256 constructions. The precise security guarantees of LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and LMS\_SHA256\_M24 thus remain unknown (and are also missing in the standards). To bridge the structural gap, we provide ICM-based security proofs for the additive-Davies-Meyer abstractions of LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and LMS\_SHA256\_M24. The security level of LMS\_SHA256\_M32 is roughly $256-\log_2 \widehat{B}$ bits, where $\widehat{B}$ is the number of blocks in SHA-256 calls internally made by LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and $\widehat{B}\ll2^{128}$. The security level of LMS\_SHA256\_M24 is roughly $\min \{ 192 - \log_2 \widehat{\Gamma} , 256-\log_2 \widehat{B} \}$ bits, where $\widehat{\Gamma}$ is the number of SHA-256/192 calls internally made by LMS\_SHA256\_M24 and $\widehat{B}$ is the number of blocks in them, and $\widehat{B}\ll2^{128}$ and $\widehat{B} \widehat{\Gamma} \ll 2^{192}$. In conclusion, LMS\_SHA256\_M32 and LMS\_SHA256\_M24 ensure a moderate (yet not ``full'') level of security.
papers.authors: Chun Guo, Hao Cheng, Bart Preneel, Meiqin Wang

papers.title: SILMARILS-MV: Information-Theoretically Secure Multi-Verifier Signatures with Dealer-Free Key Issuance and Linear Aggregation for Permissioned Blockchains
papers.abstract: Permissioned blockchains authenticate transactions, votes and quorum certificates with computationally secure signatures, and post-quantum replacements inflate consensus traffic by orders of magnitude. Information-theoretic alternatives have required a trusted authority, quantum channels, per-signature interaction, or single-use keys with bounded transfer. We present SILMARILS-MV, a multi-verifier unconditionally secure signature in which a signature is the vector $α= A\,e(m)$ and each verifier holds a secret functional $c_i = Γ^T λ(x_i)$ derived from virtual anchors $Γ$ that nobody learns. Against unbounded adversaries corrupting up to $ω$ verifiers and any signers, and observing every decision, an honest verifier accepts a forged or invalid signature with probability at most $Q/q + 1/(q-1)$, a bound that is tight in its leading term. The scheme is strongly unforgeable, non-repudiable, transferable across unboundedly many hops, and linearly aggregatable. Keys are issued by the validators through perfectly secure MPC for $t < n/3$, without broadcast. To scale, we let the committee itself sign: in threshold notarization, finality certificates have constant size $32(ω+1)$ bytes and per-validator issuance cost no longer depends on $n$. Arbiter-verified keys give clients 32-byte signatures, robust redistribution supports membership changes and share refresh, and verifiers can be enrolled retroactively. A certificate verifies in 2.4 microseconds. In an analytic normal-case model at 1000 validators, threshold notarization needs 71 KiB of authentication traffic per validator per block, 22x less than ML-DSA-44 for admitted verifiers. In a Rust HotStuff prototype with 100 validators, SILMARILS-MV commits 2.8x more transactions per second than ML-DSA-44 with 67x less cryptographic CPU, and Monte-Carlo attacks match the bounds.
papers.authors: Khadijeh Bagheri, Hassan Khodaiemehr, Chen Feng

papers.title: Cryptanalysis and Repair of "Decentralized Multi-authority ABE for NC$^1$ from BDH"
papers.abstract: We present a plaintext-recovery attack on both the DBDH-based construction and the CBDH-based variant of Datta, Komargodski, and Waters (Journal of Cryptology, 2023). The attack succeeds with probability one in the claimed static security model using one corrupt authority and two users, each unauthorized even when granted the corrupt authority's attribute. The flaw is an invalid extension of the LSSS matrix-normalization lemma originating with Rouselakis and Waters (FC,~2015): preserving complete-share distributions does not preserve coordinate-wise ciphertext masks, which a corrupt authority can expose to remove identity binding from other users' shares. For both variants, replacing these masks with independent full linear sharings of zero preserves correctness and restores ciphertext-distribution invariance. We prove static security of both repaired variants in the random oracle model under their respective BDH assumptions, using the original hardcore-bit convention for the CBDH variant. Both proofs allow adaptive identity-hash queries. The modification retains the original matrix-width and row-labeling restrictions, keys, decryption, and ciphertext size, requiring only additional encryption randomness and finite-field arithmetic. We also attack both multi-authority attribute-based inner-product functional encryption constructions of Datta and Pal (PKC, 2023) and establish correctness and matrix-substitution invariance of the same repair. We prove static security of the repaired small-universe construction under asymmetric DBDH. For the large-universe construction, we identify a missing source-group encoding in the original reduction and give a complete static security proof under an augmented $L$-DBDH assumption, whose generic bilinear group hardness we establish.
papers.authors: Xingwang Wang

papers.title: On the Subtleties of Non-Malleability in IVC: Notions, Attacks and Constructions from Falsifiable Assumptions
papers.abstract: We investigate non-malleable Incrementally Verifiable Computation (IVC), a subject that has received limited attention. We focus on whether and how simulation-sound IVC can be obtained from falsifiable assumptions. We provide additional evidence of the unique aspects of non-malleable incremental proofs, identifying definitional challenges in formalizing simulation-sound IVC, and showing how existing IVC designs from falsifiable assumptions cannot exhibit simulation-soundness "for free" (without modifications). In addition to a new family of definitions of simulation-sound IVC, our main results are the following. - A general negative result: common Valiant-style proofs are malleable. We isolate and formalize a feature shared by the dominant Valiant-style IVC designs (Valiant, TCC 2008) related to the ability to merge proofs together. We show that, assuming one-way functions, natural zero-knowledge versions of Valiant's design are malleable. As an implication of our framework of attacks, we show that the only IVC for NP from falsifiable assumptions (Datta et al., CRYPTO 2025) cannot satisfy any form of simulation-soundness; this is the case even when instantiating this scheme from non-malleable building blocks. - A positive result: first IVC from falsifiable assumptions with non-malleability features. We construct an IVC satisfying a non-trivial form of simulation-soundness under subexponential iO and either subexponential LWE or subexponential bilinear-map assumptions.
papers.authors: Matteo Campanelli, Suvradip Chakraborty, Chaya Ganesh

papers.title: Chosen Commitments and Certified Decoding Regions in the Adaptive Threshold Schnorr Attack
papers.abstract: Crites and Stewart reduce an adaptive forgery attack on threshold Schnorr signatures with $N$ parties and threshold $\tau$ to one call to a sparse linear search oracle, which they show to be bounded distance decoding of a diagonally scaled Reed–Solomon code and whose sparse answer, a witness, names the parties to corrupt. Their analysis samples the coefficient vector behind the adversary's commitment uniformly at random and leaves open whether a chosen vector does better. We bound the success of an adversary that follows their template with a chosen vector and recovers witnesses only inside regions built from the radii that seven decoding theorems, three for Reed–Solomon and four for folded Reed–Solomon codes, certify under their own setup hypotheses. When the commitment is fixed through a known coefficient vector before a fresh hash challenge, the attack target is, conditional on the history that fixed the vector, a uniform point of a line. For distinct nonzero Shamir points, our main theorem shows that every such line contains at most $M$ targets with a witness in a finite collection of coordinate and block weight regions fixed before the targets, each permitting fewer than $\tau$ nonzero coordinates, for an explicit integer $M$ depending only on $N$, $\tau$ and the collection. We call the adversary the wrapper when it makes at most $Q$ fresh challenges and no signing query, chooses each coefficient vector from its history before the challenge and keeps it afterwards, and lets its solvers make no further signature hash queries. It accepts only a witness of the same target and representation that lies in the regions of the collection within its corruption cap, corrupts parties only once it holds such a witness, and then forges from that witness and stops. Hence the wrapper succeeds with probability at most $QM/p$, with $p$ the group order, even if its solvers recover every witness in the regions at no cost. On the six pairs $(N,\tau)$ of the original attack, fixed collections built from partitions into consecutive blocks contain all seven certified regions and have $M$ below $2^{24}$, so at the field size proxy $p = 2^{252}$ the bound stays below $2^{-100}$ after $2^{128}$ challenges. For uniform targets we prove much smaller bounds on the witness probability in these regions. For the folded Guruswami–Wang and Ashvinkumar–Habib–Srivastava block regions on partitions into consecutive blocks fixed before the target, this probability is negligible for polynomially many parties, exponentially large fields and $\tau/N$ bounded away from zero. These results also classify the studied decoder theorems. The hardness of the oracle, the success of other strategies and the adaptive security of threshold Schnorr schemes are open.
papers.authors: Hüseyin Eren Demirtaş, Oğuz Yayla

papers.title: The Entire Quantum Computer on a Classical Leash
papers.abstract: We show that a classical client with no quantum hardware can use a single untrusted and potentially malicious quantum server as if it were its own trusted quantum computer. Through the server, the client can privately choose and run quantum computations, prepare quantum states, and process quantum states supplied by other parties. It can also keep quantum memory on the server, hidden from the server itself, and use that memory in later computations so its quantum state persists across rounds of interaction. Together, these capabilities let a purely classical party act as a quantum party in a variety of interactive protocols. We expect this virtual quantum computer to be a broadly useful tool. As immediate applications, we resolve two known open problems: (1) classical verification of quantum sampling with negligible computational soundness error, and (2) remote state preparation of arbitrary efficiently preparable quantum states. Underlying all of these results is a general-purpose, maliciously secure two-party computation protocol between a classical client and a quantum server, which we construct assuming only the post-quantum hardness of learning with errors.
papers.authors: Yael Tauman Kalai, Dakshita Khurana, Justin Raizes

papers.title: Private Information Retrieval with Accountability at Erasure-Optimal Server Redundancy
papers.abstract: Private information retrieval (PIR) hides which database item a client requests. We study PIR that also identifies servers that respond incorrectly. Against a coalition of at most $t$ corrupted servers, the client must retrieve the item and identify every deviating server when at most $d$ deviate. Above that threshold, it must abort and return an empty identification set, with a specified statistical error. We present SynTrace, a single-round compiler for linear PIR supporting audit queries whose honest answers belong to a public code. The client combines the retrieval query with $m$ audit queries using secret linear mixing and independent blinding. Audit syndromes identify deviations before reconstruction. We prove perfect query privacy, zero false-identification probability within the deviation threshold, and statistical realization of an accountable PIR functionality. For Shamir-based PIR, SynTrace uses $k=t+d+1$ servers. Under the stated privacy and download assumptions, tolerating $d$ missing responses already requires this many servers, so identification adds no server overhead. With this number of servers, $m=d$ audit queries suffice with a suitable field, and are necessary within the specified syndrome-span decoder class. Additional audit queries can reduce communication by allowing a smaller field. For one 32 KiB record from a 1 GiB database, with five servers, privacy and robustness against two corrupted servers, and error at most $2^{-40}$, SynTrace uses 2.25 MiB of communication, compared with 8.96 MiB for the homomorphic-MAC construction of Eriguchi, Kurosawa and Nuida (TCC 2022) under the same workload and thresholds. Batched retrievals can share the audit queries.
papers.authors: Myeongjun Kim, Hyunseok Jeong, Mincheol Son, Young-Sik Kim

papers.title: VeilDNS: Post-Quantum DNS Privacy from the First UDP Packet
papers.abstract: DNS was designed around UDP, and most DNS traffic today still follows that design: one query, one response, and no handshake. This makes DNS fast and scalable, but exposes client queries in cleartext. DoT, DoH, and DoQ provide privacy by encrypting DNS messages with TLS. This works once TLS/TCP or QUIC handshakes complete, but cold sessions spend extra round trips and CPU before the first private query can be sent—a cost that grows with post-quantum cryptography. We present VeilDNS, a DNS-native protocol that uses a post-quantum KEM and AEAD to encrypt DNS questions and answers and authenticate the resolver in a single UDP exchange. Given an authenticated resolver KEM key, clients have query privacy from their first UDP packet. VeilDNS supports stateless and stateful modes—the latter reducing recurring computation and bandwidth. An optional mode provides forward secrecy from the second query onward. By preserving the DNS wire format, VeilDNS runs on the standard UDP port 53. Compared with ML-DSA-authenticated Do(T/H/Q) on the well-provisioned network profile, VeilDNS's stateless and stateful modes achieve up to $3.5\times$ higher cold-session throughput, $4.8\times$ lower average latency, $4.7\times$ lower CPU time, $13.7\times$ fewer bytes, and $15.8\times$ fewer packets. On the constrained profile, the throughput gain reaches $12.4\times$. Tamarin establishes query confidentiality, response authentication, and forward secrecy.
papers.authors: Aditya Singh Rawat, Mahabir Prasad Jhanwar, Rei Safavi-Naini

papers.title: Quantum Cadence: Post-Quantum Consensus with Multiple Concurrent Proposers
papers.abstract: The consensus protocols of most high-performance blockchains use quorum certificates, which bundle the signatures of a quorum of validators. Signature schemes such as BLS can aggregate the signatures of a whole quorum into a single short signature, which keeps these certificates small. A large-scale quantum computer would break these schemes, and no post-quantum scheme with comparable aggregate size and aggregation time is known. Without aggregation, a certificate holds one large post-quantum signature per member of the quorum, so it becomes infeasible for each validator to broadcast certificates, as modern consensus protocols often require. We present Quantum Cadence, a post-quantum consensus protocol with multiple concurrent proposers that avoids certificates altogether: every validator counts quorums among the messages it has received itself. Its safety and liveness do not even depend on signatures, although we add signatures to obtain accountability. Quantum Cadence builds on Cadence and replaces its slot consensus, Chorus, with Quantum Chorus, which keeps the optimal fast-path latency of Chorus: dissemination followed by two rounds of votes. When its fast path fails, Quantum Chorus runs Coda, our signature-free Byzantine agreement for multiple proposers. We also outline how the Conductor, which schedules the slots of Cadence, can be adapted to Quantum Cadence. In simulations with 200 validators, Quantum Chorus has a latency comparable to that of Chorus and scales better with the number of proposers.
papers.authors: Mohammad Mussadiq Jalalzai, Tobias Klenze, Jovan Komatovic

papers.title: SynMark: Semantic-Coordinate Multi-Bit Watermarking during LLM Code Generation
papers.abstract: LLM-generated code is increasingly reused across downstream applications and often undergoes identifier renaming or structural refactoring, making robustness to functionality-preserving edits essential for generative multi-bit code watermarking. Existing methods commonly derive message routes from surface-token prefixes, so such edits can desynchronize routing and degrade watermark recovery. We propose SynMark, which replaces surface-dependent routing with learned semantic coordinates and further calibrates residual recovery errors after transformation. For watermark embedding, Scope learns semantic coordinates from aligned prefixes of functionally equivalent variants for keyed routing and applies a syntax-aware adaptive bias during generation. For watermark extraction, Traced recomputes semantic routes from transformed code and uses reliability-weighted aggregation to suppress unreliable token contributions. Under 100% identifier renaming, SynMark retains 82.27% and 83.77% BitAcc on CodeLlama and DeepSeek-Coder, respectively. Across three code LMs, it also improves clean BitAcc and Pass@1 by up to 4.53 and 11.18 percentage points over the strongest watermarked baselines.
papers.authors: Rui Xu, Weizhi Liu, Zhaoxia Yin

papers.title: A Memory-efficient Implementation of Wiedemann XL
papers.abstract: The signature schemes MQOM, SNOVA, MAYO, and UOV are third-round candidates in the NIST standardization process for additional post-quantum signatures, and their security relies on the hardness of the multivariate quadratic (MQ) problem. XL with block Wiedemann (BW) is one of the most efficient MQ solvers in practice, but its memory demand has led to a debate about its memory access cost: generating the rows of the Macaulay matrix on the fly is widely believed to save memory at a non-negligible computational cost. In this work, we evaluate the memory--time trade-off in practice. We provide the first efficient on-the-fly implementation of XL with BW. We build on the state-of-the-art implementation by Cheng, Chou, Niederhagen, and Yang (CCNY), which uses SSE instructions and supports the fields $\mathbb{F}_2$, $\mathbb{F}_{16}$ and $\mathbb{F}_{31}$; we remove its column-index tables and generate the rows on the fly in the first phase of BW (BW1). We amortize the cost of on-the-fly generation with a new algorithm that computes column indices with $O(n^2)$ instead of $O(n^3)$ table look-ups, where $n$ is the number of variables. In our experiments we observe that our on-the-fly implementation achieves running times comparable to CCNY's with up to five times less memory. We also port both implementations to AVX2 over $\mathbb{F}_{256}$, the main field of UOV, and observe a similar behavior: comparable BW1 running times with less memory for the on-the-fly variant.
papers.authors: Daniel Cabarcas, Tung Chou, Felipe Merino, Javier Verbel

papers.title: Nearly Optimal Hardness for CVP and NCP with Preprocessing
papers.abstract: The closest vector problem(CVP)and the nearest codeword problem (NCP) are fundamental computational problems with connections to learning, coding theory, and cryptography. We study hardness of approximation in the preprocessing model: an algorithm receives the lattice or code in advance, may perform unrestricted computation to produce polynomial-size advice, and must then solve the problem on any target in polynomial time. Unless $\mathsf{NP} \subseteq \mathsf{P/poly}$, no such algorithm achieves an approximation factor of $\bullet$ $M^{1−\varepsilon}$ for NCP over any fixed finite field, or $\bullet$ $M^{1/\min\{p,2\}−\varepsilon}$ for CVP in any $\ell_p$ norm, for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, where $M$ denotes the code block length or lattice dimension, respectively. We improve the subpolynomial factors of Khot, Popat, and Vishnoi [KPV14]to polynomial ones, matching the exponents that Song [Son26] proved without preprocessing for binary codes and the $\ell_2$ norm. We further extend Song’s evaluation tables to every fixed prime characteristic and the lattice reduction to $\ell_p$ with $p > 2$. Our main technical contribution is an extension of the moment method, introduced in an OpenAI report [Ope26] and improved by Song [Son26], to the preprocessing setting. In addition, we give a direct reduction from probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs) whose query locations and families of possible predicates do not depend on the formula. The resulting factor of $M^{\Omega(1/(\log \log M)^2)}$ is already larger than that of [KPV14], and the reduction may be of independent interest.
papers.authors: Giacomo Fenzi, Guy Weissenberg

papers.title: When Elliptic-Curve Semiprimality Certificates Reveal Factors
papers.abstract: Public certificates of semiprimality could support cryptographic modulus generation by proving that an integer has exactly two prime factors without revealing them. Their usefulness in this setting depends on whether the certificate preserves the difficulty of factoring. Motivated by the examples of Reble and Broadhurst, we formalize semiprimality certificates by adapting the Goldwasser-Kilian primality criterion. For certificates with a prime point order, our semiprimality theorem uses public data $(N,S,E,P)$ comprising a composite nonsquare integer $N$, an elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, a certified prime $S>(N^{1/6}+1)^2$, and a point $P\in E(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ of order $S$ modulo every prime divisor of $N$. Hasse's bound forces each prime divisor above $N^{1/3}$, proving that $N$ has exactly two prime factors. For such semiprimality certificates constructed using complex multiplication (CM), we show that a norm-lattice reconstruction factors $N$ from $(N,S,D)$ alone in expected polynomial time when the Frobenius at every prime divisor lies in a known imaginary quadratic field of fundamental discriminant $D$ or has trace zero, and $\gcd(S,2DN)=1$. Applying this reconstruction and complementary public-point and quadratic-twist attacks, we factor Reble's 1084-digit and Broadhurst's 5061-digit moduli. These attacks also defeat proposed repairs based on hidden cofactors, withheld CM maps, or private isogeny descent within a known field under the stated hypotheses. We leave open whether one can efficiently produce a public Goldwasser-Kilian-based certificate for a fixed modulus, using its privately known factors, while preserving its factoring difficulty relative to the General Number Field Sieve.
papers.authors: Giuseppe Vitto

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Loss Exploration for Vision-Based Perception under Non-IID Data
papers.abstract: Vision-based image classification models benefit from Federated Learning (FL) across vehicles, however learning accurate models from distributed vehicular cameras is challenging due to data heterogeneity and privacy concerns. To improve performance on non-IID data, advanced FL optimization approaches have emerged that share auxiliary insights, such as client gradient behaviors. While these gradient-guided optimized FL methods improve the model accuracy, their reliance on sharing additional gradient information introduces a previously unexplored privacy vulnerability. In our empirical privacy-leakage experiment, we show that a malicious server can infer clients' label sets from shared guidance matrices under heterogeneous client label distributions (simulated via Dirichlet-based label partitions), between 50% and 84% accuracy. To address this privacy leakage, we propose PPFLex that replaces the central server with three Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) servers to securely compute the global guidance matrix and perform federated averaging under semi-honest and malicious MPC server assumptions. We evaluate PPFLex on widely used traffic-sign classification datasets (e.g., GTSRB and BTSC) as representative autonomous vehicle perception benchmarks, comparing against baselines. Our results show that PPFLex achieves accuracy comparable to the plain-text FedLEx pipeline while preventing privacy leakage, incurring acceptable MPC overhead.
papers.authors: Nergiz Yuca, Christian Internò, Nikolay Matyunin, Markus Olhofer, Barbara Hammer, Stefan Katzenbeisser

papers.title: AgentTrace: Execution-Level Fingerprinting of Black-Box LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Verifying the provenance of autonomous LLM agents is a critical security challenge. Existing semantic attribution is easily obfuscated by system prompts, while active watermarking conflicts with schema-constrained tool generation. We propose AgentTrace, an active framework that identifies the foundation model behind a black-box agent via observable execution traces. AgentTrace injects structurally ambiguous probes to trigger tokenization-sensitive serialization failures at rigid tool interfaces. While these initial failures provide coarse-grained separation across model families, the temporal sequence of subsequent repair operations reveals fine-grained, model-specific recovery behaviors. By modeling these multi-step trajectories with lightweight Markov chains, AgentTrace achieves 96.0% attribution accuracy under adversarial identity spoofing. Crucially, sequential repair modeling successfully distinguishes the evaluated intra-family variants sharing identical tokenizers (e.g., Llama-3 8B/70B), substantially outperforming unordered behavioral statistics while remaining robust against prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling.
papers.authors: Gejian Zhao, Hanzhou Wu, Xinpeng Zhang

papers.title: Notes on BulletProofs++ Range Proofs
papers.abstract: We review the Bulletproofs++ construction which replaces the bit-decomposition inner-product argument of Bulletproofs with a reciprocal set-membership argument over base-$16$ digits. We present a self-contained specification of the $64$-bit range proof as well as a general batched variant parametric in the batch size $M$ and bit width $b$ and prove honest-verifier zero-knowledge and exact-form knowledge soundness. We describe the evaluation and optimizations of our Rust implementation over Ristretto255, which proves up to $7.8\times$ and verifies up to $4.5\times$ faster than regular Bulletproofs. Finally, we correct two formulas of the original paper: the affine $T^3$ term of the scalar polynomial $p_s(T)$ carries a factor of $2$, and the slot-$0$ component of the blinding vector $r_S$ carries the opposite sign.
papers.authors: Philipp Jovanovic, Arnab Roy

papers.title: Revisiting ZMAC+: Birthday-Bound Attacks and a Beyond-Birthday-Bound Repair
papers.abstract: ZMAC+ is a tweakable-block-cipher-based MAC proposed by List and Nandi in ToSC 2017 with claimed beyond-birthday-bound security. We show that a tag-swap mechanism previously observed for a hypothetical two-output extension of DoveMAC also applies to the published ZMAC+ construction. For two-block tags, we give a distinguisher with constant advantage and a fresh-message forgery with constant success probability using $O(2^{n/2})$ queries in the ideal-TBC model, where $n$ is the block length. An internal collision between two message families exchanges their tag blocks; a common extension preserves this relation and leads to a forgery with one additional authentication query. We identify a counting error in the published Lemma~4 and prove a corrected aggregate differential bound. The resulting PRF and MAC upper bounds match the birthday query threshold for bounded message lengths and two-block tags, under explicit field-order conditions. The distinguisher extends to every legal fixed output length $d\ge2$, and the forgery to every legal even $d$. We also retain ZHash and separate the output domains. Under stated field-order, length, and domain-capacity conditions, this modification admits an adaptive PRF bound of order $q^2/2^{n+\min(n,t)}$ for bounded lengths. Finally, a one-query counterexample shows that the ZAE security theorem must retain the per-message length restriction required by its counter-in-tweak encryption component.
papers.authors: Yan Jia, Peng Wang, Lei Hu, Shuping Mao, Tingting Guo, Jiadong Han

papers.title: Mikros: Bitwidth-Aware SNARKs over Extensions of Small Fields
papers.abstract: Provers for succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (SNARKs) perform arithmetic over a large field for soundness, even when the witness entries are a few bits wide, which inflates both prover time and memory usage. Recent work makes individual SNARK components bitwidth-aware, so that a lower witness bitwidth means faster proving and lower memory usage, but these techniques cover only part of the prover and exploit the structure of specific fields, typically binary ones. We introduce Mikros, a framework for end-to-end bitwidth-aware SNARK construction based on algebraic vector packing. We pack vectors of length \(N=m\kappa\) over a base field \(\mathbb{F}\) into length-\(m\) vectors over a degree-\(\kappa\) extension field \(\mathbb{E}\), which turns length-\(N\) relations over \(\mathbb{F}\) into length-\(m\) relations over \(\mathbb{E}\) and makes existing linear-time extension-field protocols bitwidth-aware. This technique thus unifies bitwidth-aware inner-product proofs, Hadamard-product proofs, and polynomial commitment schemes, previously obtained by separate constructions, and yields the first bitwidth-aware grand-product proof, hence the first bitwidth-aware permutation argument. Composing them gives bitwidth-aware SNARKs for circuit satisfiability over extensions of arbitrary small fields. For a single instance of circuit satisfiability, the prover cost is proportional to the effective bitwidth, the combined bitwidth of the witness entries and the wiring-position encodings; across instances of the same circuit, the position encoding is amortized and the per-instance cost is proportional to the witness bitwidth. Although Mikros does not rely on binary-field structure, its prover is \(2.19\times\), \(2.55\times\), and \(1.85\times\) faster on batches of \(256\) SHA-256 compressions, Keccak permutations, and BLAKE3 compressions than Flock (B\"unz \etal, IACR ePrint 2026), the state-of-the-art bitwidth-aware SNARK over binary-extension fields.
papers.authors: Mingshu CONG

papers.title: Maximum-Likelihood Decoding of Gabidulin Codes Is NP-Hard Even in Dimension One
papers.abstract: Fix a prime power q . We prove that deciding whether a received word y ∈ F^n_qm lies at rank distance at most n − 2 from the one-dimensional Gabidulin code {λg : λ in Fqm } is NP-complete. Thus maximum-likelihood decoding of Gabidulin codes is NP-hard even for k = 1, an analogue of the Guruswami-Vardy theorem for Reed-Solomon codes. In the Hamming metric, by contrast, hardness at this radius requires the dimension to grow with the length, as in the Guruswami Vardy theorem. The reduction is deterministic; consequently Rank Syndrome Decoding (RSD) and Rank Minimum Distance (RMD) for Fqm -linear codes are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial reductions, whereas the previously known reduction was randomized. The proof goes through a pivot problem that we introduce, Twisted Square Membership (TSM): given Fq -subspaces U, W in FqN , decide whether some non-zero a ∈ U satisfies a^(q+1) in W . Quadratic systems in d unknowns are encoded into TSM, then TSM into Gabidulin decoding. The last step views the received word as an Fq -linear map and decoding at radius n − 2 as the search for an Fq -plane on which it acts as a scalar. With support U + τ W in a cubic extension and map a + τ b → a^(q^2) + τ b^q , two Frobenius twists force solution planes to encode the relation a^(q+1) ∈ W . All constructions are explicit and polynomial, with N = O(qd^2 ), n ≤ N + d, and m = 3N .
papers.authors: Philippe Gaborit

papers.title: On the Inapplicability of Residue-Confined Error Attacks to CRT-FHE with Non-Degenerate Error Distributions
papers.abstract: This paper responds to the cryptanalysis presented in “Key Recovery from Residue- Confined Errors in the Pradhan CRT-RLWE Construction” (Olejnik and Naskrecki, 2026), which claims key recovery and plaintext recovery against the CRT-FHE scheme introduced in “A New CRT-based Fully Homomorphic Encryption” (Pradhan et al., 2026). We demonstrate that the reported recovery attacks rely entirely on a deliberately con- structed error distribution whose support lies in the kernel of the CRT encoding function. Consequently, the effective encryption error is identically zero, reducing the attacked con- struction to a noiseless RLWE instance. The subsequent key-recovery and plaintext-recovery results therefore follow from the deliberate elimination of the encryption noise, rather than from any cryptanalytic method capable of recovering secrets from properly noise-bearing CRT-FHE ciphertexts. Crucially, the proposed attack neither removes nor estimates errors from normally generated CRT-FHE ciphertexts. Instead, it assumes an artificial error distribution specifically chosen to guarantee their annihilation during encoding. This condition does not hold for the intended centered-binomial error distribution, under which the probability that an entire error polynomial belongs to the encoder’s kernel is negligible at the reported parameters. Thus, the presented recovery procedures do not constitute attacks against the concrete CRT-FHE instantiation with its intended non-degenerate error distribution. We conclude that the reported key-recovery and plaintext-recovery results concern a deliberately degenerate, effectively zero-error instantiation and do not demonstrate a practical security compromise of CRT-FHE under its intended error sampling.
papers.authors: Anil Kumar Pradhan

papers.title: The Exact Bit Security of Hash-Based Signatures
papers.abstract: In this work, we analyze the security of hash-based signatures in Lean4. We examine how different ways of accounting for an adversary’s work yield different notions of bit security. As our working example, we study two instances of XMSS with $128$ bit digests. Under most of the accounting modes we consider, we get $127$ bit security for strong unforgeability. However, under the most conservative convention that counts only the adversary’s direct random oracle queries, we only get $122$ bits of security. We prove these bounds in the random oracle model without computational hardness assumptions and give matching attacks. We also prove a tight bound of $127$ bits of strong unforgeability for SLH-DSA-128s. Our work is primarily motivated by recent autoresearch competitions, and it demonstrates the concrete impact of resource accounting. We hope that it helps designers of future challenges make an informed decision when choosing a notion of bit security that reflects their needs.
papers.authors: Mikhail Kudinov, Benedikt Wagner, Emile Wambsgans

papers.title: Faster Matrix Multiplication Leads to Faster Lattice Sieving
papers.abstract: Let $\omega$ denote the matrix multiplication exponent. Very recently, OpenAI showed that $\omega\le9/4$. We demonstrate that, for any fixed $\eta>0$, if $\omega\le9/4-\eta$, then there is a constant $\delta=\delta(\eta)>0$ such that heuristic lattice sieving can be improved to $(3/2-\delta)^{n/2+o(n)}$ time under the spherical heuristic used in the BDGL analysis. With known matrix multiplication algorithms, our method already yields subquadratic search within BDGL buckets.
papers.authors: Yiming Gao, Honggang Hu

papers.title: Embedding Large PQC KEMs in IKEv2
papers.abstract: Post-quantum key encapsulation mechanisms carry public keys far larger than the established VPN handshake protocol IKEv2 was designed for. At the same time, its initial exchange comprising the public keys cannot be fragmented. In response, the IETF discusses a range of protocol adjustments, yet these proposals have never been compared in terms of their performance and stability under identical conditions. We systematically screened the IETF document corpus for such proposals, added three of our own (one using forward error correction and two using IKEv2 with QUIC, namely QUIKE and QUIKE with a composite key exchange), identified two specification gaps in existing acknowledgment drafts, and implemented all eight on the same open-source codebase. Measurements across different bandwidths, latencies, and packet loss rates, and with ML-KEM, FrodoKEM, and Classic McEliece, total 126 500 handshakes in 1296 different configurations and show that no mechanism fully compensates for the effect of the key size on performance. For Classic McEliece, no approach handles challenging conditions acceptably. The approaches either congest the link or take up to nearly two minutes per handshake on average. For ML-KEM and FrodoKEM, there are two ways forward: building on already standardized extensions or delegating the transport. The former requires the larger implementation change and needs further optimization, such as acknowledgment mechanisms or error-correcting codes, but grants continuity and compatibility. The latter can use a composite key exchange to avoid these drawbacks and achieve a faster, more resilient handshake and leaner implementation, with QUIKE-composite offering the best overall performance.
papers.authors: Daniel Herzinger, Marco Thomas, Tobias Handirk, Stefan-Lukas Gazdag, Daniel Loebenberger, Marian Margraf

papers.title: SPA: Structure-Preserving Approximation of Gated Activations under FHE
papers.abstract: Nonlinear activation evaluation remains a major bottleneck in neural inference under fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). FHE supports efficient addition and multiplication, but lacks native operations for exponential functions, reciprocals, and value-dependent selection. High-degree polynomial approximations on fixed intervals are therefore commonly used to replace nonlinear activations. They can achieve small errors but often incur substantial multiplicative depth and latency. We observe that several widely used nonlinear activations share the algebraic structure $A(x)=xg(x)$ with $g(-x)=1-g(x)$. This class includes GELU, SiLU, fixed-parameter Swish, and the scalar nonlinear branches of GEGLU/SwiGLU. We propose \SPA{} (\emph{Structure-Preserving Approximation}) to exploit this shared structure. \SPA{} retains the exact odd component $x/2$ and approximates only the even residual as a polynomial in $x^2$, yielding a comparison-free arithmetic kernel. This construction removes redundant odd degrees of freedom and enables lower-cost polynomial evaluation at a given error target. Plaintext experiments with Gemma-4-E2B and Llama-3.2-3B show that SPA largely preserves downstream task performance without weight updates. Fixed-interval CKKS benchmarks show favorable error--latency trade-offs. On $[-5,5]$, \SPA{}-balanced achieves a $3.25\times$ speedup over MOAI (ICLR'~26) for erf-GELU with comparable error. On the same interval, \SPA{}-accurate achieves $79.22\%$ lower root mean squared error (RMSE) and a $10.40\times$ speedup over Euston (S\&P'~26) for QuickGELU. For SiLU, \SPA{}-accurate achieves $19.02\%$ lower RMSE and a $2.06\times$ speedup over THOR (CCS'~25).
papers.authors: Rui Li, Wenyuan Wu, Weijie Miao

papers.title: Agentic AI Defense: Decode-Time Provenance Binding for MCP
papers.abstract: Agentic AI systems using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection through untrusted tool outputs. We demonstrate cross-modal trust laundering, in which instructions concealed in an email-signature image using least-significant-bit (LSB), discrete cosine transform (DCT), or metadata steganography bypass text scanners and enter a multi-agent workflow when decoded by a tool. To counter this threat, we propose decode-time provenance binding, which combines HMAC-authenticated trust labels with an MCP-maintained provenance ledger and context-taint tracking. The mechanism labels decoded content as untrusted and blocks critical tool calls influenced by that content, even when a compromised agent substitutes a valid trusted label. We evaluate the approach using a real MCP testbed with three steganographic carriers and 24 adaptive payloads. The undefended pipeline exhibits 100% attack success, while keyword and regex defenses each permit 62.5% of attacks. Our mechanism blocks all attacks (0% success), including adversarial label substitution across mediated agent boundaries. A four-component ablation validates the roles of decode marking, cryptographic authentication, lineage tracking, and sink enforcement. An audited trusted-promotion mechanism increases legitimate-task completion from 67% to 100% without compromising protection. The approach provides carrier-independent containment within fully mediated MCP execution environments. Code and data are publicly available.
papers.authors: Eric Yocam, Varghese Vaidyan, Paris Kalathas, Patrick Tague, Bruce DeBruhl, Yong Wang

papers.title: Exact Error Bootstrapping and Comb Bootstrapping in FHEW/TFHE
papers.abstract: In FHEW and TFHE, bootstrapping evaluates the decryption function via a blind rotation, whose resolution limits the message space. We propose instead to bootstrap the \emph{error}. By rounding the ciphertext at a resolution that is a multiple of the message modulus, we preserve the message exactly. Reduction modulo a small integer then yields a noise-free encryption of the error, which a single blind rotation lifts exactly before it is subtracted. The message modulus is thus constrained solely by the noise and can be much larger than in standard TFHE. Since the error takes far fewer distinct values than the ring degree, a single blind rotation can also refresh several ciphertexts simultaneously. We call this procedure the comb bootstrap. Between refreshes, an integer remains encrypted in a single ciphertext, allowing additions modulo the message modulus and multiplications without programmable bootstrapping. Built on TFHE-rs, for $8$-bit integers on a single thread, our refresh is $3.5$ times faster than that of TFHE-rs, and $9.1$ times faster with the comb bootstrap; multiplication is $6.5$ times faster. In a residue number system, multiplication of integers modulo $\widehat P\ge 2^{32}$ is $19$ times faster than in TFHE-rs. The error bootstrap serves exclusively to refresh ciphertexts; evaluating any other function still requires programmable bootstrapping.
papers.authors: Philippe Chartier, Mohammed Lemou

papers.title: Iterative Behavioral Identification for Covert Misappropriation Attacks
papers.abstract: We present a data-driven, three-phase framework for covert misappropriation attacks on closed-loop networked control systems. A man-in-the-middle (MITM) adversary, with access only to intercepted input-output data, incrementally identifies the plant's behavioral subspace while maintaining stealth under an infinity-norm intrusion-detection system (IDS). Phase 1 collects an initial rank-deficient Hankel matrix using a low-amplitude probing signal that satisfies an analytical stealth bound. Phase 2 adapts online rank-increasing experiment design to the closed-loop setting, using causal predictor-based masking to limit IDS residuals while the Hankel rank grows from 1 to the full behavioral rank n + mL in exactly n + mL - 1 steps. We show that the identified subspaces are strictly nested and that the projection error of any desired trajectory decreases monotonically, strictly so almost surely at each rank increase. Phase 3 employs the final Hankel matrix in a DeePC-style optimization to synthesize a covert attack that tracks an arbitrary reference while respecting the IDS constraint. Simulations on a DC motor with PI control demonstrate full-rank identification and stealthy tracking. Stealth is guaranteed analytically in Phases 1 and 3 and is numerically supported in Phase 2. The method is model-free and assumes noise-free LTI dynamics.
papers.authors: Victor Mattos, Amit Bhaya, Daniel Sadoc Menasche, Alan O. de Sá

papers.title: AquaSense-ICS: A Hybrid Real-Simulated Cyber-Physical Dataset and Leakage-Aware Benchmark for Smart Water Quality Monitoring and Attack Detection
papers.abstract: Machine-learning research on water cyber-physical systems (CPS) is constrained by datasets that are either real but chemically poor, or simulated but free of sensing noise and attacks. We present AquaSense-ICS, an open dataset and benchmark that co-registers (i) a 25.4 h recording window (8.0 h of recorded data, 26% coverage) from a Raspberry Pi 5 edge node (TDS probe and BME680 ambient sensor, 1-2 s sampling, 23,688 records), with (ii) a looped network of 13 nodes (10 junctions, 2 reservoirs, 1 tank) simulated in EPANET-MSX for six water-quality species, (iii) a parameterised library of cyber-attacks (false data injection, replay, denial of service, drift) and unintentional sensor faults with sample-level ground truth, and (iv) augmented and TimeGAN-generated sequences, flagged by an origin column. The attack, fault and water-quality labels are traceable to a seeded generator, a documented rule or a simulation input. We show that the most common way of benchmarking such hybrid data, random row splits and labels computed from the input features, yields near-perfect but uninformative scores (macro-F1 = 0.9998 for Random Forest), and we replace it with a leakage-aware protocol using chronological splits and held-out attack types rather than label reconstruction. Under this protocol, no model exceeds the constant "normal" predictor for attack classification (macro-F1 = 0.465), and the best detectors reach a mean AUROC of 0.64 on attack types unseen during training (0.35-0.93 depending on the type), leaving substantial headroom. Data and simulation files are released under CC BY 4.0 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23390541, and attack generators and benchmark code under MIT.
papers.authors: Amal Neji, Mohamed Fourati, Lamia Chaari Fourati

papers.title: Non-profiled Single-Trace ML-DSA Secret Key Recovery by Horizontal Distribution Analysis
papers.abstract: During the last decade, single-trace side-channel attacks on cryptographic implementations have largely focused on profiled methods, which typically assume that the attacker has a clone device and implementation knowledge to build a leakage model for the target before launching the attack. In this paper, we demonstrate that a much weaker adversary, without the ability to profile, can also mount powerful single-trace attacks. The presented method compares the observed sample distribution with the expected Hamming weight leakage distribution using a Gaussian mixture model as a distinguisher. The horizontal nature of the attack allows us to obtain multiple observations per execution by partitioning and stacking the trace. We show how to select optimal parameters for trace preprocessing and configure the measurement setup so that the noise floor is lowered, enabling the exploitation of weak leakage. We also prove that imperfect classifications can be efficiently corrected using information-set decoding algorithms. The new method is evaluated on an optimized implementation of ML-DSA-65 on ARM Cortex-M4 using the secret key unpacking procedure as an attack point. With an enumeration budget of $2^{70}$ operations in $\mathbb Z_q$, the full secret key is recovered from a single trace in 99% of attacks.
papers.authors: Linus Backlund, Elena Dubrova

papers.title: Revisiting AES Key Wrap: Forgery Bounds, Structural Observations, and Recommendations for the Revision of NIST SP 800-38F
papers.abstract: NIST is revising SP~800-38F, which specifies the AES Key Wrap modes KW and KWP. This paper is an updated and expanded version of our technical comments to NIST. We show that the forgery probabilities stated in SP~800-38F do not account for adaptive attacks, give the resulting forgery probabilities for KW, KWP, and TKW, and show that checking the expected plaintext length can raise the security level of KWP considerably. Revisiting Kelsey's long-message observation, we correct the collision conditions, show that a successful forgery leaks a plaintext prefix, derive an encryption-only distinguisher, and conclude that KW does not have beyond-birthday-bound security. We explain the role of the step counter, analyse the single-semiblock path of KWP and the trade-off between the number of passes and the length limit, and give recommendations for the revision, for implementations, and for future key-wrap designs.
papers.authors: John Preuß Mattsson

papers.title: A Kelsey–Kohno Attack Variant against SHA-2 Message Digests in HSS/LMS and XMSS
papers.abstract: We present a multi-target second-preimage attack on the message hashing of the stateful hash-based signature schemes HSS/LMS and XMSS with SHA-256 and with the truncated SHA-256/192. The attack builds on the herding technique of Kelsey and Kohno: the attacker takes the chaining states that follow the per-signature prefixes of many collected signatures and merges them, level by level through state collisions, into a single chaining state. From that state one search serves all collected signatures at once, which defeats the commitment to the key and to the one-time-signature leaf index at the start of the hash input that is meant to rule out multi-target attacks. The search can match the final digests, which is the better choice against SHA-256/192, or, after appending a Kelsey-Schneier expandable message, the internal chaining states of long signed messages, which is effective for full SHA-256. For SHA-256 with NIST's bound of $2^{64}$ signatures, which may be spread over any number of keys, the cost in compression-function calls falls from the nominal $2^{256}$ to about $2^{166}$ for messages of up to 4 GiB and to about $2^{156}$ in the formal limit of maximal message length, a loss of 100 bits. For SHA-256/192, digest matching costs about $2^{153}$ for $2^{64}$ signatures of any length, a loss of 39 bits. Because the attack pools signatures across keys, even the first signature of an individual key contributes to a potential overall exposure of an ecosystem. The attacks exploit the chaining state of SHA-256, which is narrower than twice the targeted security level; the SHAKE256 parameter sets are not affected.
papers.authors: Falko Strenzke

papers.title: Identity Amortization: Shared Resources and the Cost of Sybil Attacks
papers.abstract: Sybil defenses commonly price identities by requiring a resource for each one. When one resource can support several identities, an adversary can pay less per identity than the defense intends. We call this identity amortization: a strict reduction in the minimum cost of provisioning identities when resources may be shared, relative to provisioning each one independently. It is a second route to the gap that a Sybil attack exploits. When influence is assigned per identity, a defense calibrated to the nominal price can overestimate the cost of a Sybil threshold by up to the number of identities one resource supports. For any resource catalogue, we give exact tests for when identity amortization occurs, where it begins, and its largest error; a sharing cap below the onset removes it. Because the tests need only prices and capacities, they apply to any defense that admits identities against a shareable resource, telling designers whether the assumed per-identity cost is paid, how wrong it can be, and which intervention restores it most cheaply for honest participants. On published phone-verification prices, per-account estimates overstate provisioning cost 1.6 to 4.3 times; Tor's raised per-address relay limit cut modeled attack cost by 8 to 72%, depending on the address-to-relay price ratio.
papers.authors: Homayoun Maleki, Nekane Sainz, Jon Legarda, Igor Santos-Grueiro

papers.title: Autonomous Cyber Weapons as AI-Enabled Digital Harms: A Platform Accountability Framework
papers.abstract: Governments govern AI-generated online harms from commercial platforms (EU DSA, AI Act, UK Online Safety Act), yet the most severe class remains ungoverned: autonomous cyber weapons (ACWs) deployed by nation-states against civilian infrastructure. We address this gap with three contributions: a digital-harm taxonomy (six ACW modes $\times$ five harm categories); the Meaningful Human Control (MHC) Model, a governance-compliance function with a closed-form IHL threshold and a proved weight-sensitivity bound; and a platform accountability architecture with treaty language grounded in ARSIWA state-responsibility doctrine, not Rome Statute individual responsibility. Applied to eleven documented state-attributed operations and one hypothetical defensive AI system, every documented case falls in an accountability vacuum; the threshold is target-dependent, and against wholly civilian targets no system studied clears it, including the hypothetical. Three further incidents are correctly excluded on autonomy/attribution grounds, a discriminant-validity check. The weights and threshold parameters are illustrative, not fitted.
papers.authors: Mansi Ganga Nayak, Samarjeet Malik, Shaurya Pratap Singh, Vaibhav Sharma, Hritika Adhikary

papers.title: Curvature-Aware Clipping: Mitigating Bias in DPSGD via Approximate Second-Order Information
papers.abstract: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DPSGD) has become the de facto standard for training deep neural networks with rigorous privacy guarantees. However, the utility of DPSGD is constrained by gradient clipping bias and DP noise. While existing work has tried to address these issues, the geometric misalignment caused by clipping bias remains a critical challenge. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework, Curvature-Aware Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (CA-DPSGD), which leverages approximate second-order information to construct an optimal, curvature-aware clipping space. CA-DPSGD integrates a rectified estimator for the curvature matrix and is coupled with an anisotropic noise mechanism to ensure privacy guarantees. Extensive empirical experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art clipping methods.
papers.authors: Xincheng Xu, Thilina Ranbaduge, Thierry Rakotoarivelo, David Smith

papers.title: Label-Budgeted Attribute Inference from Protected Features in Edge-Cloud Split Multimodal LLMs
papers.abstract: Edge-cloud split inference runs the early layers of a multimodal large language model (MLLM) on a device and sends intermediate features to a server to complete the task. While keeping raw images local is often perceived as a privacy benefit, an honest-but-curious server can still infer sensitive attributes, such as age, gender, and race, from the received features. Existing protections intervene at the input, transmitted representation, or model's responses, but their native evaluations rely on final-response refusals or fixed-classifier failures, which underestimate an adaptive server's capabilities. To address this, we propose a label-budgeted attribute-inference framework that measures representation-level privacy through a recovery curve: the share of the unprotected leakage the server recovers as a function of its labeled-sample budget, from zero (a classifier trained on unprotected features) to a full labeled set. Our evaluation across two popular MLLMs reveals two critical findings. First, in unprotected pipelines, intermediate features leak all three attributes regardless of the split depth. Second, even when protection mechanisms are deployed across different stages, sensitive information remains recoverable under limited label budgets. For example, Safe-LLaVA removes biometric content from the model's responses, but from the features it transmits in split inference, 20 labeled samples per class recover 75-85% of the unprotected leakage. This work provides a label-budgeted measure of feature-level privacy for split MLLM inference and motivates defenses that act on the transmitted representation.
papers.authors: Junguang Yao, Peichun Hua, Hanxiu Zhang, Yue Zheng

papers.title: TRACE: Data-Free Text Reconstruction Attacks against Approximate Unlearning in LLMs
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) face growing demands for data removal driven by regulatory compliance, copyright concerns, and privacy protection, approximate unlearning has emerged as a practical alternative to expensive full retraining. In practice, pre- and post-unlearning model snapshots are often maintained for auditing and rollback, introducing a previously overlooked side channel. This paper demonstrates that approximate unlearning in LLM can leave residual traces within model snapshots, which may be recoverable and thus enable the privacy breaches that approximate unlearning is intended to prevent. Here, we propose TRACE, a framework that reconstructs unlearned training data given access to pre- and post-unlearning model snapshots, without any data-specific prior knowledge. To achieve this, TRACE identifies a compact set of candidate tokens from embedding-level parameter differences to constrain the search space, and assembles sequences via a contrastive scoring mechanism based on the perplexity gap between the two models. A two-stage exploration-then-completion strategy enables the recovery of multiple distinct samples. Extensive experiments on various datasets, including TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP, across multiple LLMs and six representative unlearning methods, demonstrate that TRACE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction. This paper exposes significant privacy risks in current LLM approximate unlearning deployments and highlights the need for defenses against parameter-difference leakage and appropriate management of model snapshot access.
papers.authors: Mengying Zhang, Derui Wang, Ibrahim Khalil, Bowen Liu, Xiaoyu Xia, Minhui Xue

papers.title: LINE-Break: Cryptanalysis and Reverse Engineering of Letter Sealing
papers.abstract: We present a security analysis of the messaging service known as LINE, a popular platform used daily by millions of users in East and Southeast Asia – most notably Japan, Taiwan, Thailand, and Indonesia. More specifically, we focus on its underlying custom end-to-end encryption (E2EE) protocol, known as Letter Sealing v2. Our findings show that Letter Sealing allows a TLS Machine-in-the- Middle attacker or malicious server to violate integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality of communications. The stateless design of the protocol allows message replay, reordering, and blocking attacks without the user being notified. The lack of origin authentication facilitates impersonation attacks, in which the authorship of mes- sages in one-to-one or group chats can be forged by malicious users colluding with the adversary. Lastly, stickers and URL previews present a notable leakage of plaintext, which leads to a violation of confidentiality. To verify the correctness of our findings, we mounted a Machine-in-the-Middle attack on an iOS device, yielding the device’s outgoing traffic and the corresponding server responses. Utilizing this setup, we experimentally verified our attacks against the authentic LINE application and an independent implementation. We discuss our findings in comparison to the state-of-the-art E2EE protocols, and conclude that Letter Sealing does not satisfy the requirements expected from a modern E2EE messaging protocol.
papers.authors: Diego F. Aranha, Adam Blatchley Hansen, Thomas Kingo T. Mogensen

papers.title: Isotaxis: Optimal Asynchronous Byzantine Consensus with Ordering Linearizability
papers.abstract: Despite ensuring both consistency and liveness, state machine replication (SMR) protocols remain vulnerable to adversaries that manipulate transaction order, causing, e.g., MEV attacks. To mitigate this, researchers have proposed new variants augmented with order-fairness. However, existing protocols that employ dependency graphs, such as Aequitas (Crypto 2020), Themis (CCS 2023), and SpeedyFair (NDSS 2024), often suffer from suboptimal performance, limited resilience, or weakened security guarantees. Pompē (OSDI 2020) introduced a novel ordering notion called ordering linearizability (OL) that may circumvent those drawbacks. However, its guarantee holds only under favorable network conditions, making the protocol vulnerable to order fairness violations during network delays and susceptible to performance degradation in the presence of Byzantine faults. Also, implementing SMR under OL remains an open challenge in asynchronous settings, as no known protocol achieves this without sacrificing liveness of SMR. In this paper, we present $\mathsf{Isotaxis}$, a state machine replication with ordering linearizability; moreover, our protocol has communication complexity $\mathcal{O}(n\ell+\lambda n^2)$, where $n$ is the number of processes, $\ell$ is the input (transaction) size, and $\lambda$ is the security parameter. This is optimal when $\ell\geq \lambda n$, while previous works have cubic communication. To the best of our knowledge, $\mathsf{Isotaxis}$ is the first protocol to achieve ordering linearizability in the asynchronous setting, especially one with optimal communication complexity and optimal Byzantine resilience. We implemented $\mathsf{Isotaxis}$ and conducted extensive experiments using up to 100 EC2 c6a.2xlarge instances. The experimental results show that our protocol robustly outperforms Pompē across all system scales, ranging from 4 to 100 nodes.
papers.authors: Vincent Gramoli, Zhenliang Lu, Qiang Tang, Pouriya Zarbafian, Xinrui Zhang

papers.title: Iterated-Logarithmic Additive Hardness for Bin Packing
papers.abstract: The question of obtaining a constant-additive approximation for bin packing was highlighted in the third of ten open problems in Williamson and Shmoys' The Design of Approximation Algorithms [SW11, Chapter~17, Problem~3]. We prove that there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$, no deterministic polynomial-time packing using at most $\mathrm{OPT}+c\log^*\mathrm{OPT}$ bins, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the minimum number of bins. In particular, no such algorithm has additive error $o(\log^*\mathrm{OPT})$. The best known upper bound, due to Hoberg and Rothvoss [HR17], is $\mathrm{OPT}+O(\log\mathrm{OPT})$, achieved by a randomized algorithm with expected polynomial running time. OpenAI [Ope26] previously showed that, unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$, no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm guarantees a packing using at most $\mathrm{OPT}+O(1)$ bins. We conjecture that the optimal additive approximation error for bin packing is $\Theta(\log \mathrm{OPT})$.
papers.authors: Zhao Song

papers.title: Extraction meets Distillation - cryptanalytic techniques to recover parameters from a Deep Neural Network
papers.abstract: We study fully connected neural-network reconstruction by combining cryptanalytic weight-direction extraction with learning from predicted labels. We adapt a ReLU extraction implementation to Leaky ReLU, compare sign-search methods, and estimate biases and output layers. We prove conditional bounds for direction recovery with approximate prefixes, preservation of local distance votes, prediction changes from aligned parameter errors, and sign selection with independent scoring data. We also specify exact row restoration and distinguish its guarantee from that of gradient masking. The experiments evaluate assisted extraction, with privileged access to gradients, hidden activations, and victim parameters, followed by label-based reconstruction. Across eight search seeds on the largest synthetic architecture, Leaky ReLU recovers 51--57 neurons in the deepest hidden layer, while ReLU recovers none. This advantage does not hold uniformly across architectures and layers. Removing victim-weight access from the sign walk gives less accurate signs, despite high final prediction agreement. Across 40 seeded runs on the two smallest synthetic victims, agreement on 5,000 inputs excluded from fitting and selection ranges from $0.9890$ to $0.9992$. On two CIFAR-10 victims, the reconstructed models achieve $56.40\%$ and $58.29\%$ agreement and exceed the distillation baseline on three functional metrics. We report label requests separately from privileged access and explain why prediction agreement does not identify network parameters.
papers.authors: Biprarshi Biswas, Arya Anshuman Ojha, Yubaraj Das, Devansh Khosla, Kamran Rais, Saankhya Samanta, Subhamoy Maitra, Pantelimon Stanica

papers.title: Faster Polynomial Factorization over Finite Fields via Batched Modular Composition
papers.abstract: In the algebraic model, where one counts operations in $\mathbb{F}_q$ uniformly in the characteristic, the best published algorithm for factoring a polynomial of degree $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, due to Kaltofen and Shoup with the rectangular products of Huang and Pan, uses $n^{1.80535+o(1)}\log q$ operations, and its bottleneck is the modular compositions of the giant steps. A new algorithm is presented for these compositions. Like the algorithm of Neiger, Salvy, Schost and Villard, the new method is based on the relation matrices of the argument. Since all compositions at one level of the giant steps share one argument, the relation matrices and a table of remainders are computed only once, and the remaining work consists of rectangular matrix products. For the two-matrix evaluation, we prove that a random change of basis puts every Frobenius image in good position. This reduces the cost of factorization in this model $$\text{from}\quad n^{1.80535+o(1)}\log q\quad\text{to}\quad n^{1.5532+o(1)}\log q,$$ and to $n^{3/2+o(1)}\log q$ if $\omega=2$; with the compositions of Neiger, Salvy, Schost and Villard performed one at a time, the exponent would be $1.7147$. In the bit model, and algebraically in small characteristic, Kedlaya and Umans obtained the exponent $3/2$. For a single composition with an arbitrary argument modulo a separable polynomial, the content of one short relation separates large value fibers, which gives a Las Vegas algorithm for every input at the exponent $(\omega+3)/4<1.3429$, previously known only for generic inputs, and a fourth evaluation level, with truncated powers obtained by transposition, lowers it to $1.3309$. As applications, we obtain faster algorithms for normal bases, minimal polynomials and irreducibility testing, and, for large $q$, factorization in $O(n^{1.5983})+n^{1+o(1)}\log q$ operations.
papers.authors: Zhenyu Xiong, Mingsheng Wang

papers.title: The Covering Radius of $\operatorname{RM}(2,8)$ is Between $88$ and $91$
papers.abstract: Let $\operatorname{RM}(r,n)$ be the $r$th order Reed--Muller code of length $2^n$, and let $\rho(r,n)$ denote its covering radius. The values $\rho(2,6)=18$ and $\rho(2,7)=40$ are known, whereas the exact value of $\rho(2,8)$ remains open. Starting from the current state of the art bound $88\leq\rho(2,8)\leq96$, we give a computer-assisted reduction of the upper bound $\rho(2,8)\leq91$. We first show that every even-weight Boolean function on eight variables is within distance $90$ of a quadratic function. Changing one value then gives the bound $91$ for odd-weight functions. Our main lemma addresses rank-four seven-variable quintics: when their second-order distance is $36$ and their maximum quadratic-shift first-order distance is $56$, they have at least $60$ minimizing quadratic cosets and at most $12$ cosets of cost $56$. The complete proof covers all $68443$ quartic classes. For every rank-four quintic, the distance-$56$ cosets are enumerated outright, and the $5199$ words are examined individually. Profile counts, hyperplane contractions, and support moments then give the even-weight bound. We describe the calculations and enumerations, together with the classification upon which the proof depends. Instructions to verify the computer search portion may be found at $\texttt{https://github.com/EvelynSabo/RM28}$.
papers.authors: Xiang-dong Hou, Evelyn Sabo, Freeman Slaughter

papers.title: Bounds on polynomial approximations of the discrete logarithm function
papers.abstract: We revisit a classical result of Coppersmith and Shparlinski [CS00] showing bounds on how well polynomials can approximate the discrete log function. They showed that for any univariate polynomial $f(X) \in \mathbb{F}_p[X]$ with $\deg(f) \leq D$, we have: $$ |\{ x \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times \mid f(x) = \mathsf{dlog}(x) \}| \leq \sqrt{2 D p}.$$ We show two improvements: (1) For all $D$, we improve the upper bound above to $(1+o(1)) \cdot \sqrt{Dp}$. In particular, we give nontrivial upper bounds on the approximation even for $D > p/2$. This new upper bound is the Johnson bound from the theory of list-decoding of error-correcting codes, and in fact our proof uses a connection to that problem, as well as other combinatorial ideas. (2) For $D = 1$, where both the above bounds are $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{p})$, we give an asymptotically improved upper bound of $\mathcal{O}(p^{2/5})$. This is based on the sum-product phenomenon of additive combinatorics. We also improve the [CS00] bounds on the number of points of the form $(x, \mathsf{dlog}(x)) \in \mathbb{F}_p^2$ that any bivariate polynomial $Q(X,Y) \in \mathbb{F}_p[X,Y]$ with $\deg(Q) \leq D$ can vanish on, with our new bounds approaching the analogue of the Johnson bound for this problem.
papers.authors: Swastik Kopparty, Rishabh Kothary, Ashutosh Shankar

papers.title: STROKE: Simple Sparse Structural Occlusions for Black-Box Adversarial Attacks
papers.abstract: We introduce STROKE, a query-efficient score-based black-box adversarial attack that constructs perturbations from simple oriented rectangular occlusions. STROKE optimizes these perturbations through a lightweight greedy add-and-refine procedure. Across diverse image classifiers, STROKE achieves high attack success with low query counts at nominal 1--2\% area settings, showing favorable performance relative to existing patch-based attacks in several configurations. Matched comparisons further demonstrate substantial reductions in wall-clock attack time, while ablation studies examine the key design choices and effectiveness across structural primitives. These findings suggest that simple structural occlusions offer an effective and computationally efficient search space for black-box adversarial attacks.
papers.authors: Ankit Gupta, Akshat Pandya, Paul Lin, Christoph Adami, Emily Dolson

papers.title: Developing Security Metrics for Automated Compliance Checking
papers.abstract: To automatically check for compliance with security-related standards, prose requirements must be translated to technical properties to make them measurable. A multitude of metrics have been proposed in past literature, but they are lacking a systematic methodology for their elicitation. Without such a methodology, metrics remain inconsistent in their data models and abstraction levels, they exhibit considerable overlaps and are difficult to combine to comprehensively cover a standard's requirement.
