In this paper, we develop a data model for security metrics based on a systematization of compliance requirements, and we propose a methodology for their elicitation. The method is based on an ontology that enables a systematic development of metrics with a comparable degree of abstraction. We also present our initial work on an open-source effort that demonstrates that our approach also supports a collaborative development of metrics.
papers.authors: Immanuel Kunz, Nico Haas, Angelika Schneider, Christian Banse

papers.title: Data-Efficient Backdoor Attacks on Code Models via Trigger-Neutralized Counterfactual Scoring
papers.abstract: Pre-trained code models are exposed to backdoor poisoning, in which crafted training samples make the model misbehave on a trigger. A capable attacker minimizes the number of such samples, since each adds cost and exposure and a lower poisoning rate leaves a smaller footprint for defenses. Which samples to poison therefore matters, but existing data-efficient selection methods target image classification, offer no scoring mechanism for autoregressive generation, and have not been studied on code. We propose Trigger-Neutralized Counterfactual Scoring (TNCS), which isolates a trigger's contribution to the target behavior by comparing the scoring model's output on a triggered input with its output on a trigger-neutralized counterfactual, covering classification and generation alike. TNCS attains higher attack success rates than the baselines at very low poisoning ratios, across three CodeXGLUE tasks and five trigger families, without degrading clean-task performance, and its margin grows as the ratio decreases. It is the only method effective on every trigger family, and its selected poison set transfers to mismatched victims.
papers.authors: Yu-Yu Lee, Ming-Feng Tsai, Tomohiro Morikawa, Chun-I Fan

papers.title: Democratic Accountability for Autonomous Systems: A Legislative Notification Framework and Comparative Institutional Design
papers.abstract: No domestic legislature has ever reviewed a state's decision to authorise an autonomous cyber weapon before it acted. Closing the international attribution gap is necessary but not sufficient for democratic accountability. We formalise the Tripartite Attribution Framework's three attribution levels and add a fourth, non-legal Democratic Accountability level ($A_{dem}$): a 72-hour legislative notification requirement. Scoring six democratic oversight bodies against five adoptability dimensions yields a counter-intuitive result: the statutes granting these bodies privileged access to classified material are often the same statutes withholding particular ongoing operations from them, so at most one could lawfully receive such a notification today, and the carve-out Level 4 needs is required in nearly every jurisdiction rather than only the least-equipped. Retrospective analysis of Stuxnet, NotPetya, and Volt Typhoon shows one pattern: legal attribution resolvable, domestic democratic review absent.
papers.authors: Samarjeet Malik, Mansi Ganga Nayak, Mugdha Raje Ashiya, Hritika Adhikary, Vaibhav Sharma

papers.title: Tracing Money Laundering Across DeFi, Bridges, and Mixers on Ethereum
papers.abstract: Illicit actors exploit Ethereum's deep liquidity and diverse on-chain services to launder criminal proceeds by combining decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols, cross-chain bridges, and mixers in multi-stage processes. Existing anti-money laundering tracing methods fail to disentangle the underlying asset-flow paths in complex transactions, potentially misdirecting subsequent tracing; cannot identify cross-chain intent without pre-collected bridge information; and treat mixers as generic exit services, overlooking post-mixer laundering flows. We present FPTracer, a framework for tracing illicit assets across Ethereum services. First, we propose a method based on the Context-Aware Transfer Tree (CATT) to recover intra-transaction asset-flow paths, which guide accurate tracing and service analysis. Second, we extract discriminative features from asset-flow and execution-evidence perspectives and train a classifier to identify transactions with cross-chain intent. Third, we leverage evidence from the upstream laundering network to analyze potential post-mixer laundering activities. Evaluation on 20 real-world laundering cases demonstrates FPTracer's effectiveness. It achieves the highest recall for both known laundering addresses (98.6%) and destinations (94.2%). It identifies all known uses of bridges in these cases and uncovers 30 previously unreported ones. Among 18 cases with identified Tornado Cash usage, FPTracer can identify potential withdrawal-side activities, which are corroborated by public reports where available.
papers.authors: Huan Xing, Gaohe Jin, Bang Fu, Yue Li, Baoning Niu, Xing Fan

papers.title: The 3DS Oracle: BIN Attack via the Network
papers.abstract: EMV 3-D Secure (3DS) requires a client-visible continuation boundary in browser-mediated flows; in some deployments, that boundary exposes a pre-authorization classification channel. This paper studies 3DS as a protocol, integration surface, and governance problem, combining standards analysis, architectural reconstruction, formal modeling, a documentation audit, disclosure history, and a bounded live evaluation. We show that client-visible integrations can reflect routing and authentication state before financial authorization, allowing 3DS to function as a profiling and screening channel for issuer controls and cardholder/account state rather than only as a defense. In the tested browser-channel Braintree/Cardinal path, the first client-visible result separated researcher-owned anchor cards from bounded adjacent same-range comparison PANs in six of seven distinct ACS/card-range cohorts; separate public evidence, including openly accessible attacker tooling, rotating-proxy support, and illicit paid 3DS card-testing services, shows that comparable signals are already operationalized in the wild. Our live study was deliberately bounded for ethical reasons, so the empirical ceiling reported here reflects researcher restraint rather than an attacker-side scalability limit, although we do not claim network-wide prevalence or candidate issuance. The deeper issue is systemic: decoupled pre-authorization authentication, weak requestor-boundary assumptions, identifier-linked routing invariants, and fragmented accountability let the exposure persist even when individual actors appear locally conformant. Meaningful remediation therefore requires consortium-level reform, including stricter minimization of client-visible pre-authorization responses, more uniform continuation behavior, and stronger client authenticity and session binding.
papers.authors: Wasif Faisal, Suprava Saha Dibya

papers.title: Depth-Dependent Safety Geometry in Vision-Language Models: Layer-Wise Localization and Bidirectional Refusal Control
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are widely deployed, yet the internal mechanisms behind their safety behavior remain poorly understood. We present a lightweight inference-time framework for localizing and manipulating safety-sensitive representations in frozen VLMs, without retraining or modifying parameters. On Qwen3-VL-4B, layer-wise activation divergence analysis reveals non-uniform safety geometry across depth. Causal interventions show that early vision layers support strong bidirectional refusal control through activation steering along a learned safety direction, with unsafe rejection spanning 6%-96%, whereas later layers respond more to activation magnitude scaling and exhibit a substantial safety-selectivity trade-off. Deeper layers remain well separated along the safety direction yet are largely insensitive to steering, distinguishing representational separability from causal controllability. InternVL2.5-4B shows qualitatively similar depth-dependent activation geometry despite differences in layer location and magnitude. Our results expose a white-box, representation-level refusal-bypass attack surface in VLM vision encoders and motivate inference-time stabilization of safety-sensitive representations.
papers.authors: Muhammad Zeeshan Karamat, Syed Talal Hassan, Christiana Chamon Garcia

papers.title: Detecting Insecure Compositions of Clean Agent Skills via Capability-Flow Graph Analysis
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly extend their capabilities by invoking third-party skills, where each skill encapsulates instructions, scripts, and resources for agents to execute on demand. This paper reveals that deploying many benign skills together introduces compositional security risks: multiple individually clean skills can compose into safety-violation chains, because the agent passes an upstream skill's output to a downstream skill's input across invocations. The risk arises not from any single skill, but from the agent's runtime orchestration, and thus cannot be captured by existing malicious skill detection methods. To this end, we develop KnotScryer to detect insecure skill compositions by treating skills as typed capability flows. In particular, we abstract each skill into a capability summary, and construct the Skill Capability-Flow Graph (SCFG), where edges denote cross-skill information flow. Moreover, we design a search policy that tracks protected or untrusted data along handoff edges to locate paths reaching insecure operations. Finally, a two-layer verification method replays the insecure information flow for reachability analysis and applies a task-anchored LLM chain audit to confirm the semantic plausibility of the identified violation chains. We deploy KnotScryer to analyze 13,598 clean skills from ClawHub, and validate the detected chains across three agent frameworks and three LLMs. KnotScryer identifies 612 insecure compositions, which are consistently exploited across agent frameworks. Meanwhile, under GLM-5.1, it outperforms tag-match and graph-only baselines by improving the exploitation rate from 16.5%-18.2% to 85.6%, while reducing the search space by 85.3%. Furthermore, 13.7% of the detected chains consist entirely of skills labeled safe by a single-skill scanner, showing that KnotScryer effectively identifies insecure compositions that per-skill auditing cannot.
papers.authors: Yihao Li, Chuanpu Fu, Yizhou Zhao, Miao Chen, Qi Li, Ke Xu

papers.title: Concept Acupuncturist: An Efficient and Precise Concept Erasure Method for Diffusion Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based image generation models produce high-quality images but may generate harmful or policy-violating content, motivating machine unlearning (MU) to selectively remove target concepts while preserving general capabilities. However, existing MU approaches often struggle with the distributed and entangled nature of concept representations, leading to inefficient optimization and imprecise edits when applied through large-scale fine-tuning over full diffusion trajectories. To bridge this gap, we propose Concept Acupuncturist (ConceptACP), a novel MU framework that integrates interpretability-guided analysis with inference-free fine-tuning for efficient and precise concept removal. By establishing mappings between semantic concepts and cross-attention blocks in the U-Net denoiser and localizing the most concept-relevant block for targeted optimization, ConceptACP avoids full diffusion trajectory optimization, thereby improving fine-tuning efficiency. To mitigate concept entanglement, we propose a feature-level correction mechanism based on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), where SAE-derived sparse, semantically meaningful feature activations are manipulated to construct targeted correction signals, which are then projected back to the output space of the corresponding block and used as supervision for precise concept removal. Consequently, ConceptACP eliminates the need for external inference-time modules while achieving efficient and fine-grained unlearning. Instantiated on SDXL-Turbo, ConceptACP improves the forgetting success rate by 36.34 percentage points in the standard one-step generation setting on average over the best-performing baseline, while preserving image quality and prompt fidelity, and generalizes effectively across other Stable Diffusion backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/Eran-Xia/ConceptACP.
papers.authors: Yiran Xiahou, Siliang Qin, Kai Chen, Shengzhi Zhang, Renyang Liu

papers.title: Incomparable Minima in Agent Tool Authorization
papers.abstract: An agent that needs a tool needs authority to call it, and every proposal for governing that authority has to answer one question: of two grants that both let the agent finish a task, which one is smaller? Over-privilege benchmarks score agents against this answer, and permission solvers compute it. We check the question against the authorisation tables that Microsoft and Google publish, covering 22,305 Microsoft Graph endpoint bindings and 23,852 Google API methods, on tasks generated from each table's own resource structure. For 29.8-33.3% of Graph tasks and 3.2% of Google resource tasks the question has no answer, because the minimal sufficient grants form an antichain, a set of grants none of which authorises a subset of what another does. In its two main authorisation modes, Microsoft's shipped privilegeLevel rates 67.4-74.4% of these incomparable pairs equal. Google ships no such scale, so on Google we apply a reconstruction of the FORTIS privilege ladder, which rates 90.7-98.7% equal. Applying the same reconstruction to Graph attributes much of that difference to the scale rather than the corpus: its form based on the HTTP verb alone rates 92.0% of Google pairs and 89.0-92.0% of Graph pairs equal. Four risk measures (operations, writes, services reached, administrative surface) order 28.7% of incomparable Google pairs and 15.7-23.4% of Graph pairs in opposite directions, so for those pairs the ranking has no measure-independent answer. Offered pools of minimal and larger grants, 6 frontier models pick a minimal grant on 99.0% of 1,708 decisions, a grant smallest under all four measures on 66.7%, and on 22.1% a grant that another option matches or beats on every measure. We propose that benchmarks report which minimal grant an agent chose and that deployments show the alternatives to whoever approves the grant.
papers.authors: Xin Xu

papers.title: Fooling LLM Safety Guards into Judging the Wrong Text
papers.abstract: Safety guards check content before an LLM application acts on it, and most paste that content into a plain-text prompt. Content that imitates the prompt can append a second task, and the guard answers that one instead. We call this target rebinding. Our explanation is that the guard grades the last complete task in its input, here a harmless decoy, so the harmful request goes through unchanged. In a pre-registered test, an appended forged query and decoy clear all 75 held-out AdvBench requests that Shieldstral-1.0-3B flags. The guard is not persuaded: a directive to ignore the text above clears none of them, and in a follow-up run a harmful decoy stops the attack. On our GuardRebind benchmark, each of five guards has an attack family, chosen per guard, that clears at least 93% of its flagged items. Rebinding explains this best on Shieldstral and gpt-oss-safeguard; on ShieldGemma and Llama Guard 3, generic evasion and trailing text respectively do part of the work, and Qwen3Guard falls mainly to a forgery of its whole task. Training the guard to score content no lower than its most harmful part cuts attack success from 75% to 0.8-1.6% on attack families, decoys and forged queries held out of training. All of these attacks append the forged structure after the request, and we added the held-out-decoy evaluation after a first round of test runs. Clean AUROC falls by at most 0.01, but our test of non-inferiority is inconclusive. A score-guided search still beats this trained guard on 47 of 50 items, usually by placing forged structure before the request. On about half of the items where the search wins, the same search also finds benign text, with no forged structure, that clears the guard.
papers.authors: Utkarsh Kanwat

papers.title: Beyond Copying: Lifelong Smart Contract Security Task Construction via Protocol Mutation
papers.abstract: AI agents can inspect code and run tests to support smart contract security. SlowMist reports about $38.6 billion in losses across the broader blockchain ecosystem. Existing evaluations can reward memorized or copied answers, including attack code recovered from public blockchain transactions. Reconstructing contracts and validating tasks also require costly manual effort. To address these issues, we propose CONSTRAINTDIAL, a framework for lifelong construction of smart contract security tasks via protocol mutation. It automates local contract reconstruction and uses attack execution to select changes to the required calls or inputs. Execution checks guide revisions that make the original attack fail while preserving exploitability, the security objective, and normal functionality. New incidents and audit findings enter the same procedure. With CONSTRAINTDIAL, we construct 3,045 task inputs from 203 public cases, covering detect, exploit, and patch. Compared with reconstruction alone, protocol mutation reduces success with supplied public answers by 10.9 percentage points on average across detect, exploit, and patch. The fraction of tasks solved by copying online answers falls by 9.3 points.
papers.authors: Zifan Peng, Peng Huang, Jingyi Zheng, Yingjie Xue, Xuechao Wang, Xinlei He, Xia Hu, Dongrui Liu

papers.title: DeepAVR: Deep Analysis via Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Vulnerability Repair
papers.abstract: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has emerged as a critical defense against software security flaws, aiming to triage and fix bugs autonomously. Early LLM-based approaches focused on patch generation under the assumption of perfect fault localization, while recent end-to-end methods attempt to repair vulnerabilities directly from sanitizer logs. However, these methods often fail when the root cause is deeply hidden--either physically distant from the crash site or logically masked by interdependent errors--making the initial report insufficient. We propose DeepAVR, a multi-agent framework for end-to-end AVR that performs deep analysis by transforming intermediate repair outcomes into structured diagnostic feedback. DeepAVR decomposes repair into specialized roles--Fault Localization, Patch Generation, Compile Validation, Security Validation, Functionality Validation, and Patch Review--and routes feedback across these roles to iteratively refine both localization and patch hypotheses. In particular, DeepAVR introduces patch-conditioned re-localization, which treats execution results from intermediate patches as diagnostic signals to uncover hidden root causes, and a root-cause-oriented patch review stage that detects symptom-level fixes and incomplete repairs beyond execution-based validation. Evaluation on the real-world C/C++ vulnerability repair dataset VulnLoc shows that DeepAVR significantly outperforms prior methods, generating correct patches for 92.3% of vulnerabilities. Furthermore, results on SAN2VULN demonstrate strong generalization, with DeepAVR effectively repairing vulnerabilities unseen during training.
papers.authors: Woorim Han, Hyunjun Kim, Brian Junekyu Lee, Kyeongmin Kim, Younghan Lee, Hyungon Moon, Yunheung Paek

papers.title: Automated Post-Exploitation Attack Chain Exploration Based on a Phase-guided Hybrid Planning-Monte Carlo Tree Search Algorithm
papers.abstract: Advanced attackers in post-exploitation scenarios increasingly craft attack chains that combine benign operations, configuration errors, and vulnerability exploitation to achieve objectives like privilege escalation. While such chains pose significant threats, manually discovering them in complex modern host environments is prohibitively labor-intensive. Automating this discovery is therefore essential for proactive defense, yet existing methods still suffer from inefficiency and lack diversity when exploring these attack chains. To address these limitations, we present APEX, an Automated Post-EXploitation attack chain exploration system. This system transforms attack chain discovery into a planning problem and solves it with a novel phase-guided hybrid Planning-Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm. By organizing attack actions into semantic phases and integrating symbolic planning with MCTS, APEX enables efficient exploration of the state space while generating multiple diverse chains. Evaluations on a benchmark comprising 5 virtual machines, 30 synthetic problems and 291 cloud instances demonstrate that APEX successfully discovers both known and previously unreported attack chains--including 9 novel privilege escalation vectors--providing actionable intelligence for hardening complex production environments.
papers.authors: Jie Ying, Mengce Zheng, Ruoxi Chen, Wenrui Cheng, Tiantian Zhu, Zhongjie Zhu

papers.title: Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence
papers.abstract: Pipelines that combine large language models (LLMs) with static analysis let the model consume the analyser's output as evidence, but whether the model distinguishes true from false evidence, and whether its scrutiny depends on what the evidence claims, has not been measured. We built an intraprocedural analyser for C/C++ that produces proof obligations and audited vulnerable and patched functions from PrimeVul under six evidence conditions that differ only in the notes, including fabricated assurances that a missing check exists and fabricated alarms that an added check is missing. The study covers 916 pairs in four disjoint sets, eleven model configurations from four vendors and 16,572 audits; no model is trained or fine-tuned. True evidence barely improved accuracy (+0.02). False evidence acted asymmetrically: relative to true notes about the same operations, false assurances lowered the detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points, whereas false alarms never significantly lowered accuracy and were disputed far more often. An internally registered replication on seven new models confirmed that false assurances move verdicts towards their claim more than false alarms do (mean asymmetry +0.16, 95% CI +0.10 to +0.24). Instructions in the audit prompt did not reliably reduce deference; the best one failed to replicate. Verifying each claim in a separate call and showing the refuted claims raised accuracy under false assurances by 12 points in a pre-specified test (p=0.002) without loss under true evidence; for a second model the gain was smaller and not significant. Pipelines should therefore verify a tool's guarantees before the model relies on them, and studies should measure deference in a direction-aware way.
papers.authors: ZhiHong Liu, Shuyao Gao

papers.title: WADE: An LSTM-Based Anomaly Detection Engine for WebAssembly Applications
papers.abstract: WebAssembly (Wasm) enables near-native performance for web applications through a portable and sandboxed execution model. However, its limited runtime protection mechanisms (e.g., the lack of stack canaries and address space layout randomization (ASLR)) leave Wasm applications vulnerable to traditional attacks. We present WADE (WebAssembly Anomaly Detection Engine), a system that detects anomalous runtime behaviors in browser-executed WebAssembly applications. WADE monitors function-level execution traces collected under benign conditions and trains a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to learn the normal execution behavior of each application. At runtime, the model flags deviations from these learned patterns as potential attacks. Unlike signature-based approaches, WADE builds application-specific behavioral models, enabling detection of both known and previously unseen attacks without per-vulnerability signatures. We evaluate WADE on a dataset of 67 WebAssembly applications spanning ten vulnerability classes, achieving zero false negatives and a 0.42% false positive rate.
papers.authors: Ilaria Campestrini, Stefano Zanero, Engin Kirda

papers.title: Not an Accident: Exploiting Safety Filter Inadequacy in Humanoid Robots
papers.abstract: As humanoid robots move from research laboratories toward deployment in human-centered environments such as homes, hospitals, and warehouses, safe operation around nearby people and objects becomes a fundamental requirement. Safety filters have emerged as a promising technique to address this challenge by providing mathematical guarantees that generated control actions do not result in collisions. This paper shows that these guarantees hold only when the safety parameters are configured correctly. However, correct parameter configurations are task- and environment-specific, and no general method exists to determine them across diverse deployments. As a result, safety filters shipped with humanoid robots can fail after deployment in specific scenarios. We show that attackers can exploit these failures through only normal user interactions without any additional privileges or capabilities. To demonstrate this risk, we present goal insertion attacks and develop SIREN, an automated tool that identifies vulnerable inserting goals for a given task and environment. Experimental results show that SIREN identifies attacks in all vulnerable scenarios in the SPARK dataset. Compared with a baseline approach, SIREN discovers three times as many attacks. We also show that SIREN is able to generate attacks against a real humanoid and cause it to collide while executing tasks. These results demonstrate that current safety filters introduce exploitable vulnerabilities that can cause safety violations, which reveals that existing safety mechanisms can themselves become a source of safety risk for humanoid robots.
papers.authors: Tiffany Bao, Shangtao Li, Yifan Sun, Mengwen He, Bowei Li, Alden Wang, Changliu Liu, Ruoyu Wang, David Brumley

papers.title: Ulysses: A Security Harness For Synthesizing Verifiable Web Exploits
papers.abstract: How can an AI agent automatically discover security vulnerabilities in any software repository? Existing approaches use LLMs to generate software vulnerability exploits. However, it is challenging for an LLM to reliably verify its own generated exploits. In this paper, we propose Ulysses, a multi-agent security harness to synthesize verifiable vulnerability exploits for web applications. Ulysses converts candidate vulnerability findings into verified Proofs of Exploitability by iteratively exploring exploit hypotheses and establishing success in independently observed execution effects. We evaluated Ulysses on WebExploitGym, a curated benchmark of exploitable instances from 25 real-world web applications that span 5 languages and 7 frameworks. Ulysses produces verified proofs for 10 of 25 real-world advisories. It also discovered 4 new proofs of exploitability that have never been previously reported.
papers.authors: Aditya Oke, André Vicente Duarte, Rui Melo, Shubham Gandhi, Nachiket Kotalwar, Charmi Khandor, Danqing Wang, Carolyn Rosé, Lei Li

papers.title: On Task, Off Track: Benchmarking LLM and Agent Robustness to Near-Target Prompt Injection
papers.abstract: Prompt injection benchmarks assess whether large language models (LLMs) and agents resist malicious instructions embedded in external content. However, a system could perform well by rejecting attacks that obviously abandon the user's request, while still accepting changes that retain most of a legitimate answer but make it incorrect or harmful. Testing more instructions for unrelated outcomes would not necessarily reveal this weakness. We call attacks seeking responses designed to resemble legitimate answers while introducing incorrect or harmful changes near-target prompt injection. We introduce NTBench, the Near-Target Benchmark, which builds on legitimate tasks from existing datasets. For each task, a legitimate reference outcome guides the generation of target--instruction pairs, with separate tracks targeting incorrect and harmful outcomes in responses or agent tool invocations. Harmful targets can also accompany otherwise correct task completion. We combine LLM-based checks with human validation of the intended deviations, then assess whether injected instructions induce them using response judgments or tool-call checks, excluding deviations already observed without injection. We evaluate seven LLMs on ten datasets for language tasks and two agent benchmarks. Under a common budget of three attack executions per sample, both tracks achieve higher overall attack success rates than the fixed-target baseline for every evaluated model in each setting. On language tasks, the increases range from 9.3 to 35.8 percentage points for incorrect targets and 1.7 to 17.3 percentage points for harmful targets. These results show that resistance to the tested fixed-target attacks does not imply resistance to related incorrect or harmful outcomes, and that reference-guided targets broaden the failures revealed by robustness evaluation.
papers.authors: Yuyang Gong, Zihao Wang, Jiawei Liu, XiaoFeng Wang

papers.title: SEMPRE: Semantic-Aware Protocol Reverse Engineering via Consistency-Driven Joint Optimization
papers.abstract: Protocol reverse engineering (PRE) is essential for understanding undocumented or proprietary communication formats, enabling security-critical tasks such as vulnerability discovery, malware C2 analysis, and IDS signature generation. However, existing PRE techniques rely on brittle hand-written rules, under-model contextual dependencies among neighboring fields, and often fail on messages with nested sub-protocols. We present SEMPRE, a fully automated PRE framework that replaces ad-hoc heuristics with recursive LLM reasoning grounded in fine-grained dynamic program analysis. SEMPRE uses taint-flow and loop traces to guide an LLM-driven tree-of-thought search that slices messages into fields while detecting nested sub-payloads, producing a hierarchical layout. It then infers each field's type and role and iteratively refines boundaries by freezing high-confidence segments and re-running detection under semantic constraints, yielding an EM-style procedure that monotonically improves structure and semantics until convergence. Evaluated on a broad corpus of mainstream protocols against six state-of-the-art (vs. <0.4 for all baselines) and 0.72 for semantic inference (vs. 0.13 for BinPRE). Ablations confirm the contribution of each component, and a case study on a prolific real-world botnet demonstrates practical utility.
papers.authors: Yihua Xu, Weijie Huang, Xiaofeng Wang, Hang Zhang, Binghui Wang, Yue Duan

papers.title: Omni-UBench: Benchmarking Omni-Modal LLM-based Guardrails Across Safety, Utility, and Reliability
papers.abstract: Advances in Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs) have enabled increasingly seamless human-AI interaction, but their unified processing of heterogeneous modalities also expands the attack surface, allowing adversaries to exploit richer input compositions to circumvent safety alignment. To counter such risks, omni-modal guardrails have been proposed to detect and filter unsafe queries across arbitrary modalities. However, their capabilities and limitations remain insufficiently understood due to the absence of a comprehensive evaluation benchmark. In this paper, we present Omni-UBench, the first comprehensive framework for omni-modal safety assessment, evaluating guardrail models along three critical dimensions, i.e., safety, utility, and reliability. Omni-UBench curates over 183k samples drawn from 35+ heterogeneous sources spanning text, image, audio, video, and their cross-modal combinations, annotated with safety labels under a unified risk taxonomy. Benchmarking under Omni-UBench on 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails yields several key findings, including: (1) modern OLLMs exhibit strong content moderation potential even without guardrail-specific tuning; (2) existing guardrails still struggle to identify cross-modal queries that conceal harmful intent or involve sophisticated jailbreaks; (3) they further exhibit substantial safety hallucination and over-sensitivity to textual patterns, revealing a deficient understanding of cross-modal safety semantics. Our findings provide valuable insights for developing more trustworthy omni-modal guardrails in future research.
papers.authors: Junhao Wang, Yidou Chen, Li Lu, Hongwei Yao, Xiaodan Li, Mengjie Wu, Yuefeng Chen, Zhan Qin, Kui Ren

papers.title: EVSEFuzz : A Tool for Automated Testing of Protocol Implementations
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption and development of electric vehicle (EV) networks has required the expansive deployment of EV charging infrastructure (EVCI) which relies on communication protocols such as the open charge point protocol (OCPP) to coordinate data transfer between charging network operators and the EV supply equipment. In this paper, we present EVSEFuzz, a tool for automatically building fuzzers to test the security of protocol implementations. To achieve this we make a novel use of Python datatype validation packages and tools to ``understand'' datatypes and message structures and generate both compliant and non-compliant messages. To date, EVSEFuzz has been tested successfully with several open and closed-source implementations and has found several vulnerabilities leading to the publication of two CVEs.
papers.authors: Soham Gumaste, Michael Khan, Roland Varriale, Rigel Gjomemo

papers.title: Faster and Smaller Anonymous Credentials from Standardized Signatures
papers.abstract: We present GordieHowe, a system comprising a language, a certifying compiler, and a zero-knowledge proof protocol. GordieHowe is especially suitable for building anonymous credentials on top of standardized signature schemes like ECDSA, RSA, and ML-DSA. GordieHowe is the first system to achieve the following three properties simultaneously: provable security against quantum attackers, efficiency for statements spanning multiple fields—including proving and verifying in parallel—and automatic batching of structured computations. GordieHowe is high-assurance by design. The language is designed to enable static checking of bounds safety, preventing integer overflows. Its compiler emits a Lean certificate that its optimization decisions are semantics-preserving for the input program. The proof system's security theorems are machine-checked in Lean. GordieHowe is faster and has smaller proofs than comparable prior work. It proves, in parallel on four cores, an ECDSA-signed mobile driving license presentation in 64.8 ms with a 276 KiB proof, 10.1× faster and 22% smaller than Google's Longfellow. With at least 101 bits of knowledge soundness in the random oracle model, GordieHowe proves knowledge of a 1 KiB SHA3-256 preimage in 5.0 ms with a 60 KiB proof, and of an RSA-2048 signature on a private 2 KiB message in 25.9 ms with a 210 KiB proof. With at least 116 bits against quantum adversaries, GordieHowe proves knowledge of an ML-DSA-44 signature on a private message in 87.3 ms with a 549 KiB proof, 70.2× faster and 29% smaller than an optimized Longfellow circuit. In building GordieHowe we make a number of contributions of independent interest. We define a new notion of an interactive oracle proof (IOP) whose messages are partially ordered, which we call a series-parallel IOP. We extend the BCS transformation to series-parallel IOPs, and give knowledge soundness and ZK proofs in the QROM. We also show our BCS extension satisfies a form of simulation extractability in the QROM; we believe this is the first simulation extractability result of any kind for BCS in the QROM.
papers.authors: Chad Sharp, Paul Grubbs

papers.title: Learning with Quantization and Worst Case Lattice Problems
papers.abstract: Motivated by the MAMBA proposals, we study the worst case hardness of learning with quantization (LWQ) with public dither. We allow any efficiently computable dither function and efficiently samplable seed distribution; the matrix is uniform and independent of the secret and the seed. Using the randomized polar lattice quantizer of Lyu et al., we construct explicit families with polynomial power of two moduli. For the search family, polynomial time recovery of the uniformly chosen secret with inverse polynomial probability yields quantum polynomial time algorithms for the gap shortest vector problem (GapSVP) and the shortest independent vectors problem (SIVP) on arbitrary \(n\) dimensional lattices, with approximation factors \(O(n\log n)\) and \(O(n(\log n)^2)\), respectively. Under stronger parameter conditions, a second family admits a decision reduction: a polynomial time algorithm with inverse polynomial distinguishing advantage yields quantum polynomial time algorithms for the same lattice problems with factors \(O(n(\log n)^3)\) and \(O(n(\log n)^4)\), respectively. Conditional on the public seed, the comparison output is uniform in the prescribed dither coset and independent of the matrix. We also examine extensions to learning with errors (LWE) with interval uniform errors, as arising in MAMBA Frost. We identify obstacles caused by deterministic quantization boundaries and give a local perturbation bound with explicit dependence on the number of observations. This analysis does not establish a complete worst case reduction for these errors or hardness at the concrete MAMBA parameters.
papers.authors: Ziwei Hong, Zhongqiu Fang

papers.title: PPAD Hardness from SIS
papers.abstract: Understanding the hardness of the complexity class PPAD is an important question in complexity theory given that it contains problems such as computing a Nash equilibrium. Evidence of hardness, however, has come primarily from cryptography, through a long line of work. Most recently, Chen, Freitag, Jin and Wichs (STOC 2025) based the hardness of PPAD on the polynomial hardness of the Learning with Errors (LWE) problem, together with a fine-grained average-case hardness assumption. In this work, we base the hardness of PPAD on a different lattice problem, the Short Integer Solution (SIS) problem, which, unlike the assumptions underlying prior work, is not known to imply public-key encryption. Specifically, we show that PPAD is hard on average assuming either: (i) polynomially hard SIS with a quasi-polynomial norm bound and a fine-grained average-case hardness assumption; or (ii) subexponentially hard SIS alone. Our main technical contribution is a succinct, incrementally updatable proof system for a class of exponentially large circuits with short descriptions. Building on the work of Wee (CRYPTO 2025) for succinct proof systems for circuits from SIS, we show how to make such proof systems satisfy these properties while preserving the unambiguity guarantee of the underlying scheme: it is hard to find two distinct accepted states for the same computation and time. Together, these are crucial for our PPAD hardness reductions.
papers.authors: Arka Rai Choudhuri

papers.title: Efficient Laconic Oblivious Transfer with Malicious Security
papers.abstract: Laconic Oblivious Transfer (OT) enables a receiver to compress a large database into a short digest, allowing a sender to generate a succinct ciphertext that reveals only a single indexed message. While prior works achieve efficient constructions in the semi-honest model, known solutions for malicious security rely on inherently heavy non-black-box techniques, such as garbled circuits or succinct arguments, resulting in impractical schemes. In this work, we present the first construction of maliciously secure laconic OT that makes fully black-box use of its underlying primitives. Our construction is based on a simple and widely used paradigm combining vector commitments with witness encryption, previously known to yield efficient semi-honest protocols. We show that this approach can in fact achieve malicious security by introducing two minimal yet powerful enhancements: equivocal vector commitments and maliciously secure witness encryption. We prove that these properties suffice to obtain laconic OT with security against malicious senders in the universal composability model and against malicious receivers in the context model. We instantiate our framework from standard assumptions, including LWE and bilinear Diffie-Hellman variants, obtaining schemes in the standard model. Notably, our constructions avoid heavy non-black-box tools mentioned before, and therefore achieve efficiency comparable to the state-of-the-art black-box constructions with merely semi-honest security. In particular, in certain settings, we obtain malicious security at essentially no additional asymptotic cost. Our results resolve a central question on the feasibility of practical, maliciously secure laconic OT, and provide a unifying pathway for efficiently achieving malicious security in laconic cryptography.
papers.authors: Yijian Zhang, Zuoxia Yu, Rupeng Yang, Willy Susilo

papers.title: A Post Quantum Vector Commitment Scheme with Efficient Insertions and Deletions
papers.abstract: Vector Commitments (VCs) are a cryptographic primitive that allows users to commit to a tuple and later provide proofs about entries of the committed tuple. Literature on VCs provides many secure constructions with properties attractive for decentralized applications. These include fast commitment/proof update algorithms after a value in the committed vector changes, algorithms to aggregate position proofs, generating proofs for subvectors, commitment hiding, and many more. However, these works assume a static setting, where only vector values change and the length of the committed vector never changes. We initiate the study of designing VCs which support efficient updates to commitments and proofs after a change in vector length occurs (i.e. an insertion or a deletion of a vector value at an \textit{arbitrary} position). In order to construct such a primitive, we formalize a VC framework implicitly considered in VC based verifiable decentralized storage constructions. Parties control a subset of positions in the committed vector. A proof for an inserted vector value at a given position may only be generated via participation from enough honest parties. We call such primitives \textit{Multiparty Dynamic Vector Commitments}. Our work provides formal definitions for multiparty dynamic VC functionality and security. In particular, standard VC binding does not extend to our dynamic setting. This motivates us to define the \textit{dynamic multiparty binding} security notion. We also comment on how multiparty dynamic VCs can be applied to extend existing VC based instantiations of verifiable storage. Finally, we provide a vector commitment construction and show that it possesses multiparty dynamic binding under standard lattice assumptions.
papers.authors: Vir Pathak, Sushmita Ruj

papers.title: A Crypto-Agile Mixed-Radix NTT Accelerator for Negacyclic and Trinomial Rings
papers.abstract: Hardware accelerators for lattice-based post-quantum cryptography (PQC) have largely converged on the radix-2 number-theoretic transform (NTT). The spectrum of standards that crypto-agility must accommodate, however, extends beyond NIST. In response to advances in cryptanalysis and to reduce the attack surface, national authorities are standardizing or recommending lattice-based algorithms with alternative algebraic structures, as well as schemes built on entirely different primitives. For instance, NTRU+, selected in the Korean PQC competition and currently undergoing standardization, is defined over a trinomial ring whose degree is divisible by three and thus requires a mixed-radix NTT comprising both radix-2 and radix-3 layers, whereas SMAUG-T employs an NTT-unfriendly modulus. Support for heterogeneous algebraic structures is therefore no longer optional but a prerequisite for crypto-agile design; existing radix-2-centric accelerators, however, fail to meet this requirement. In this paper, we present a crypto-agile mixed-radix NTT accelerator that performs transforms over both negacyclic and trinomial rings on a single datapath. Our contributions are threefold. First, we design a unified butterfly unit that integrates two parallel radix-2 butterflies, one radix-3 butterfly, and the trinomial transform on shared arithmetic resources, in which a generic 17-bit Montgomery path and an ML-DSA-specific 23-bit reduction path share the same two DSPs. Second, we propose a conflict-free memory mapping that guarantees in-place parallel access across all mixed-radix layers with a single 1-bit bank-selection function, namely address parity for radix-2 and a fixed address bit for radix-3, and requires neither mapping tables, nor coefficient reordering, nor additional BRAMs. Third, we introduce a generalized modular constant division that combines the multiple alignment of Montgomery reduction with the quotient estimation of Barrett reduction to perform the $3^{-1}$ scaling of the radix-3 inverse NTT without any DSP. Implemented on an Artix-7 FPGA, the proposed core supports all security levels of ML-KEM, ML-DSA, HAETAE, SMAUG-T, and NTRU+ using 5,279 LUTs, 4 DSPs, and 9 BRAMs at 141.5~MHz. For NTRU+, it achieves a $4.1$--$13.0\times$ improvement in area-time product (ATP) over approaches that resort to radix-2-only cores via degree lifting, and new moduli of up to 17 bits can be integrated at the cost of fewer than 20 LUTs.
papers.authors: JaeSeok Lee, DongHyun Shin, YoungBeom Kim, Seog Chung Seo

papers.title: Mímir: A Stateless Private Search Engine
papers.abstract: Private search engines allow a user to retrieve documents from a public database that are similar to a text query. Our cryptographic protocol Mímir employs state-of-the-art homomorphic ciphertext switching techniques to realize the first stateless semantic private search engine for highly dynamic databases. The security of Mímir relies on (Ring) Learning with Errors. Mímir requires no offline communication, and it trades higher but highly parallelizable server computation for low per-query communication. When the database may change between queries, Mímir matches Tiptoe's search quality with 84$\times$ less per-query communication (0.24 MiB). At Tiptoe's per-query communication, it reaches 64$\%$ instead of 36$\%$ of non-private search quality and is 4.2$\times$ faster (0.87s on a single multithreaded machine). Against PACMANN, Mímir improves search quality from 76$\%$ to 81$\%$ of non-private with 72$\%$ of its per-query communication and a 9.54 MiB instead of 2.68 GiB one-time cost, but is 2.1$\times$ slower. Mímir can achieve 59$\%$ of the non-private search quality with 8.13 MiB of per-query communication and 0.77s of total latency. This matches PACMANN's latency at a 7.6$\times$ smaller per-query communication, and outperforms Tiptoe in all three metrics.
papers.authors: Gökberk Erdoğan, Emma Munisamy, Kamil Kluczniak

papers.title: Balsamic: One-round Threshold UOV from GPU-Accelerated FHE
papers.abstract: Universal thresholdizers offer one-round threshold signatures, but require evaluating an entire signer under fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). We present Balsamic, a complete homomorphic Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) signer and its application to one-round threshold UOV signature. UOV's short salted target hash shifts the encrypted workload to finite-field linear solving, which we integrate with coin derivation and hashing in a packed discrete-CKKS circuit. Our paired-pivot solver selects both pivots before first-pivot normalization, then applies their coupled update with one inversion stage per pair and cubic field work. Pivot-success certificates enable encrypted retry selection without residual evaluation. In 2-out-of-3 semihonest threshold UOV signing, each partial signing (online) takes $10.7$ seconds on NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada and $7.77$ seconds on NVIDIA GB300, with $5.25$ MB per response. These measurements demonstrate that complete homomorphic signing can provide the computational core of one-round threshold signatures without intermediate openings or per-signature interactive preprocessing.
papers.authors: Jaehyung Kim, Charles Gouert, Jean-Luc Watson, G. Edward Suh

papers.title: Efficient (Functional) Bootstrapping for CKKS over the Conjugate-Invariant Ring
papers.abstract: The CKKS fully homomorphic encryption scheme enables efficient encrypted computation over complex-valued data. In many real-world cases, however, the computation only involves real data, and storing them inside complex slots wastes the encoding ability. This motivated the design of conjugate-invariant CKKS (CI-CKKS) instantiated over the conjugate-invariant ring (CIR), which provides the same number of real slots while halving the RLWE dimension. Despite its better efficiency in handling real data, CI-CKKS cannot be bootstrapped directly in CIR, since the CoeffToSlot and SlotToCoeff linear transformations used in bootstrapping require storing complex values in both plaintexts and ciphertexts. Existing methods bootstrap CI-CKKS ciphertexts via conversion to standard CKKS, perform bootstrapping there, and convert back. For example, Lattigo bootstraps two CI-CKKS ciphertexts by combining them into a CKKS ciphertext with doubled ring dimension, while Bae et al. convert a single CI-CKKS ciphertext to a CKKS ciphertext in the same dimension. The former is efficient only for batched inputs and suffers from limited flexibility, while the latter consumes additional layers in packing. Another issue with CI-CKKS is that many existing functional bootstrapping methods encode intermediate values using complex roots of unity, whereas CI-CKKS provides only real-valued slots. Our first contribution is a real FFT algorithm over the conjugate-invariant ring, thereby enabling native bootstrapping in CI-CKKS. Our second contribution investigates functional bootstrapping over CI-CKKS. We adapt the real-valued AKP interpolant with radial correction and develop a single-cosine Hermite interpolation method using a single real ciphertext. We show existing complex-valued interpolation methods can be implemented using two real ciphertexts to simulate complex arithmetic. We also study the numerical behavior of real-valued interpolation and evaluate the tradeoffs between computational efficiency and precision. We implement our methods in Lattigo. Our native CI-CKKS bootstrapping achieves a $1.14$--$12.86\times$ speedup in single-ciphertext bootstrapping across different baseline methods and total linear transformation depths. Compared with state-of-the-art functional bootstrapping methods over standard CKKS, our methods achieve $1.16$--$1.68\times$ higher throughput.
papers.authors: Jiaming Liu, Shihe Ma, Anyu Wang, Xiaoyun Wang

papers.title: Tight Post-Quantum Multi-Key Security of the FX Construction
papers.abstract: The FX construction (FX) is one of the simplest key-length extension schemes for block ciphers, introduced by Kilian and Rogaway as a generalization of DESX. By extending the key length without modifying the underlying block cipher, FX can improve security against adversaries that perform quantum computation but are restricted to classical queries to the keyed construction. Recently, Shiba and Iwata showed in their ToSC 2026 paper that FX with an $n$-bit block and a $\kappa$-bit internal key is secure up to approximately $2^{(n+\kappa-\log_2\mu)/3}$ total classical and quantum oracle queries in the quantum ideal cipher model, where $\mu\leq2^\kappa$ is the number of independently keyed instances. In this paper, we improve this bound to approximately $2^{(n+\kappa)/3}$ total oracle queries in the same model against fully adaptive adversaries, for every $\mu\geq1$ and $1\leq\kappa\leq2n$. The known attack based on the offline Simon's algorithm can target a single keyed instance and matches our bound in the exponent. Thus, the exponent of the total query complexity required to break FX is independent of the number of keyed instances in this parameter regime.
papers.authors: Rentaro Shiba, Tetsu Iwata

papers.title: On the $s$-projected Goppa Codes and their Application to the Interactive Oracle Proofs of Proximity
papers.abstract: Error-correcting codes are a useful tool in cryptography, being used both to design schemes whose hardness relies on coding theory problems (the area typically known as code-based cryptography) and as a building block in other contexts, such as proof systems and associated cryptographic argument systems. Among all codes used in cryptography, Goppa codes stand out, notably in the well-known McEliece encryption scheme, where they have withstood the test of time as one of very few classes of codes to be considered secure for over 40 years. Therefore, a natural question is whether Goppa codes can also be used in the construction of proof systems or cryptographic argument systems. In the context of probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs), codes are used to transform proofs into a format that requires only a constant number of queries for verification. This efficiency is often achieved using low-degree polynomial codes, which enable the verifier to check consistency through interpolation, ensuring correctness with minimal effort. This application underscores the importance of good codes in enhancing the robustness and verifiability of proof systems. Given their critical role, we take a closer look at how error-correcting codes are used in proof systems to find a new way of obtaining an interactive oracle proof system of proximity (IOPP) from Goppa codes.
papers.authors: Abhraneel Dutta, Veronika Kuchta, Edoardo Persichetti

papers.title: Integer Coordinate Families and Threshold RSA Signatures for Any Prime Exponent
papers.abstract: At CT-RSA 2026, Ng and Lau introduced $(t,n)$-integer coordinate families for threshold RSA signatures with $e=3$, and found some families by heuristic search for $2\le t \le n \le 9$. They asked whether such families always exist and, if so, can they be constructed efficiently. We answer both of these questions positively. We prove that a $(t,n)$-integer coordinate family is also a $(t+1,n)$-integer coordinate family. We construct such families for $t=2$, and $2\le n < 19$, using a polynomial time algorithm in $n$ and its output bit length. Answering another question raised in the Ng-Lau work, we prove super-polynomial lower bounds on coordinates of pairwise families. We also find the minimum families for $n \le 9$. Ng and Lau proposed a threshold signature scheme based on integer coordinate families. We show that the Ng-Lau scheme admits trivial forgeries, and has a flawed proof. We give a repaired scheme $\mathrm{PiIC}$ which does not suffer from these issues. Finally, we propose an integer secret-sharing scheme $\mathrm{PiZ}$ that works for every prime $e$ and every $(t,n)$, without relying on any special coordinate family. We prove that both the schemes $\mathrm{PiIC}$ and $\mathrm{PiZ}$ are TS-UF-CMA secure under the standard RSA assumption.
papers.authors: Shivansh Jaiswal, Somitra Sanadhya

papers.title: Sotto Maschera: Masking the Sota-Voce Fixed-Weight Vector Sampling
papers.abstract: Sparse fixed-weight vector sampling is a highly critical primitive in several post-quantum cryptography schemes. It has also been the target of multiple side-channel attacks, demonstrating the need for robust implementations. While such implementations do exist, they are not necessarily practical in terms of runtime, and some have already been shown to be insecure. At CHES 2026, Filho et al. presented a runtime-optimized, but not side-channel protected, sparse fixed-weight vector sampling algorithm named Sota Voce. It consists of the Sota support sampler and MWSupport support-to-vector conversion, where the latter is planned to be included in the next HQC implementation. This work explores how both parts of Sota Voce can be transformed into a power side-channel protected implementation using masking gadgets for embedded devices. At the same time, we aim to preserve its competitive performance advantage over other masked implementations. By bitslicing core components of the algorithm, including sorting, merging, and compaction, we achieve high parallelism of the computation, improving the overall runtime. Moreover, we avoid slow masking conversions by masking exclusively in the Boolean domain. Thereby, our masked implementation is orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art, while showing no power side-channel leakage in TVLA evaluations. For instance, for HQC, we achieve a speedup of up to 45x in comparison to previous work.
papers.authors: Ben Brooksnieder, Dina Hesse, Markus Krausz, Tim Güneysu

papers.title: Smaller Share Size for Evolving Secret Sharing: General Thresholds and Threshold Three
papers.abstract: Evolving secret sharing allows participants to join indefinitely without modifying previously distributed shares. We study the share size of perfectly secure evolving threshold secret sharing schemes and obtain two improvements. For general thresholds, we introduce a polynomial sharing method that shares two secrets with adjacent reconstruction thresholds using one polynomial. Combining this method with the evolving scheme of Cheng et al.\ (ASIACRYPT 2025), we obtain an evolving $k$-threshold scheme whose $t$-th share has size \[ \left\lfloor \frac{k}{2} \right\rfloor \log_2 t + O_k\!\left(\ell+\log_2\log_2 t\right) \] bits for an $\ell$-bit secret. This reduces the leading coefficient of their general construction from $k-1$ to $\lfloor k/2\rfloor$. For threshold three, we give a separate construction that reduces the lower-order terms of the scheme of Cheng et al. We mask the short shares in all generations with the same random $\ell$-bit value $R$, which is shared through an evolving $2$-threshold scheme, we obtain \[ \log_2 t+(2+o(1))\log_2\log_2 t \] bits per share for fixed $\ell$. Both constructions satisfy correctness and perfect information-theoretic security.
papers.authors: Xiaozheng Wang

papers.title: Quantum Cryptomania with Classical Communication without One-Way Functions
papers.abstract: In classical cryptography, one-way functions are necessary for most of cryptography. In the quantum world, however, Kretschmer at TQC'21 and subsequent works have demonstrated that quantum versions of various primitives in minicrypt, such as signatures and private-key encryption, do not require quantum-computable one-way functions (qOWFs). However, the question of the necessity of qOWFs for primitives in Cryptomania like public-key encryption with classical public-keys and ciphertexts (qPKE) has remained open. We provide a comprehensive picture of the relationship between qPKE and qOWF. First, our main result is a black-box separation between qOWFs and qPKE. In particular, we show that relative to a unitary, real, and self-inverse oracle, there exists a qPKE scheme (with classical keys and ciphertexts), but qOWFs do not exist. Further, our oracles admit a point-function obfuscation construction, thus ruling out black-box construction of qOWF from point function obfuscations. On the positive side, we construct qPKE from quantum indistinguishability obfuscation for quantum circuits with classical obfuscated descriptions and efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles, which is known to be a potentially weaker assumption than qOWFs, due to an existing black-box separation. Our construction is the quantum analog of the classical construction of PKE from one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation in the quantum computation with classical communication (QCCC) setting.
papers.authors: Mohammed Barhoush, Amit Behera

papers.title: The Distributed Producer-Consumer Model Is All You Need: A Compiler for Asynchronous BFT
papers.abstract: Building an Asynchronous Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) protocol requires establishing payload availability with total order despite Byzantine faults and arbitrarily delayed messages. Although many BFT systems separate payload dissemination from agreement, they often couple their composition to protocol-specific selection or scheduling mechanisms. We present the Distributed Producer-Consumer Model (DPCM), an event-driven abstraction that separates payload-specific certified availability from payload-oblivious binary finalization. We prove that DPCM compiles any producer–consumer pair satisfying interfaces specified herein into an asynchronous BFT object log. DPCM batch-finalizes certified heights, deterministically refining failed batches until each height yields a normal or evidence-backed dummy entry. We instantiate DPCM as Octopus, which combines parallel consistent broadcast producers with batched asynchronous binary agreement (ABA). To achieve performance advantages, Octopus lets producers certify blocks without waiting for consumer decisions and keeps payload recovery off the agreement path. One ABA optimistically finalizes multiple consecutive producer columns, while failures trigger parallel row-wise refinement with logarithmic bisection depth. Across an eight-region WAN with $n\in\{8,16,32\}$ and 2200-transaction blocks, Octopus remains within 6.5% of Dumbo-NG's (ACM CCS'22) fault-free throughput. With the maximum tested number of silent faulty parties, it outperforms Dumbo-NG by 25.9% and 18.7% at $n=8$ and $n=16$, respectively, and remains within 1% at $n=32$. At $n=16$ and $n=32$, Dumbo-NG's latency is 1.9--2.5$\times$ that of Octopus. Across all evaluated settings, Octopus achieves 2.9--16.8$\times$ the throughput of Alea-BFT (USENIX NSDI'24), whose latency is 2.4--15.2$\times$ that of Octopus.
papers.authors: Liang Zhang, Binyang Hou, Zhengxuan Guo, Xiaohai Dai, Haibin Kan, Jiheng Zhang, Moti Yung

papers.title: ANNULAR: Post-Quantum Private Transactions from Isogenies with Recursive Batch Verification
papers.abstract: ANNULAR is a shielded pool built on isogeny-based primitives. Notes are committed in a Merkle tree and spent by nullifier with hidden amounts, following the structure of Zcash's Sapling, but every primitive is post-quantum: spends are authorised by the prime-degree PRISM signature of Basso et al., note ciphertexts are keyed by the MIKE non-interactive key exchange, and each transaction carries a STARK proved natively over the isogeny field. The transaction proofs of a block are then folded into a single recursive proof. A ledger need record and verify only this one proof, 426 KB in 15 ms, whatever the batch holds, and check each transaction's two signatures alongside it. A transaction's body is the size of Sapling's at the same memo length (2,685 bytes against 2,756 with a 512-byte memo); its share of the batch proof adds under 500 bytes. A move to post-quantum primitives is generally expected to raise a pool's operating cost. We argue that the post-quantum change and the scaling change are complementary: with a STARK as the proof system, proofs fold, and with isogeny keys, the per-transaction data remains small. The cost moves to the sender, whose proof takes 1.4 s on sixteen cores, and to one aggregator per batch, which we measure: 1,248 transactions in 99 s on one GPU. Each proof in the tree carries 100 bits of round-by-round soundness and the batch about 90 under a union bound; under Fiat–Shamir that is the work an adversary needs. The constraints of the leaf circuit are proven in Lean 4 to encode the spend statement, while the soundness of the STARK itself rests on a paper argument. The scheme's claims rest on the signature's existential unforgeability; its strong unforgeability, argued by the construction's authors and not yet proved, is not relied on.
papers.authors: Dustin Ray

papers.title: Registered Functional Encryption for Circuits with Dynamic Bounded Collusion
papers.abstract: Registered Functional Encryption (Reg-FE) eliminates the key escrow issue in traditional functional encryption by allowing users to generate their own public/secret keys without the help of a central authority. The public key is then registered to the system along with a function, and all the registered public keys will be aggregated to a compact master public key by a transparent key curator. Messages are encrypted under the master public key, and users can learn functions of encrypted data from the ciphertext using their own secret keys. Prior constructions of Reg-FE either become insecure when more than one malicious users collude or require the heavy machinery of indistinguishability obfuscation. In this work, we construct the first collusion-resistant Reg-FE without obfuscations. The schemes are secure if the number of colluded users is bounded, and the collusion bound can be either a global parameter or specified by the encryption algorithm dynamically. In both settings, we provide generic constructions of Reg-FE from registered attribute-based encryption and instantiate them from either the standard $k$-Lin assumption or the succinct LWE assumption.
papers.authors: Yijian Zhang, Rupeng Yang, Zuoxia Yu, Willy Susilo

papers.title: Tritone: Pairwise Garbled Disputes for Multi-Party Proof Verification on Bitcoin
papers.abstract: Bitcoin Script lacks native pairing operations for efficient direct verification of Groth16 proofs. Conventional federated bridges instead authorize withdrawals through a signing quorum, whose collusion can release funds without valid evidence. We present the Tritone protocol, which lets Bitcoin enforce the outcome of verifying a Groth16 proof for an NP relation fixed in a one-time trusted setup, with the locked funds secure as long as one of a fixed set of $N$ operators is honest. Verification is optimistic and off-chain, and every transaction is standard under current relay policy, so Tritone runs on Bitcoin today without consensus changes. Tritone generalizes the two-party BABE protocol to a fixed committee of $N$ operators, with one dispute instance per ordered pair. Cut-and-choose protects against malicious garblers, while Feldman verifiable secret sharing correlates input keys across candidates. Our new Lamport-adaptor gadget forces a challenging verifier to disclose the shares selected by the prover's committed proof element, providing the transaction-level binding left unspecified by BABE. A single set of disclosed shares then unlocks all retained candidates. We formalize the multi-party primitive, prove the protocol secure against up to $N-1$ statically corrupted operators, and specify its complete pre-signed transaction graph. We implement Tritone in Rust. On Bitcoin mainnet, when one verifier disputes a claim at every stage, the prover-candidate posts 9,607 vB and the verifier 18,160 vB of protocol transactions. In local benchmarks at 40-bit statistical security, the prover-candidate of each dispute instance retains as little as 112.83 MiB. Tritone thus replaces trust in a signing quorum with a single-honest-operator assumption wherever locked bitcoin is released to an operator against a Groth16 proof, with Bitcoin bridges as our showcase.
papers.authors: Oleksii Avramenko, Alessandro Baccarini, Torben Poguntke

papers.title: High-Precision Bootstrapping for GCKKS
papers.abstract: Generalized CKKS (GCKKS) trades slot count for reduced modulus consumption in high-precision approximate arithmetic. However, designing a GCKKS bootstrapping algorithm with reduced modulus consumption throughout its computation remains a challenging problem. We construct high-precision bootstrapping for GCKKS using low-precision overflow extraction followed by iterative precision enhancement. Our main ingredient is a ciphertext-conversion framework for changing the decryption factor and slot count without requiring the factors to be units. A slot-aware analysis bounds unused-slot magnitudes proportionally to the corresponding evaluations of the decryption factor, which is essential to ensure the unused-slot values remain well-bounded after conversion. We combine precision doubling with ciphertext splitting and develop a joint evaluation procedure that produces two error-cleaned outputs at the cost of only one evaluation of the cleaning polynomial. We also give a useful-slot-preserving conversion from CKKS to GCKKS that simultaneously resets unused slots through component-wise re-encoding. Underlying these constructions, we also improve the construction of the decryption factors by searching directly in the canonical embedding and obtain depth-free conjugation with non-unit factors. For target encoding precision $p$ and $2N/k$ useful slots in a ring of dimension $N$, the precision-dependent stages of the bootstrapping use $O(k)$ homomorphic operations and consume $O((p/k)\log k)$ modulus bits.
papers.authors: Shihe Ma, Jiaming Liu, Anyu Wang, Xiaoyun Wang

papers.title: For Thirty Pieces of Silver: Overcoming Non-IID via ZKP Sample-Level Auditing and Forcing Attackers into Traitors in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: As a privacy-preserving distributed learning paradigm, federated learning faces severe security threats, especially data poisoning, gradient tampering, distributed attacks, and adaptive attacks. Existing gradient-based detection methods encounter three major bottlenecks in practical applications. First, they cannot distinguish between benign and malicious gradients under distributed attacks in non-IID scenarios. Second, defenders lack prior knowledge of trigger patterns. Third, attackers can launch adaptive attacks against these defense mechanisms. To address these challenges, we propose a novel defense paradigm. This paradigm shifts away from gradient detection, instead leveraging zero-knowledge proofs to conduct sample-level inspections on the local datasets of clients, eliminating the defense degradation caused by distributed attacks under non-IID settings. Then, through a staking mechanism, attackers are forced to train on discovered malicious samples with flipped labels, generating counter-gradients to neutralize hidden malicious samples, achieving targeted backdoor removal without requiring any prior knowledge of backdoor features. Furthermore, through zero-knowledge proof commitments, training gradients must be generated based on the same locked data. This prevents dynamic adaptive attacks based on reference model parameters and precludes gradient tampering. Experimental results demonstrate that under the highly non-IID setting of $\text{Dir}(0.1)$, our proposed scheme successfully defends against distributed backdoor attacks and edge-case attacks on CIFAR-10, suppressing the attack success rate to below $6\%$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first framework to achieve such defense results.
papers.authors: Jinghao Zhao, Hongwei Yang, Bobo Wang, Meng Hao, Hui He, Weizhe Zhang

papers.title: SoK: Optimization Tools for the Hydra Multiplayer Channel
papers.abstract: Blockchain technology allows parties to use a consensus protocol to add transactions and data to a decentralized ledger that are immutable. However, the amount of transactions that can be processed within a consensus protocol and thus added to the ledger within a given time frame is limited. This is a scalability issue. Layer-2 protocols are a class of approaches that process transactions off-chain, i.e. without involvement of the consensus protocol, but allow usage of the consensus protocol as a backup for security. This potentially reduces the processing of $n\in\mathbb{N}$ transactions to only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ transactions being committed to the ledger. The basic building blocks of Layer 2 protocols are Payment Channels, whereas newer protocols as Hydra (FC'21) allow for multi-party channels that are not limited to payments but can execute smart contracts, i.e. program code. There has been substantial research proposing tools and improvements to Layer 2 protocols, but most assume the original two party Payment Channel design. This makes it unclear to what degree existing techniques can be utilized with Hydra style multi-party channels. This work (1) presents a survey of such such existing two party channel protocols and tools built on top of them. We use a didactic approach with a focus on explaining their core ideas. (2) This work identifies uses cases for which novel protocols for Hydra should be developed. (3) This work analyzes open problems for Hydra, lists relevant related work and proposes which existing tools can be used to address them or serve as a starting point for further research.
papers.authors: Maxim Jourenko, Mario Larangeira

papers.title: Pairwise Independence of Ten-Round AES
papers.abstract: We prove that ten rounds of \AES{} with independent and uniform random round keys are $\varepsilon_{10}$-close to pairwise independent, with \[ \varepsilon_{10}\leq\frac{3017}{2^{141}}<2^{-129}. \] For every two distinct plaintexts, the joint ciphertext distribution is therefore within this statistical distance of the uniform distribution on ordered pairs of distinct ciphertexts. The same sampled key tuple is used for both encryptions. The construction retains the \AES{} round transformations, including the omission of MixColumns in the final round, with input and output whitening. Let $E_{10}$ denote this random permutation and $\Omega$ the set of nonzero differences. We establish the result through the induced one-norm bound $\norm{\Dten-U}_1\leq3017/2^{140}$ on its averaged difference-distribution matrix restricted to $\Omega$, where $U$ projects onto the uniform distribution on $\Omega$. The proof groups the ten rounds into five superbox layers and decomposes the deviation from uniformity into fourteen orthogonal subspaces according to the number of active words and residual factors. Local Gram moments and MDS code constraints control the dependencies between word differences. Bounds for the distributions produced by the first rounds preserve their common source variables, while joint estimates for the last four rounds retain the constraints across two linear layers. The final conversion to statistical distance uses the support size of each component. Exact rational evaluation of the resulting finite recurrence establishes the stated bound.
papers.authors: Zhongfeng Niu, Kai Hu

papers.title: Descent-PBS: Programmable Bootstrapping beyond the Ring Dimension
papers.abstract: Programmable bootstrapping (PBS) in FHEW/TFHE evaluates a lookup table (LUT) while refreshing a ciphertext, but a t-entry negacyclic table must fit, with redundancy, into the 2N signed rotation positions of a ring accumulator. Module bootstrappings, namely extended bootstrapping (PKC'23), monomial-matrix bootstrapping (TCC'25) and their successors, rotate a redundant table once in a module of rank tau, at a cost linear in both the rank and the redundancy. Meta-PBS (CCS'26) removes the redundancy by iterating the rotation in the ring, but supports plaintext moduli only up to 2N, and running it inside the module pays the rank in every rotation. We present Descent-PBS, which pays the module rank of a large table only in its first rotation. We prove that for a module secret embedded from the subring, truncation commutes with the secret, so one public functional key switch with merged columns repacks all tau_0 components of a module accumulator into the ring and removes the per-component factor tau_0 of repacking. The bootstrapping then continues with Meta-PBS refinements in the ring, at tau_0 + K instead of (K'+1) tau_0 external products per key. For block one-hot secrets, the first-rotation exponents are multiples of tau_0, so every combined key is a scalar matrix: the tau_0 components share one key per block, and since all exponents are public in advance, one pass over the bootstrapping key builds the keys of all rotations of a negacyclic table. Ties-to-even gadget rounding removes a refinement bias that we trace to half-up rounding on the FFT grid. In a TFHE-rs-based engine, Descent-PBS evaluates a 16-bit negacyclic LUT in 196 ms on one thread at 128-bit security and a model-predicted failure probability below 2^-64. With the same keys and failure budget, the descent alone makes it 1.44-2.40x faster than Meta-PBS run inside the module for dense secrets; for block one-hot secrets, the descent and the shared keys together make it 1.51-3.32x faster, and 1.37-3.57x against the same baseline re-planned for more conservative 131-bit parameters. General 13-16-bit LUTs take 179-368 ms, 3.8-6.6x faster than WoP-PBS in its authors' configuration on the same single-ciphertext interface, at about twice its memory. The failure probabilities are predictions of a model that we validate where failures are observable, and the 16-bit keys take 1,208 MB.
papers.authors: Zhenyu Xiong, Mingsheng Wang, Han Wang, Zhedong Wang

papers.title: Linear Cryptanalysis of TFHE-Friendly Cipher FRAST in the Average Key Setting
papers.abstract: In the average key setting, a linear attack of Bak et al. on the TFHE-friendly stream cipher FRAST let wrong guesses pass, which they left as an open problem. The S-boxes of FRAST are public and random for every keystream block. For the mask on the least significant bit, we show that key differences fall into five indistinguishable classes per round. The filter of Bak et al. gives some wrong classes of the right parity a nonzero expected score. We compute the trail correlation exactly through the real cipher and bound the success of our statistic for every fixed master key. We bound its false alarms for a fixed master key with the last round kept and no filter, and for every attack against an ideal keystream. With known XOF inputs, our algorithm Contract recovered the classes of a branch pair of 15 rounds and the master key of ten rounds. A cost model gives class recovery for every sampled key at 26 rounds with known inputs and for a third at 38 rounds with chosen inputs. In the accounting of Bak et al., it reaches full FRAST on weak master keys of density $2^{-11.8}$ to $2^{-5.4}$ within the claimed security. A distinguisher of full FRAST has a proved advantage on these keys, and its time over the advantage stays below the claimed security as well. Independent branch S-boxes remove the cheap classes at a cost in TFHE.
papers.authors: Xingwei Ren, Zhenyu Xiong, Bo Xu, Yongqiang Li, Mingsheng Wang

papers.title: Mutual Correlated Agreement and List-Decoding: Improvements and Separations
papers.abstract: At a high level our contribution is threefold: we improve the quantitative MCA error bound for polynomial generators, we prove a refinement of the implication from list-decodability to MCA, and we clarify that in general, these two notions are distinct. We show that, for every finite field $\mathbb{F}$, every nonempty seed set $S\subseteq\mathbb{F}$, every linear code $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathbb{F}^{n}$ of relative minimum distance $\delta_{\mathcal{C}}$ and every degree $d \geq 1$, the univariate powers generator $G_{d}(x) := (1,x,\dots,x^{d})$ has mutual correlated agreement for $\mathcal{C}$ at relative proximity parameter $\gamma$ with error $O(d\max\{1,n\gamma\}/|S|)$ below the smaller of the unique decoding radius and the generalized Johnson radius $J_{d+2}(\delta_{\mathcal{C}}) := 1-(1-\delta_{\mathcal{C}})^{1/(d+2)}$, with a one-coordinate margin below the latter when it is smaller. Then, we show that list-decodability at radius $p$ with list size $L$ implies MCA slightly above $1-\sqrt{1-p}$ (the improvement on the radius is dependent on the list size).
