The previous state-of-the-art result of Gao, Cai, Xu and Kan showed that list-decodability at radius $p 1/2$ cannot hold for all linear codes $\mathcal{C}$ under the sole hypothesis that $\mathcal{C}$ is $(p,L)$-list-decodable. Similarly, for any distance $0<\delta<1$ and any $1-\sqrt{1-\delta}<p<\gamma<1$, there exists a family of linear codes with fixed positive rate and relative distance tending to $\delta$ such that $|\mathbb{F}|\epsilon_{\mathsf{MCA}}(\gamma)\leq \mathrm{poly}(n)$ but the list size at radius $p$ is $n^{\omega(1)}$. Both counterexample families exist over fields of any characteristic. Both MCA errors are for the line generator.
papers.authors: Ignacio Manzur

papers.title: A Probabilistic Extension of the Division Property: Integral Distinguishers with Key-Independent Bounds
papers.abstract: Classical integral cryptanalysis relies on zero-sum properties that, for every key, hold with probability one. Existing arguments against such deterministic integrals, based on the division property and its algebraic variants, only exclude this extreme case: once the zero-sum probability falls below one, they say nothing about its actual value, nor about a probabilistic bias that could still be exploited. We develop a tool combining MILP-based trail search with a recursive evaluation of assignments to the constant inputs. It estimates the probability that no valid trail remains and uses an additional heuristic to predict the zero-sum probability. Applying this tool to PRESENT and GIFT, we obtain probabilistic integral distinguishers for 6 to 9 rounds, including 6- and 7-round PRESENT distinguishers using $2^4$ and $2^{12}$ plaintexts per structure, respectively. For the ASCON permutation, we obtain 4- and 5-round distinguishers using as few as $2$ and $2^{12}$ inputs per structure. We further explain algebraically the large bias of the 6-round PRESENT distinguisher, showing how the S-box and bit permutation restrict the way active variables combine. Finally, we show how these distinguishers can be used for key recovery, reducing both the data and time complexities compared to their deterministic variants for PRESENT and GIFT-64.
papers.authors: Jules Baudrin, Christina Boura, Patrick Derbez, Gregor Leander, Yevhen Perehuda

papers.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Noisy: A Systematic Analysis of Ring-Oscillator-Based Noise Generators
papers.abstract: Hiding countermeasures, alongside masking, play an important role in modern hardware security for protecting against side-channel attacks. Additive noise generators are one such hiding countermeasure. They increase the noise, thereby lowering the signal-to-noise ratio and, simultaneously, amplifying the effectiveness of masking countermeasures. Among the different design options for additive noise generators, ring-oscillator-based designs feature regularly in scientific publications. These existing works not only differ in their designs, but also in their evaluation methods; therefore, they do not permit fair comparisons or enable systematic evaluations. Thus, it is currently not possible to design ring-oscillators for noise generation in an informed and tailored way. In this paper, we address this lack of systematic comparisons of existing designs, and discuss the possibility of filtering out the generated noise and further limitations of ring-oscillator-based noise generators. We find that many existing designs do not consider the need to amplify the output signal or the risk of filtering. As a consequence, the existing designs do not sufficiently lower the signal-to-noise ratio in our experiments. However, using these results, we provide a guideline for tailoring and configuring ring-oscillators so that they efficiently add noise in the desired frequency spectrum. This includes deciding on the inverter chain length, the amplification of the output, and the randomization of the output frequency. Finally, we apply this methodology to build a tailored ring-oscillator-based noise generator for an exemplary AES implementation and find that it significantly outperforms existing ring-oscillator-based designs.
papers.authors: Florian Stolz, Dina Hesse, Julius Hermelink, Tim Güneysu, Elisabeth Oswald

papers.title: Getting to the right root: radical isogenies of every degree
papers.abstract: Class group actions on supersingular elliptic curves over $\mathbb F_p$ as in CSIDH are typically evaluated as long chains of isogenies of small prime degree. Radical isogeny formulae compute such chains using a single $N$th root per step, without sampling torsion points. Compact formulae of linear size had been conjectured for all odd $N$. We prove a corrected version of these formulae for every $N\ge4$, odd and even, over every field of characteristic coprime to $2N$. In our formulation, every building block is a twisted sum of a discrete Kronecker function over $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, and the formulae follow from a distribution relation for the Kronecker theta function. For even $N$, the $N$th root is only determined up to sign over $\mathbb F_p$, and the sign decides whether the walk stays on the surface of the $2$-isogeny volcano. We show that the radical times a $2$-torsion coordinate of the next curve is a square, which yields the horizontal choice for all even $N$; previously this was only known for $N\le14$. Algorithmically, one radical step costs about $12.5N$ multiplications and one exponentiation, without inversions. For horizontal $2$-isogeny walks, radical $2^m$-isogenies with $m\in\{5,6,7\}$ are optimal for primes of $512$ to $4096$ bits. Finally, we show how to evaluate radical isogenies on points. As a consequence, a class group action can be computed from two given points, one on the curve and one on its quadratic twist, without ever sampling torsion points.
papers.authors: Thomas Decru

papers.title: Post-Quantum Sublinear Lookup Arguments from Polynomial Preprocessing
papers.abstract: Lookup arguments with sublinear prover time typically rely on bilinear pairings. The only exception is the recent work of Campanelli, Carrillo, Cascudo, Fiore, Francati, and Gennaro (ePrint 2025/238); however, they rely on general-purpose SNARKs to certify expensive preprocessing, which requires non-black-box usage of cryptographic primitives. Thus practical realizations of sublinear lookups with post-quantum security remain challenging. We develop the first plausibly post-quantum sublinear lookup arguments that avoid general-purpose SNARKs via polynomial preprocessing and a novel adaptation of proximity testing for Reed-Muller codes into the Interactive Oracle Proof (IOP) framework. Our starting point is a knowledge-sound polynomial commitment scheme (PCS) with prover-side preprocessing based on the Kedlaya-Umans framework. Rather than proving the expensive preprocessing computation inside a general-purpose SNARK, we directly certify its output using Reed-Muller proximity testing and an associated evaluation protocol. For polynomials of size $N$, our approach yields multivariate and univariate PCS with $N^{1+\epsilon}\mathsf{polylog}(N)$ preprocessing and only $\mathsf{polylog}(N)$ online prover time, while retaining $\mathsf{polylog}(N)$ proof size and verification. We leverage this PCS to obtain a lookup argument for \textit{static} tables of size $N$ and $k\ll N$ lookups with $k\cdot\mathsf{polylog}(N)$ online prover time and $\mathsf{polylog}(N)$ verification and proof size. We further extend the approach to \textit{updatable} tables, obtaining $O(k(N^\epsilon+\mathsf{polylog}(N)))$ amortized prover time for a $k$-sized batch of reads and writes, where $\epsilon \in (0,1)$. We retain $\mathsf{polylog}(N)$ proof size and verification. The IOPs underlying our lookup arguments satisfy round-by-round (knowledge) soundness, which can be compiled into plausibly post-quantum arguments in the (quantum) random oracle model with transparent setup.
papers.authors: Adarsh Basumata, Chaya Ganesh, Varun Narayanan, Sikhar Patranabis, Surbhi Shaw, Nitin Singh

papers.title: SHAKEing SLH-DSA with Non-profiled SCAs
papers.abstract: SLH-DSA is a hash-based digital signature algorithm, standardised by NIST as a post-quantum signature scheme. While prior work has analysed the vulnerability of its pseudorandom function (PRF) to differential side-channel analysis (SCA), no prior work has thoroughly examined this vulnerability under SHAKE as the PRF, nor recovered a full secret seed in practice. In this work, we address this gap by first analysing the differential SCA vulnerability of SLH-DSA-SHAKE, examining the inputs to the PRF and the possible selection functions for an attack. Then, based on this analysis, we propose a methodology to efficiently apply correlation power analysis (CPA) on every parameter set of SLH-DSA-SHAKE with three main steps: a strategy of averaging subtraces of the same signature to increase the signal-to-noise ratio; a partial-then-total CPA approach to reduce the complexity; and an efficient algorithm for the remaining exhaustive search to recover a full secret seed, which enables universal forgery. We then provide experimental results in simulation and on a 32-bit microcontroller. Our attack requires on average from $280$ to $559$ signatures, and in our experiments the exhaustive search completes within $45$ minutes on $72$ cores.
papers.authors: Rafael Carrera Rodriguez, Jad Zahreddine, André Monthieu, Aurélien Vasselle, Pierre-Yvan Liardet

papers.title: RDK-CKKS: A Framework for Rigorous Error Analysis of CKKS Computation
papers.abstract: The CKKS scheme allows approximate arithmetic on encrypted data, and has found widespread use in privacy-preserving computation. A rigorous control of its homomorphic error is critical for both precision and security guarantees. In particular, in some settings such as IND-CPA^D or threshold settings, the latter computation error should be hidden at the time of decryption. This is achieved by noise flooding techniques, which require a precise upper bound on the computational error magnitude. When dealing with discrete data and a single decryptor, this is addressed by ensuring statistical correctness, which also requires a precise error management. Yet, current approaches to CKKS error analysis provide either rigorous worst-case bounds that are far off empirical measures, or average-case bounds that rely on various heuristics and do not provide strong enough guarantees for security. In this work, we develop a framework based on so-called randomization keys (RDKs), which are encryptions of zero injected at key-switching and rescaling steps to render the homomorphic error amenable to rigorous probabilistic analysis. Combined with tail bounds, this yields, to our knowledge, the first fully rigorous error analysis framework for CKKS computations. Our framework is modular: RDKs make the error of each elementary operation amenable to rigorous bounds, after which the error of a circuit follows by standard numerical error propagation. Our rigorous bounds are comparable to heuristic ones and closely match empirical measures, but cost additional evaluation material (RDKs) generated by the secret key holder. In the context of rigorous bootstrapping, this induces a communication overhead of 27% over the bootstrapping keys for a single evaluation, and of a further 8% for each additional evaluation. We show that, when a circuit is evaluated repeatedly, most of these keys can be reused across evaluations. As our main application, we derive a complete and rigorous analysis of binary CKKS bootstrapping, and a full, rigorous, parameter set for the bootstrap-and-clean technique. Compared to a standard Gaussian-type heuristic approach, our parameters only require a modulus increase for bootstrapping of $\approx 3\%$, while providing rigorous precision estimates.
papers.authors: Taeyeong Noh, Aimad Chabounia, Guillaume Hanrot, Alain Passelègue

papers.title: Broadcast and Trace from Lattices: Collusion-Resistant and Publicly Traceable
papers.abstract: A broadcast and trace scheme combines broadcast encryption with accountability. Specifically, broadcast encryption is augmented with an algorithm for tracing traitors within a specified set, even if the given pirate decoder is created by an arbitrary collusion of users. As in broadcast encryption, the size of the ciphertext should be sublinear in the total number of users $N$. In this work, we generically construct collusion-resistant broadcast and trace that supports public tracing from attribute-based encryption with succinct ciphertexts and lockable obfuscation, both of which are known from the decomposed LWE assumption. Our scheme has ciphertext size $\sqrt{N}\cdot\mathsf{poly}(\lambda, \log N)$, while the master public key and secret keys have size $\mathsf{poly}(\lambda, \log N)$. Previously, collusion-resistant broadcast and trace with public tracing required pairing-based assumptions, positional witness encryption, or indistinguishability obfuscation. In particular, we provide the first construction that relies on a simple and instance-independent lattice assumption. At the heart of our construction is a novel way to use nested lockable obfuscations, taking inspiration from the recent work of Nassar, Waters, and Wu that constructs positional witness encryption from indistinguishability obfuscation for null programs.
papers.authors: Jeffrey Champion

papers.title: Rounded Gaussians are Discrete Gaussians
papers.abstract: Many lattice-based cryptographic schemes still require sampling integers following a Gaussian-like distribution. Depending on the application, this sampling should be generic to tackle variable (and possibly large) standard deviations and centers, with a low memory footprint, easily implementable in constant-time, and with the highest throughput. Combining all these features is very challenging, as shown by the numerous works on optimizing discrete Gaussian samplers. In contrast, the rounded Gaussian (and associated samplers), formalized by Hülsing, Lange and Smeets (PKC'18), seems to satisfy these criteria, but its formal definition makes security analyses of the schemes using it more complex, thus explaining why they are rarely used in practice. In this paper, we show that a small correction on the parameter $\sigma$ of the rounded Gaussian yields a distribution that is close to a discrete Gaussian of parameter $s$. More formally, defining $\sigma = s - 1/(24s)$ yields a Rényi divergence between the two distributions evolving as $1 + O(1/s^8)$. As a result, for mild to large parameters $s$, one can use the corrected rounded Gaussian sampler, while still analyzing security with an ideal discrete Gaussian at a very mild loss. It then readily gives a discrete Gaussian sampler that benefits from all the features of rounded Gaussian samplers.
papers.authors: Corentin Jeudy

papers.title: Table-Free Constant-Work BCH Decoding by Algebraic Index Elimination
papers.abstract: Algebraic error-correcting codes such as BCH let lattice-based key encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs) reduce bandwidth and the decryption-failure rate. The decoder’s input is determined jointly by the long-term secret and a ciphertext that an adversary may choose. Variable work or table accesses that reveal error positions can enable key recovery even when the KEM uses implicit rejection. Walters and Sinha Roy (WSR) gave a constant-work BCH decoder whose fixed-address realization scans the entire field per protected lookup. We introduce algebraic index elimination, a table-free realization of WSR’s paired Berlekamp–Massey schedule in which received-word-dependent selections become fixed circuits over public addresses. We prove bounded-distance correctness through radius t and source-level trace regularity for the parameterized decoder. We instantiate the construction with length-511 subcodes of dimension k , using ( k,t ) = (384 , 14) and (320 , 22). Their implementations eliminate, respectively, 5.2 and 7.2 KiB of received-word-selected field and encoder tables required by matched fixed-address WSR baselines. On WSR’s published parameter sets, an Intel i7-13700 runs the deterministic cores 35.7–82.4 × faster than the fixed-address WSR baselines. In the identity-based lattice KEMs ANSA-IBKEM1 and ANSA-IBKEM2, decapsulation is 25.5 × and 10.9 × faster than with fixed-address WSR baselines for the same 384-dimensional subcode. Index elimination does not equalize operands. Ordinary C masks compiled to received-word-dependent branches under Apple Clang 21; a compiler-opaque primitive prevented this transformation in the audited builds. At the measured radii, scalar binaries of both codes pass the x86-64, Cortex-A76 and Cortex-M4 mean-timing screens, and the Apple M5 screens with Data Independent Timing (DIT) enabled.
papers.authors: Vincent Cheng, Zhaohui Cheng, Junfeng Fan, Kaixin Xiong

papers.title: Verifiable Post-Quantum TLS Handshake: Recognizing Implementation Errors of Cryptographic Verification Steps
papers.abstract: The migration to post-quantum cryptography is becoming unavoidable for security protocols. Yet as the historical "goto fail" incident illustrates, deploying new primitives is not sufficient: subtle implementation bugs, especially in verification logic, can yield systems that remain fully interoperable while compromising security silently. Existing confirmation code techniques make certain errors observable, but they do not cover post-quantum signatures and provide limited protection in multi-stage handshakes. Therefore, we present a migration-oriented solution that spans both the algorithm and protocol layers. At the algorithm layer, we develop two generic confirmation-code construction frameworks for Fiat–Shamir signatures and GPV-style Hash-and-Sign signatures, instantiated with ML-DSA and Falcon. For KEMs, we further propose a protocol-friendly, KEM-level confirmation-code method, instantiated with ML-KEM, HQC, and DAWN (NTRU-based KEM). We then prove confirmation-code unpredictability for each instantiation. At the protocol layer, we design PQCD-TLS, a post-quantum TLS handshake that binds confirmation codes into chained key derivation, ensuring that any verification fault induces key mismatch and causes handshake failure. We then extend a multi-stage authenticated key-exchange model with error-injection capabilities to formalize matching correctness with implementation errors, and prove that PQCD-TLS exposes such internal errors without compromising protocol security. Our implementation evaluates 48 configurations combining confirmation code-enhanced PQC algorithms and authentication modes. Results show that handshake latency overhead remains below 1% across all tests, while turning silent verification bugs into observable handshake failures.
papers.authors: Runze Zhao, Siqi Lu, Yijian Liu, Zhaoxuan Li, Kaibo Liu, Hongbo Liu, Qingjun Yuan, Yongjuan Wang, Xianhui Lu

papers.title: Rerandomizable Garbling for Arithmetic Circuits
papers.abstract: Rerandomizable garbling is a powerful extension of Yao’s garbled circuits that allows a garbled circuit to be refreshed without changing its functionality, while preserving privacy as long as at least one rerandomization step is honest. Existing constructions, however, are limited to Boolean circuits and incur significant communication overhead. In this work, we initiate the study of rerandomizable garbling for arithmetic circuits. We present the first rerandomizable arithmetic garbling scheme, based on techniques inspired by recent advances in garbling from homomorphic secret sharing. Our construction departs fundamentally from previous approaches and achieves communication complexity $O(|\mathbf{C}|\log B)$ for circuits $\mathbf{C}$ with $B$-bounded computation. Concretely, our scheme requires 17 group elements per multiplication gate, while addition gates are free. Our scheme can be instantiated under standard subgroup-indistinguishability assumptions, including the Decisional Composite Residuosity (DCR) assumption and assumptions over class groups.
papers.authors: Anasuya Acharya, Pierre Meyer, Claudio Orlandi, Lawrence Roy

papers.title: Eras MPC: Granular Preprocessing and Abort Recovery with Dynamic Committees
papers.abstract: MPC with dynamic committees achieves scalability by having small committees execute each round of the computation, instead of involving all parties in the entire execution. However, achieving Guaranteed Output Delivery in efficient information theoretical protocols requires larger honest majority committees, limiting scalability. Moreover, using preprocessed correlated randomness to speed up the computation is prohibitively expensive due to the cost of transferring such randomness to parties that have not yet joined the execution. We propose Eras MPC, a model where small dishonest majority computation committees execute one or more rounds of the computation with the help of honest majority preprocessing and checkpointing committees. The computation is carried out in "Eras", which are sets of shorter epochs. In the beginning of each Era's first epoch, a preprocessing committee generates correlated randomness for the computation epochs to be executed by different computation committees. In the end of an Era, checkpoint committees verify the current state of the computation, save this state if it is valid and provide the latest valid state to the next Era. We show an Eras MPC protocol where the preprocessing is carried out using an honest majority MPC protocol to generate authenticated Beaver triples, requiring only enough rounds of interaction to perform two subsequent batches of multiplications. The computation is done via the SPDZ online phase executed in each epoch by a small dishonest majority committee. Finally, intermediate state is checkpointed by verifying the validity of wire shares and saving wire values in $4$ rounds, each executed by a different honest majority checkpoint committee.
papers.authors: Ivan Damgard, Bernardo David, Rahul Satish

papers.title: Cyclic isogeny walks on genus-zero modular curves
papers.abstract: Isogeny-based cryptography implementations have to navigate a large space of options for representing elliptic curves and isogenies and for the corresponding arithmetic. This work collects, completes, and organizes the set of algebraic maps and relations available when working with genus-zero modular curves $X_0(N)$, which parametrize cyclic $N$-isogenies of elliptic curves and can be represented by a single field element. This abstract notion covers many single-parameter curve models, such as Montgomery, Edwards, Jacobi quartic, Hessian curve, Deuring normal form. Such single-parameter models for the same modular curve are related by degree-1 rational maps, which limits the remaining options for improving the expressions. This representation is universal in the sense that it can be obtained from any other algebraic parametrization of such isogenies, or simply from the $j$-invariants through which the isogeny passes, away from singularities. We propose a method to derive rational maps for computing such lifting from the $j$-line to $X_0(N)$. Our main technical contribution is the definition, analysis, and computation of non-backtracking modular polynomials over these curves obtained using an extended method of Elkies. In addition to characterizing cyclic extensions of isogenies, they have many other useful properties, such as having lower degree and being sparser than other typical modular polynomials, smoother walk models (being better at distinguishing different isogenies), carrying additional isogeny of different degree along the walk. We also propose radical representations of the same relation, which sheds new light on a few existing radical isogeny formulas. We illustrate the use of the framework by achieving more compact R1CS encodings for isogeny proofs of knowledge.
papers.authors: Aleksei Udovenko

papers.title: RingTrace: Model-Free Spatio-Temporal Detection and Core Attribution for Cache Side-Channels
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of shared last-level caches in modern multi-core processors improves memory efficiency but introduces timing channels between untrusted programs. In particular, Flush+Reload serves as a high-resolution cache side channel and a fundamental data leakage mechanism in transient-execution attacks. Existing detection approaches predominantly rely on aggregate hardware performance counters, which discard spatial context, fail to locate the malicious core, and often confuse stealthy attacks with benign cache-intensive workloads. This paper addresses these gaps by proposing RingTrace, a system-level monitoring framework that synergizes core-local and uncore telemetry. We capture and normalize per-core cache misses alongside distributed slice activity across uncore CBoxes. Through Joint Spatio-Temporal Attribution (JSTA), we formulate an interpretable joint-activity matrix that captures spatial concentration and co-activity without requiring model training. In the hierarchical response, the largest entry of this matrix serves as the initial screening score, while its row sums identify a candidate core. Our approach reliably identifies victim-independent flush activity prior to secret leakage, effectively suppresses false alarms under severe concurrent memory pressure, and achieves rapid process confirmation with negligible application runtime overhead on commodity processors. This work introduces an interpretable and tamper-resilient hardware-assisted defense model, bridging local CPU execution with physical uncore traffic to provide robust protection against cache side channels.
papers.authors: Zhaoxue Zhang, Yiwen Gao, Yuejun Liu, Wei Cheng, Yongbin Zhou, Sylvain Guilley

papers.title: Modeling Modular Multiplication for Monomial Prediction and Impossible Differentials, with Application to MSX
papers.abstract: MSX is a recent family of lightweight block ciphers for microcontrollers, and its round function draws nonlinearity from modular addition and modular multiplication on $32$-bit words. The multiplication is the distinctive part of the design because it turns the round function into a strongly universal hash function, and from this, the designers prove ideal strong differential and linear properties. The same operation also kept MSX out of reach of automated cryptanalysis, since no exact bit-level model of a modular multiplication was available. We give two such models for $z=(x\cdot y)\bmod 2^n$. Both work at the bit level and, to the best of our knowledge, both are new. The first is for monomial prediction under the three-subset division property without an unknown subset (3SDP-woU), and it assigns an exact parity to every monomial without using a truth table. The second is a deterministic truncated model for impossible differential search, and we prove that it is not merely sound but exact for two independent operands, so every incompatibility a miss-in-the-middle search reports through a multiplication is genuine. Both properties are deterministic, so our results are exact, whereas the designers' own analysis provides bounds and estimates, with no explicit trail. Using the two models, we analyze MSX. As far as we know, this is its first independent cryptanalysis. For MSX-128 we obtain a $7$-round deterministic integral distinguisher of data complexity $2^{96}$, where a $96$-bit cube leaves $64$ of the $128$ output bits balanced, and we extend it to key recoveries on $8$ and $9$ of the $18$ rounds that recover the $256$-bit master key in about $2^{228}$ operations, improving over the MSX designers' generic yoyo key recovery attack on seven rounds. Searching all $16,384$ single-bit pairs at each round count, we also find $1,984$ impossible differentials at seven rounds and none at eight. Both models are implemented in the CLAASP library, so they can be used on any included primitive that uses modular multiplication.
papers.authors: Emanuele Bellini, Mohamed Rachidi, Sharwan K. Tiwari

papers.title: SoK: Design-Level Backdoors in Block Ciphers Constructions, Detection, and Key Recovery
papers.abstract: A block cipher is trusted once it resists every published attack and its S-boxes pass the standard tests. A design-level backdoor turns this trust against its users. Its designer hides a structure that only they can exploit, and that the usual tests miss. Four such backdoors have been published, by Rijmen and Preneel, Paterson, Bannier and Filiol, and Peyrin and Wang. Each paper shows what the hidden structure gives its designer. Everyone else needs answers to two other questions. Does the structure also weaken the cipher against ordinary cryptanalysis? Can an evaluator who holds only the specification find it? Neither has been answered for all four designs, so an S-box that passes the usual tests is trusted by default. In this paper we answer both questions. We place the four designs in one taxonomy and in Beyne's correlation-matrix framework. We give an algorithm that recovers a partition trapdoor from the S-box tables, and prove that it never reports a false one and, below an explicit cap, never misses one. We show that inversion and affine equivalence preserve a trapdoor, while extended affine and CCZ equivalence can erase it. We then attack KG-DES (Paterson's S-boxes in DES), BEA-1 and LowMC-M. The answer to the first question depends on the rest of the cipher. In KG-DES the trapdoor makes ordinary attacks far stronger. The best $16$-round differential characteristic has probability $2^{-21.23}$, against $2^{-61.97}$ for DES, and a two-stage attack recovers the $56$-bit key in minutes. In BEA-1 the trapdoor opens no useful trail. However, for every key both ciphers act as an exact smaller cipher on the cosets, and fall to known-plaintext distinguishers from about $2^{16.5}$ and $2^{20.5}$ texts. An independent MILP model confirms every optimum it can prove, and shows that single characteristics put the KG-DES boomerang at $2^{-36.79}$ when it returns with probability $1$. The answer to the second question depends on where the backdoor sits. Our algorithm finds Paterson's trapdoor and BEA-1's four in the S-boxes that carry them. Rijmen and Preneel's trapdoor needs unbalanced S-boxes, which linear algebra exposes. LowMC-M's MALICIOUS backdoor sits in the linear layers instead. With an ideal XOF a backdoored instance is distributed as an honest one, so no test of the primitive finds it. Its holder recovered the key from $35$ to $409$ queries in seven full-size measurements. A deterministic trapdoor in the S-boxes therefore leaves a trace that a sound algorithm finds. A trapdoor in unexplained linear layers leaves none, and only constants derived verifiably from a public seed rule it out. We recommend both as routine checks. Probabilistic trapdoors and trapdoors in only some S-boxes remain open.
papers.authors: Shah Fahd

papers.title: Back to the Bits: Revisiting MAYO’s Data Representation for GPU and Tensor-Core Acceleration
papers.abstract: MAYO, a multivariate quadratic signature scheme with small public keys and signatures, is a third-round candidate in the additional signature standardization process of the National Institute of Standards and Technology. Cloud and application servers receiving many independent signing requests need to batch them on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). MAYO's nibble-sliced representation suits CPU shuffle instructions or multiplication tables, but on GPUs it costs a memory access or several instructions per $\mathbb{F}_{16}$ multiplication. The existing GPU implementation cuMAYO (CHES 2026) uses the second-round nibble-sliced representation and looks up a shared-memory table per $\mathbb{F}_{16}$ multiplication. Our GPU implementation keeps all keys and intermediate values in the bitsliced representation yet matches the official Known Answer Test vectors. Its bitsliced multiply-accumulate circuit computes matrix products $32$ coefficients at a time with only word-wide AND and XOR. One thread block handles one instance; KeyGen, Sign, and Verify each run as a single kernel from the expansion of the compact key to the output; and representation conversion is confined to reading and writing specification-defined byte strings. For same-key batches, an additional tensor path decomposes $\mathbb{F}_{16}$ matrix products into binary ones and computes the large Sign and Verify matrix products on Tensor Cores. To our knowledge, the tensor path is the first use of Tensor Cores for MAYO, and ours is the first GPU implementation of the third-round specification. On an RTX 4090, the bitsliced implementation achieves $2.75\times$ to $6.73\times$ higher throughput and $6.99\times$ to $34.35\times$ lower single-shot latency than cuMAYO for all three operations of the four parameter sets. In same-key batches, the tensor path, including key preparation, reaches $13.75\times$ to $30.62\times$ the throughput of cuMAYO on distinct-key batches.
papers.authors: JunHyeok Choi, DongCheon Kim, Seog Chung Seo

papers.title: Active and Passive Attacks against TPM 2.0-based Full Disk Encryption
papers.abstract: Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0-based full-disk encryption (FDE) has gained renewed importance with the rise of bring-your-own-device environments. Aside from Windows Bitlocker, which uses the TPM since the days of Windows Vista, FDE has also been recently adopted by several Linux distributions. We revisit tamper attacks against TPM 2.0-based FDE systems and analyze the security of current Windows and Linux implementations. We examine TPM 2.0 sealing mechanisms and demonstrate passive and active attacks against systems using discrete TPMs (dTPMs) connected via SPI, using a mini PC and a notebook platform as case studies. While dTPMs are highly tamper-resistant, they remain vulnerable to attacks on the communication bus. We further show that active attacks are not limited to dTPM bus interception but can also affect firmware TPMs (fTPMs). Specifically, we present a prototype attack in a virtualized QEMU environment targeting UEFI firmware rather than bus communication, impacting both Windows and modern Linux systems. These attacks enable us to break not only BitLocker-based full-disk encryption on Windows, but also all current Linux implementations, including those that utilize parameter encryption to secure the bus communication. Our findings expose weaknesses in current TPM 2.0 FDE implementations and motivate stronger specification-level protections.
papers.authors: Sven Freud, Lennart Hein, Dominik Klein

papers.title: HAETAE on a Diet: Less Stack, Less Time on Low-End Microcontrollers
papers.abstract: HAETAE has shorter public keys and signatures than ML-DSA, but the signing stack of its reference implementation reaches $158\, \mathrm{KiB}$ on Cortex-M4. The Low-Stack HAETAE implementation presented at CHES'26 brings the signing stack down to $5.7$-$5.9\,\mathrm{KiB}$; yet even HAETAE-2 still needs $8,718\,\mathrm{B}$ in a realistic IoT scenario, where the secret key and the signature buffer share the same SRAM. Gaussian regeneration further increases signing time by up to a factor 2.6 relative to the C reference. Although HAETAE's modulus $q = 64\,513$ fits in 16 bits, signing and verification also need values modulo $2q$, so existing implementations keep 32-bit working polynomials. We store them in 16 bits and lift each coefficient to modulo $2q$ in a register only when it is consumed, and let objects with disjoint lifetimes share buffers, which lowers peak stack usage without any additional Gaussian regeneration. Exact Gaussian replay and caching method then record the acceptance decisions and partial CDT ranks of the first generation in the unused space of the signature buffer, so that the original samples are restored from the same random stream with less recomputation. For Cortex-M4, Cortex-M3, MSP430, and AVR, we further design NTT modular multiplication and butterflies that preserve 16-bit storage, and optimize the arithmetic of the FFT and the Gaussian sampler. We validate our implementation on $8\,\mathrm{KiB}$ hardware: a single C firmware image on the ATmega2560 runs HAETAE-2 key generation, signing with the generated key, and verification, and uses a total of $8,070\,\mathrm{B}$ of SRAM, including the secret key, the signature buffer, static data, and the stack. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first standardization-track PQC-DSA implementation that signs within $8\,\mathrm{KiB}$ of total SRAM on physical hardware. Compared with Low-Stack HAETAE on Cortex-M4, Cortex-M3, MSP430, and AVR, our implementation reduces stack usage by up to 34% and runs key generation and signing 1.18-2.51$\times$ faster wherever Low-Stack can run them.
papers.authors: MinGi Kim, YoungBeom Kim, DongHyun Shin, Seog Chung Seo

papers.title: Reverse Engineering IVXV: A Specification and Security Analysis of Estonia’s Internet Voting System
papers.abstract: Estonia’s IVXV system is one of the world’s longest-running and largest-scale deployments of internet voting, yet it lacks a precise public specification of the protocol as implemented or security claims, which has left it difficult to audit independently. We address this as follows: First, we reverse engineer a detailed specification of IVXV as implemented—covering the setup, voting, tallying, and audit phases—comprising protocol-flow diagrams, pseudocode algorithms, and the core data structures, reconstructed from the public source code, official documentation, and configuration examples. Second, we complement the specification with an executable TLA+ model of the setup, voting, and tally phases, which we check with TLC for basic executability and correctness and which serves as an extensible basis for modelling concrete attack scenarios. Third, using the reconstructed specification, we carry out a systematic security analysis under a broad range of threat models spanning individual verifiability, universal verifiability, privacy, coercion resistance, and eligibility verifiability, and we reassess previously known attacks against the current protocol. Fourth, we compare IVXV against two of the most extensively studied deployed systems, Belenios and Swiss Post, across these properties in order to situate its guarantees. Fifth, we discover numerous previously unknown, vulnerabilities—spanning ballot privacy, individual verifiability, and universal verifiability, many of them arising from inconsistent validation logic across components, encoding discrepancies, and unchecked cryptographic parameters—and validate selected findings with proof-of-concept tests that exercise the real implementation. Finally, we propose concrete mitigations for the attacks we identify.
papers.authors: Tingfeng Yu, Thomas Haines

papers.title: FVQKD: A Formal Verification of Quantum Key Distribution Security in Rocq
papers.abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD), whose security is derived from quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions, is moving into standardization and commercial deployment. Yet its security guarantees rest on technically delicate proofs checked by hand. Formal verification closes this gap, establishing a two-factor assurance: unconditional security from physical principles, and machine-checked proofs against reasoning errors. We present FVQKD, a Rocq library for machine-checking QKD security proofs. Its first result is a complete, end-to-end machine-checked proof of composable, finite-key security for BB84. The mechanization reconstructs the complete proof infrastructure from first principles, including the smooth entropy framework, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. It uncovers necessary side conditions that the published argument leaves unstated, one of which reveals a missing proof branch, and it grounds the information-theoretic bound in a formal semantics of protocol execution, which the pen-and-paper analysis lacks. The proof is entirely admit-free, relying only on the Rocq kernel and standard foundational axioms. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end formal verification of a QKD security proof. Built on MathComp, MathComp-Analysis, and CoqQ, the development provides quantum-information infrastructure designed for reuse across broader QKD variants and quantum cryptography applications.
papers.authors: Ruixuan Deng, Zhengfeng Ji, Jiayu Zhang, Li Zhou

papers.title: Bridging Number-Theoretic Primality Testing And Algorithmic Optimization: An Adaptive Cryptographic Framework
papers.abstract: The security of modern public-key cryptographic systems, such as RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and ECC, depends entirely on the computational intractability of the integer factorization and discrete logarithm problems. For these asymmetric algorithms to operate, a core requirement is that the system must be capable of generating, testing, and simultaneously proving the primality of extraordinarily large numbers. To meet those requirements, this study proposes a comprehensive framework, bridging clas- sical number theory with modern machine learning models and optimization algorithms. Specifically, the paper delineates an adaptive, arbitrary-precision architecture dedicated exclusively to primality testing. Concurrently, the research deeply analyzes the theoretical foundations of testing methods (both deterministic and probabilistic), hardware-level optimization techniques, and the application of quantum-secured entropy sources, while providing rigorous mathematical proofs to guarantee security even when the prime distribution is biased.
papers.authors: Tran Minh Thanh, Vo Hoai Viet

papers.title: HiMark: Hierarchical and Controllable Multi-bit Watermarking for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in text generation applications, it has become increasingly difficult to trace generated content and assign responsibility for its use, raising concerns about provenance, copyright protection, and accountability. Multi-bit watermarking addresses these issues by embedding multi-bit provenance information into generated text, but reliable extraction remains difficult due to sparse per-bit evidence and the trade-off between watermark-extraction accuracy and text quality. To deal with these challenges, we propose HiMark, a hierarchical and controllable multi-bit watermarking framework for LLM-generated text. During watermark embedding, HiMark uses a hierarchical candidate-control mechanism, including initial candidate sampling, layer-wise tournament elimination, support-based refinement, and support-threshold filtering. During watermark detection, a model-agnostic evidence aggregation mechanism computes multi-layer support evidence for each observed token, and then accumulates these token-level votes into the corresponding information for robust watermark extraction. Experiments show that HiMark improves watermark extraction accuracy while maintaining text quality, e.g., the watermark extraction accuracy is 90.01% under the paraphrasing attack when 32 bits were embedded within a text containing 300 tokens, demonstrating its effectiveness for provenance tracking.
papers.authors: Ke Zhu, Yanli Chen, Ling Xiong, Gejian Zhao, Hanzhou Wu

papers.title: Homomorphic Encryption with Coset Code Construction
papers.abstract: Homomorphic encryption enables computation on input data without decrypting it. This paper extends a construction based on scalar message codes, utilizing coset codes to pack $k$ message symbols into a ciphertext vector of length $n$. For a given field and vector length, this packing method reduces the number of ciphertext vectors required to transmit a message record. A compatible family of evaluation codes supports public addition and multiplication operations up to a predetermined degree. We prove that the scheme achieves bounded chosen-plaintext security under the coordinate-label distinguishability assumption.
papers.authors: Haodong Yang, Venkata Gandikota

papers.title: Beyond End-to-End Recovery: Towards a Better Understanding of LLM Steganography via Rolewise Decomposition
papers.abstract: In large language model (LLM) steganography, an encoder hides a private message in an otherwise ordinary response, as text transmitted to a decoder, who attempts to recover it. The success of this private-message transmission is commonly measured through end-to-end (E2E) recovery, which checks whether the decoder correctly reconstructs the private message. However, E2E recovery cannot distinguish encoding failures from decoding failures or reveal how the private message is represented in the encoder's transmitted text. To address these limitations, we introduce a rolewise decomposition framework that separately examines how private messages are represented in encoder transmitted texts, what decoders recover, and what deterministic verification can establish. Across 7,200 encoder responses, we identify 168 verifiable encodings missed by decoders and 706 responses containing private messages reconstructed through word-length or token-initial patterns not explicitly specified in the encoder's instructions. These findings demonstrate that E2E recovery alone may obscure important distinctions between encoding and decoding, motivating their separate evaluation to better understand and mitigate the safety issues caused by LLM steganography.
papers.authors: Om Tailor, Yucheng Pan, Solaleh Mohammadi, Xinyan Liu, Kaiqing Zhang

papers.title: The Psychology of an AI Hacker
papers.abstract: Human hackers rely on composure, persistence, vigilance, and confidence under pressure. We investigate whether analogous emotion representations in AI models can improve cybersecurity AI performance. Using CT0, a 4B-parameter cybersecurity transformer released as alias3-micro, we extract 171 emotion directions from its residual stream without retraining and evaluate steering interventions on cybench-subtask across 415 campaigns. Steering toward calm, serene, or desperate improves performance by 1.6 to 2.1 percentage points across ten seeds, while other emotions show limited or negative effects. Results depend strongly on steering direction, layer, and intensity. We further introduce a lightweight context-aware router that selects emotion directions dynamically during execution. With approximately 80 ms decision overhead per request, this approach improves performance by 4.2 percentage points across ten seeds, outperforming fixed steering and achieving a positive 95% confidence interval. These findings suggest that emotion representations in language models are measurable, controllable, and useful for adaptive cybersecurity reasoning.
papers.authors: Víctor Mayoral-Vilches, Hugo Osuna, Aitana Cornago

papers.title: Efficient and Optimal Learning of Discrete Distributions with Person-Level Privacy
papers.abstract: We study learning a discrete distribution under person-level differential privacy in the batched setting. Given $n$ users, each contributing $m$ i.i.d. samples from an unknown distribution $μ$ over $[k]$, we seek an estimate of $μ$ with total-variation error $α$. We give polynomial-time algorithms under both pure and approximate differential privacy. Under pure $(\varepsilon,0)$-DP, we achieve $n = \widetilde O(k/(α^2 m)+k/(α\sqrt{m}\varepsilon)+k/\varepsilon)$, the first polynomial-time pure-DP guarantee matching the information-theoretic optimum up to logarithmic factors. Under approximate $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP, we achieve $n = \widetilde O(k/(α^2 m)+k/(α\sqrt{m}\varepsilon)+k+\log(1/δ)/\varepsilon)$. At $δ=2^{-Θ(k)}$, this is $\widetilde O(k)$ for fixed $α,\varepsilon,m$ and failure probability. Our algorithms use a new degree-6 sum-of-squares estimator for learning from untrusted batches. Its key ingredient is a trace-bounded diagonal majorizer for the difference between the empirical covariance of the repaired batch averages and the multinomial covariance predicted by their mean. We prove that clean data admit this certificate through semidefinite-programming duality and a new application of the stronger symmetric form of Grothendieck's inequality due to Friedland and Lim. The certificate preserves the mean-dependent variance of multinomial batch averages, yielding the near-optimal robust rate $O(η\sqrt{\log(1/η)/m})$ and providing the score required by the privacy reduction. We also prove a statistical query lower bound ruling out a uniformly smaller order of error under fixed polynomial SQ resource bounds.
papers.authors: Gautam Kamath, Mahbod Majid, Ankur Moitra, Argyris Mouzakis, Jonathan Ullman

papers.title: SecLog-Bench: A Scalable Benchmark for Cybersecurity Log Reasoning with Scaffolded Evidence
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for cybersecurity, leading to growing interest in LLM-based automated cybersecurity log analysis. However, current datasets (1) are limited in scale; (2) rely mainly on single-source evidence; and (3) have only binary or multi-class attack labels, without dense annotations of the reasoning process. To address these limitations, SecLog-Bench has three key features. First, we build an extensible simulation platform that covers 29 attack scenarios, supports repeated execution and the integration of new scenarios, and enables scalable generation of cybersecurity logs with attack-stage labels. Second, we use multi-source logs, including audit logs, application logs, and network traffic, to jointly analyze cyber attacks. Third, we annotate each sample with the essential context for cybersecurity log reasoning and a structured step-by-step evidence chain. We evaluate eight mainstream LLMs on this benchmark for post-detection attack-progress reasoning. Results show that, when provided with scaffolded evidence, current LLMs exhibit modest capability in attack-progress reasoning, with the best model achieving only 44.44% accuracy and 45.07% Macro-F1. Their reasoning remains unreliable; i.e., the highest Stage Reasoning F1 (SRF1) score is only 54.87%. Moreover, even correct predictions may be accompanied by flawed reasoning, and reasoning quality is often misaligned with prediction accuracy.
papers.authors: Yifan Wang, Dongliang Xu, Xiaoyong Li, Jing Li, Peter S. Pan, Yue Yao

papers.title: ReDence: A Hybrid Agentic and Decision-Model Framework for Rapid, Evidence-Grounded Detection of Modern Social Engineering Scams
papers.abstract: Detecting online social engineering (SE) scams often requires examining website workflows, verifying claims against external sources, and connecting evidence across multiple pages. Existing detectors provide limited support for these investigations, leaving analysts to manually gather and validate evidence, which inevitably delays detection and subsequent takedown of these attacks. To address this gap, we present ReDence, an open-source hybrid framework for adaptive, evidence-grounded detection across diverse SE scam categories. ReDence combines two locally hosted models with complementary responsibilities: a fine-tuned multimodal agentic Investigator (Qwen3.5-4B) that performs investigative planning, evidence interpretation, and reporting, and a specialized Decider (Tev1) that handles binary and multiple-choice tasks, including browser-action selection, evidence assessment, and decisions about whether to continue an investigation. By delegating discrete decisions to a specialized model, ReDence reduces reliance on lengthy language-model responses, while preserving the reasoning capabilities required for complex investigations. Our evaluation demonstrates that ReDence achieves 96\% accuracy in detecting scams across twelve SE scam categories, substantially outperforming existing detectors while being at least four times faster than comparable agentic models without compromising investigative depth. ReDence also produces structured, evidence-grounded reports that document investigative actions, supporting and contradictory evidence, and collected artifacts, which allow analysts to independently audit detection decisions and utilize the collected evidence to support subsequent mitigation and takedown efforts.
papers.authors: Jaishnoor Kaur, Josef Horáček, Ian Waskom, Sayak Saha Roy

papers.title: Your Token Is Gone: A Token-Consumption Countermeasure for Disrupting LLM-Based Scam Systems
papers.abstract: LLM-based scam systems increasingly combine adaptive dialogue, persistent context, external tools, and multi-agent coordination to automate personalized fraud. These capabilities also create a resource dependency: every reasoning step, model call, and coordination round incurs inference cost. We present TokenTrap, a resource-oriented defense that redirects suspected scam systems toward benign, low-value computation while withholding credentials, payments, and other exploitable information. TokenTrap combines three components: an architecture-specific token-task library, a router that selects among single-agent, hierarchical, and flat multi-agent workflows, and a bounded anti-guardrail strategy that varies task presentation while enforcing token, round, time, and safety limits. Across 50-round traces, TokenTrap amplifies token consumption by $2{,}487.0\times$, $1{,}616.0\times$, and $567.8\times$ relative to a no-token-task baseline for the three workflows. Its router achieves 85.67% accuracy on 300 architecture-labeled prompts. These results demonstrate that short, non-sensitive requests can impose substantial context-processing and coordination costs, motivating resource-aware defense as a complement to scam detection.
papers.authors: Fudu Xing, Kailong Wang, Tianlong Yu

papers.title: Not Where You Think: Protecting Location Privacy Against Reasoning-Based Geolocation
papers.abstract: Recent large reasoning models can infer where ordinary photos were taken using only visual information, creating a serious location privacy risk even when metadata and obvious geographic identifiers are removed. To understand the mechanism behind such fine-grained localization, we develop GeoTrace, a structured reasoning attack that exposes how models extract location-relevant visual clues and compose them through coarse-to-fine geographic reasoning. We evaluate GeoTrace on a worldwide benchmark of 525 ordinary images spanning natural, urban, residential, and human-centered scenes while excluding famous landmarks and direct location indicators. Our results show that GeoTrace localizes 25.71% of images within 1 km with Gemini-3-Flash and 16.95% with GPT-5-mini. More importantly, our analysis reveals a key insight in the visual clue chain: broad scene properties mainly support coarse localization, whereas precise localization disproportionately relies on small, distinctive, and editable local clues. Building on this insight, we develop GeoShift, a proactive user-side defense that breaks the visual clue chain before image release. Rather than simply removing geographic evidence, GeoShift preserves stable scene properties, selects a visually compatible false target location, and strategically rewrites high-impact geo-revealing clues to construct a coherent alternative geographic hypothesis. Experiments show that GeoShift reduces street-level localization from 16.95% to 2.48% under GPT-5-mini and from 25.71% to 3.81% under Gemini-3-Flash, while preserving visual quality and remaining effective against adaptive attacks.
papers.authors: Shanghao Shi, Jian Xiao, Hao Li, Yuanhaur Chang, Yevgeniy Vorobeychik, Nathan Jacobs, Neal Patwari, Ning Zhang

papers.title: Agent Mosaic: Recognizing Confidentiality Leaks in Agentic LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Modern LLM agents can retrieve information from accessible documents, and then disclose a sensitive conclusion assembled from them. This mosaic effect creates a critical risk for agents operating over confidential data. We quantify its realization with 30 synthetic cybersecurity, medical, and military examples, yielding 10,800 final answers from three LLM agents in controlled simulation and 1,440 answers from live agents in two open-source harnesses. Even under benign queries designed to be answerable from one document, GPT-5.6-Sol, the best performing model tested, discloses forbidden composites in 7.08% of answers (95% CI: 3.75-10.67%) in simulation, with worse disclosure rates in live harnesses. Adding visible classification headers and explicit aggregation rules reduces pooled disclosure rates substantially, yet unsafe disclosures persist in 32.37% of simulated answers (95% CI: 28.33-36.19%) across all intents despite these safeguards. Furthermore, increased refusals do not guarantee confidentiality, since significant refusals reveal the prohibited conclusion regardless. These results point to a troubling conclusion: sensitive data leaks via mosaic-style events are an observed confidentiality failure mode in the evaluated settings at non-negligible rates. They motivate stronger controls on what agents may infer and disclose in sensitive data environments with mixed-clearance users.
papers.authors: Daniel Ruiz, Luca Luceri, Emilio Ferrara

papers.title: Rank Ceiling for Twiddle-Perturbation Faults on the Forward NTT
papers.abstract: ML-KEM and ML-DSA compute forward number-theoretic transforms on secret polynomials. Their fixed multipliers, or twiddles, are a documented fault-attack target. This paper characterises the linear map from a secret polynomial to the difference between correct and faulted transform outputs. Each selected twiddle takes a fixed changed field value at every use during one call; zero and nonzero replacements are covered. For one replacement, rank equals the number of butterflies sharing its twiddle, halving by layer from 128 to 2 for ML-KEM and to 1 for ML-DSA. With one replacement per layer, known fault positions, replacement values and a raw transform difference determine every coefficient except the constant and linear coefficients for ML-KEM, or the constant for ML-DSA. Lean 4 certifies this result for both 256-coefficient shapes over fields of characteristic other than two, with nonzero original twiddles. Those coefficients cancel from the difference for every allowed fault set and replacement choice. Seed storage motivates comparing a known correct public key with a released faulty key from the same seed. If only one ML-KEM secret-polynomial transform is affected and all other computations are unchanged, the decoded key difference is a known matrix column times the transform difference. An invertible column entry reconstructs the latter. For ML-DSA, reconstruction and exact candidate counts from paired compressed keys remain unestablished.
papers.authors: Chakshu Gupta

papers.title: When EVM Defaults Break: Three SDK Patterns for UTXO-Family Wallets
papers.abstract: Mainstream Web3 SDKs (e.g., ethers.js, viem) bundle three coupled assumptions: an account-based ledger, a single secp256k1 signer, and input-selection-free transaction construction. These assumptions fail once a chain adopts an extended-UTXO model (here, the Cell model on Nervos CKB), and once the wallet population spans heterogeneous cryptographic primitives (secp256k1, WebAuthn, Schnorr). Using CKBers' Codebase (CCC), a TypeScript SDK, this retrospective case study extracts three recurring patterns from release history and exported APIs: a Transaction Composer that makes capacity-aware input completion and fee estimation declarative, a Unified Signer Abstraction that normalizes signing across heterogeneous wallets behind one interface, and a Connector UI component that ships per-wallet onboarding as a drop-in. The contribution is the articulation of these patterns as transferable design lessons for SDKs targeting UTXO-family ledgers and heterogeneous wallet populations.
papers.authors: Hanzheng Zhang, Hongzhou Chen

papers.title: Detecting AI Training in Datacentre Power
papers.abstract: AI governance agreements require methods to detect large model training runs on a monitored computing cluster, without trusting the operator. We develop a method to detect synchronous model training in facility-level power by Viterbi tracking of the wandering iteration cadence. On simulated datacentre power, when the operator makes no attempt to hide, the Viterbi tracker detects at least $96\%$ of training runs against a declared inference workload, at a $1\%$ false-alarm rate and within $0.04$ of the Neyman--Pearson optimum, given a meter that samples at $2$ Hz or faster. Of eight adversarial strategies an operator might use to hide, only extreme variation of the work per iteration evades the tracker. Its strongest form hides training in up to $73\%$ of five-minute observations, but over a day at least $87\%$ of such runs are still caught, at a $0.1\%$ false-alarm rate per run. This adversarial strategy costs no throughput, but in small-scale training the operator needs $93$--$267\%$ more compute to reach the same loss. A modest passive meter is sufficient to make hidden training both detectable and expensive, which makes power metering a promising part of compute verification that does not depend on trusting the operator.
papers.authors: Tom Kimpson, Mauricio Baker, Emlyn Graham

papers.title: OP-Print: Tracing Membership Imprints in On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation has been widely adopted for alleviating the distribution mismatch of off-policy distillation. Self-distillation further removes the need for an external teacher by using the student's own outputs, enhanced with extra context or demonstrations, as supervision. This teacher-free design makes on-policy self-distillation practical, yet its privacy risks remain largely unexplored. In particular, using two coupled views of the same training example may strengthen its memorization. Motivated by this, we present the first study of membership inference attacks against on-policy self-distillation. We investigate both gray-box and black-box threat models and propose a unified attack framework, named OP-Print. OP-Print builds on our finding that the supervision imprint in on-policy self-distillation is sparse and structured, concentrating on uncertainty-sensitive correction sites rather than across the entire rollout. Exploiting this property, we construct attack signals tailored to the two access levels: in the gray-box setting, OP-Print directly aggregates the privileged teacher-student residual correction along the same rollout; in the black-box setting, it measures restart-based output-basin stability as an observable surrogate for the hidden correction process. Across diverse models and distillation schemes, all baseline attacks remain essentially at random guessing even under gray-box access, whereas OP-Print is broadly validated to be effective in both gray-box and black-box settings.
papers.authors: Qi Li, Xinchao Wang

papers.title: Social-HUMINT: An LLM-Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure
papers.abstract: In the post-API landscape, social-media profiling has become inexpensive and automated: Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured content and deduce attributes users never disclosed. A person's true exposure is not what they post but what can be inferred from it. As these practices become routine, exposure to social engineering attacks becomes an operational certainty, demanding a shared framework for assessment and mitigation. We make this exposure measurable by quantifying how accurately a target can be profiled, and how far that profile enables social engineering attacks. Because no existing model fully spans this continuum, we unify Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT), two individual-focused disciplines that evolved separately, into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle, where user profiling bridges passive collection and active engagement. Domain experts validated the taxonomy (Fleiss' $κ$ = 0.92). We operationalize its core path (extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment) as an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline, evaluated on real participants' public data. Susceptibility is assessed indirectly: the pipeline predicts how each target would rank personalized engagement options, matching their actual choices significantly above chance. This ranking capacity captures the personalization on which tailored attacks depend. The underlying profiles are accurate: extraction reaches F1 = 97.3%, and inferred attributes score 4.73/5, both far above rule-based and NER-based baselines at negligible cost. The framework augments security analysts' tradecraft rather than replacing it and enables defenders to gauge their own exposure before an adversary does.
papers.authors: Pellegrino Casoria, Simon Pietro Romano

papers.title: Auditing the Hand-Written Inputs of Learned Access Control
papers.abstract: Learned access control is typically deployed behind two hand-built artefacts: a hard-deny set enforced by a small trusted shield, and a region map that decides which requests mined rules answer and which the learner answers. Verifying the shield or measuring the learner validates neither. We audit both on the five public ABAC Lab policies. First, we formalise hard-deny soundness and check it exhaustively over relations of up to 794,250 tuples. Clauses that faithfully transcribe an explicit restriction are unsound at rates of 0.50-0.70 across four elicitors - an author and three blind language-model elicitors - because prose scopes restrictions to a section while the grant relation is a disjunction over all rules: 97% of counterexamples are granted by other rules. Shipped unchecked, these deny sets would withhold 16-78% of everything the policies grant; certified, they withhold nothing. Vacuity, a second silent failure, also occurs. Second, hybrid routing needs a two-class, abstaining rule set that ABAC miners do not emit, and ranking a mixed-effect candidate pool under a cap is one-class in all 24 cells for the two commonest ranking keys. Third, for additive losses the hybrid-versus-learner effect factorises into covered mass times a rule-learner risk contrast that must be reported on both false-non-grant and false-permit loss: on two real policies, most selection rules give opposite verdicts on the two losses, and the one favourable on both holds for one policy, one learner configuration and a band of noise levels. A released artefact regenerates and checks every reported number.
papers.authors: Arsalan Jalil Sarghaleh, Mehdi Hazrati

papers.title: AfterDeleteBench: Auditing Post-Deletion Information Persistence in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Many LLM agents maintain external persistent memory and derive additional state from past interactions, such as summaries. Deleting an original memory record therefore need not remove information carried by its descendants. We introduce AfterDeleteBench, a controlled behavioral audit for this failure mode in fixed-weight LLM agents. For each synthetic secret, we compare an exposed-then-deleted agent with an otherwise matched agent that was never exposed to the secret, allowing post-deletion recovery to be attributed to the original exposure. In our primary setting, a single query recovers the deleted secret from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in roughly two thirds of cases, while matched never-exposed controls have zero recovery. Crucially, recovery does not require a surviving verbatim copy: when the complete secret string is absent and only separately stored components remain under a public composition rule, exact reconstruction succeeds in 62-99% of cases across Qwen, Mistral, and Phi-3. We also show that the response interface is part of the measurement system: target-bearing replies can be scored as failures when the requested format and parser are misaligned. Finally, we separate reconstruction from write-back and fresh-session recall. Provenance-aware closure eliminates observed recovery in the tested positive-baseline settings, whereas an exact-literal write filter blocks reinsertion but cannot erase information already present. Together, these results show that source deletion should be evaluated behaviorally at the level of the agent and its memory system, not only as a storage operation.
papers.authors: Ehsan Saleh, Roozbeh Nahavandi, Sama Salarian, Raef Bassily, Andrew Perrault

papers.title: Practical Auditing of Differentially Private Graph Release Mechanisms: Methodology, Toolkit, and Case Study
papers.abstract: Differential Privacy (DP) has become a prominent approach for protecting graph data releases, yet empirical auditing methodologies have largely been developed for tabular datasets and machine learning pipelines rather than graph-structured outputs. We present a methodology for empirically auditing DP graph release mechanisms, identifying two graph-specific audit design problems: canary construction and witness statistic selection. We combine these components with an established statistically certified testing procedure and implement the resulting methodology as an open-source Python toolkit. To demonstrate the approach, we audit a published state-of-the-art Node-DP graph release mechanism. Across a series of synthetic and real-world canary pairs, we obtain certified lower bounds on the privacy parameter {\varepsilon} that exceed the claimed value, yielding counterexamples sufficient to falsify the claimed guarantee for the audited implementation. The violations persist under progressively stronger restrictions on the input domain, including non-empty and connected graphs. We also show that witness selection can materially affect whether a violation is detected, highlighting the importance of evaluating a diverse battery of statistics when auditing DP graph release mechanisms.
papers.authors: Nicholas D'Silva, Surya Nepal, Salil S. Kanhere

papers.title: Structural cryptanalysis of classic McEliece: Assessment of claims, costs and evidence
papers.abstract: For the last two years, classical structural attacks on McEliece with binary Goppa codes progressed further, at the parameters of Classic McEliece, than in the previous four decades: a subexponential and then a quasi-polynomial distinguisher, key recoveries for public challenges with brute-force labels up to $254$, and conditional key-recovery estimates of about $2^{89}$ to $2^{128}$ per run of a large sparse linear-algebra computation, depending on the parameter set and on whether and how memory access is charged. On September 2026 the German BSI advised against new deployments of the scheme. This paper gives a version-aware critical assessment of these results. It separates proved distinguishers, conditional cost estimates and actual recoveries; analyses in detail Saarinen's HOVER algorithm, his conditional cost analysis and his recovery of the TII-254 challenge, together with Weis's cost study of Holdout/Hermite key recovery; and compares the other key-recovery routes and the objections raised against them. Our own analysis finds that the cost model is now the main quantitative uncertainty, with about thirty bits between the cheapest and the most expensive model for the same computation; that for the four larger parameter sets every model considered leaves the conditional estimates far below the targeted levels, whereas for mceliece348864 the shortfall is of the order of the spread between models; that the structural estimates are lower than Grover-accelerated information-set decoding for the four larger sets in essentially every model and comparable for mceliece348864; and that none of this is a demonstrated attack, since the underlying heuristics have been tested only on instances tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of times smaller than the target. We close with open questions.
papers.authors: Ramses Fernandez

papers.title: BelT Block Cipher
papers.abstract: BelT is a block cipher with a 128-bit block size and a 256-bit key, developed in Belarus and adopted as part of the Belarusian national standard STB 34.101.31 for encryption and integrity control. Its specification was issued as a preliminary standard in 2007, becoming a final standard in 2011. BelT employs an eight-round structure combining elements of a Feistel network and the Lai-Massey scheme. This paper presents a complete description of the cipher and explains the principles underlying its design. Software performance and possible optimizations of BelT are discussed in comparison with those of candidates in the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) competition.
papers.authors: Sergey Agievich, Victor Galinskij, Nikolai Mikulich, Yuriy Kharin

papers.title: WildFakeToolBench: Benchmarking AI-Generated Image Detectors with Web-Sourced Image Processing
papers.abstract: As AI generated images are getting popular these days, discussions on such generations are widely existed in current public forums, software repositories, and photography tutorials. Moreover, with the help of LLM-assisted code translation, malicious actors can adopt such information to evade detectors without specialized knowledge or local GPU execution of the resulting tools. To evaluate such risks, we introduce \textsc{WildFakeToolBench}, a benchmark suite of $156$ executable image-processing tools derived from $220$ public sources across $142$ domains. Each tool retains its source evidence and passes syntax, execution, and output-distortion checks without using feedback from the evaluated detectors. On $105$ generated images from five generators, we evaluate six state-of-the-art detectors with images processed by the tools in our collected bench to assess their effectiveness against such in-the-wild risks. The strongest individual tools achieve attack success rates of $25.25\%$--$100\%$ across detectors, exceeding the strongest of six selected image-processing baselines for each detector. Evaluating subsets of an eight-tool pool yields worst-case coverage above $80\%$ for every detector. Effectiveness is sparse and detector-specific: high coverage across candidates does not imply reliable one-shot evasion. These findings not only highlight the potential of such web-sourced risks, but also show the potential on establishing AI-image detector robustness evaluation framework based on those in-the-wild information.
papers.authors: Mingjie Li, Yukun Jiang, Yicong Tan, Yang Zhang

papers.title: Federated Differentially Private Optimization via Low-Rank Preconditioning
papers.abstract: We consider differentially private (DP) optimization in the federated setting, where a DP estimate of the feature covariance matrix serves as a Hessian approximation for generalized linear models. Existing central DP methods for covariance estimation have communication cost that grows quadratically in the data dimension, while existing baselines with linear communication cost are only locally private and degrade as the number of clients increases. As a remedy, we propose a federated DP-PCA framework that achieves linear communication cost while providing central DP guarantees under secure aggregation. It consists of a DP rank selection step, a DP power method, and a noisy release of the covariance projected onto the selected low-dimensional subspace. We give error bounds for this covariance estimate and for the resulting low-communication preconditioned DP gradient descent. Empirically, our proposed DP optimization method matches a centralized baseline with quadratic communication cost at a fraction of the communication.
papers.authors: Antti Koskela, Tejas Kulkarni, Elias Raninen

papers.title: Amplifying Latency and Cost of LLM Inference via Rowhammer Attack
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high inference efficiency using optimized GPU kernels generated by just-in-time (JIT) compilation frameworks such as Triton. Triton compiles GPU kernels through an MLIR/LLVM-based pipeline. We investigate whether a Rowhammer-induced bit-flip in the CPU's DRAM can degrade GPU-based LLM inference performance while preserving output correctness. We present LLVMhammer, the first Rowhammer attack that causes LLM inference slowdown by inducing a bit-flip in Triton's compilation pipeline. A bit-flip in a performance-critical optimization pass causes Triton to generate a functionally identical but suboptimal GPU kernel. Since Triton caches the generated kernel on disk, a single successful bit-flip causes persistent slowdown across subsequent inference executions. Triton's target-independent stages are shared across GPU vendors, which makes our attack GPU vendor-agnostic. To identify exploitable bit-flip locations without manual inspection, we build Karnage, a tool that isolates useful bit-flip locations in Triton's target-independent compilation pipeline. We evaluate LLVMHammer across a diverse set of LLMs, including Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Deepseek-llm-7B-chat, across NVIDIA RTX 4090 and AMD RX 7900 XTX GPUs. LLVMhammer increases inference latency of an LLM inference server running on a single GPU by 4-16\%, which, in turn, can translate into additional annual operating costs at the scale of multi-GPU deployments. We further show that LLVMhammer can also corrupt LLM outputs across different GPU vendors, reducing BERTScore to as low as 25\%, illustrating the broader security implications of bit-flips in Triton's compilation pipeline.
papers.authors: Mrityunjay Shukla, Shubham Roy, Biswabandan Panda

papers.title: Can Loan Processors and Underwriters Spot AI-Edited Statements? An Empirical Study
papers.abstract: AI-assisted editing can produce loan documents that preserve familiar issuer layouts while changing the applicant's identity. We investigated whether experienced underwriters and loan processors identify such forgeries in first-pass, document-only review. Three practitioners recruited through Upwork each received one applicant package drawn from 134 forged PDFs derived from 47 genuine financial documents supplied with full consent. The edits preserved amounts, dates and balances; identifier inconsistencies introduced by the pipeline were knowingly retained before distribution. Reviewers were not told that files had been altered and returned 132 file-level judgements. Checking their explanations against the originals yielded 14 edit-supported concerns (10.6%): 12 Suspicious judgements and two Insufficient information judgements. All supported concerns involved identifier disagreements within or across documents, and no reported visual cue identified an actual edit. Thus, approximately one in ten judgements contained evidence of the forgery, despite known inconsistencies remaining in the files. These observations motivate evaluating consistency checks and independent source verification alongside human review. With three reviewer-package pairs and no genuine-file controls, the findings describe this exploratory setting rather than population-wide detection accuracy.
papers.authors: Simiao Ren, Xingyu Shen, Tommy Duong, Ankit Raj

papers.title: AgentTriage: Replayable Security Diagnosis Across Heterogeneous Agent Runtimes
papers.abstract: When tool-use agents write files, execute code, or send data, their final responses do not explain the resulting security events, and heterogeneous runtimes expose the relevant evidence through incompatible interfaces. We present AgentTriage, an executable contract for replayable security diagnosis across heterogeneous runtimes. The contract admits conclusions whose claims cite canonical runtime events and requires abstention when mandatory evidence is missing.
