We interpret our attack as showing that even the slightest power given to the adversary in choosing unrestricted private coins in the evasive LWE family of assumptions, renders it insecure.
papers.authors: Shweta Agrawal, Anuja Modi, Anshu Yadav, Shota Yamada

papers.title: A Note on the Security of ECDSA with Presignatures or Biased Nonces
papers.abstract: Over the years, several ECDSA security experiments have been proposed to enable faster distributed ECDSA signing. These experiments are not known to reduce to the standard ECDSA game, and recent work (Groth and Shoup, Eurocrypt 2022) shows that some are vulnerable, especially when combined with raw signing (signing hash digests directly, rather than pre-hashed messages) and additive key derivation. Furthermore, several of these variants are implemented in public libraries and used by companies, sometimes in commercially deployed products, yet lack sound security foundations. In this note, we revisit the security landscape of these alternative modes of operation for ECDSA. As our main result, we show that the security of some of these variants, which are used in the wild, is equivalent in the generic group and random oracle model to a standard conjecture from fine-grained complexity on the average-case hardness of the $k$-SUM problem. We complement our study by proving lower bounds, conditioned on fine-grained complexity conjectures, on the running time of generic group model attacks against other standard modes of operation analyzed in (Groth and Shoup, Eurocrypt 2022). Overall, our results provide a complete picture of the security landscape of ECDSA variants, and reveal an elegant connection with (old and new) conjectures from the field of fine-grained complexity.
papers.authors: Geoffroy Couteau, Nikolaos Makriyannis

papers.title: Auditor-Assisted Summary-Channel Verification for Hosted LLM Identity Substitution
papers.abstract: Hosted LLM services increasingly expose model identity as a product claim, but external users and auditors often cannot inspect which model configuration served a request. We study an auditor-assisted regime in which a trusted auditor enrolls claimed identities and prepares verification material before deployment, while audit-time verification uses only the claimed identity and released output, without runtime access to model internals, inference logs, routing decisions, or provider metadata. We propose SUMMARK, a summary-channel watermarking framework that uses user-visible reasoning summaries as a keyed audit surface. During setup, SUMMARK constructs identity-specific vocabulary carriers, trains lightweight summary adapters, and calibrates per-identity thresholds. At deployment time, a keyed statistical test assesses whether the released summary is consistent with the claimed identity and, when needed, attributes the most likely enrolled identity. Across model families, scales, and task domains, SUMMARK reliably detects cross-family and cross-scale substitutions at low false-positive rates while preserving task-facing answer quality. We further study FP16->INT8/INT4 precision-consistency diagnostics and robustness under bounded post-processing, rewriting stress tests, and text-only spoofing, revealing both strong performance and clear failure boundaries. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/trinitr0toluene/Summark.
papers.authors: Ziyi Zhang, Ziyao Wang, Guoheng Sun, Ang Li, Jian Li

papers.title: Provable Lattice Reduction in Nearly the Time of QR Factorization
papers.abstract: We propose a deterministic lattice-reduction algorithm with bit complexity matching QR factorization up to logarithmic factors, and an implementation that uses fewer instructions than \texttt{flatter} (CRYPTO 2023) in our benchmarks. The key technical innovations are iterative precision management, a finer-grained potential analysis, and a new representation for bases and transformations, all integrated into a recursive framework. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of our algorithm, and show that, for fixed reduction and output accuracy, the running time is $\widetilde O\!\left( n^\omega\bigl(1+\log\kappa_{\rm col}(\mathbf B)\bigr)\right)$, where $\mathbf B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}$ is a nonsingular lattice basis and $\kappa_{\rm col}$ is the optimally column-scaled spectral condition number. This gives a finer complexity than prior art, by allowing a tighter condition number $\kappa_{\rm col}$. Besides, through a new observation on the recursive structure, we demonstrate that the algorithm is free from heuristic assumptions. We compare our implementation with \texttt{flatter} on q-ary, NTRU-like, scaled q-ary, and Coppersmith inputs. Our implementation uses fewer instructions in all 153 executions. The median ratios of \texttt{flatter}'s instruction count to ours are 1.55 for ordinary q-ary inputs and 1.86 for NTRU-like inputs.
papers.authors: Yang Zhou, Zhedong Wang, Mingsheng Wang

papers.title: PQC Migration of IPsec: Reliable Composite Key Sharing Mechanisms in IKEv2
papers.abstract: The threat of quantum computers breaking classical cryptographic is accelerating the adoption of quantum- resistant cryptographic algorithms. Several government agencies have set a tight time-line for upgradation of all system to support post quantum cryptographs. We study post-quantum migration of IPSec protocols and their impact on network performance. The large key lengths in Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) cannot fit in a single IP packet leading to IP fragmentation. This can cause failure of security associations and degrade performance of IKEv2 under poor network conditions. To tackle this problem, we study a new key- sharing mechanism for IKEv2 and evaluate its performance. Unlike current hybrid key-sharing approaches, which send the classical and quantum keys sequentially over UDP or TCP (as in RFC 9370), the new approach concatenates them into a single composite key and transport them over TCP to ensure a reliable handshake. We implement and benchmark the new composite key-sharing handshake mechanism against existing hybrid algorithms that use either UDP or TCP. Extensive experiments under various network conditions demonstrate that the new approach significantly improves handshake time and energy consumption by avoiding the severe retransmission penalties of the Hybrid handshake mechanism. At 1% packet loss, the handshake time of composite key sharing mechanism is better by atleast 20% than hybrid mechanisms, and the improve- ment get better with higher packet loss reaching 30% at 10% packet loss. Energy consumption follows the same pattern achieving reduction of 29% at 10% packet loss
papers.authors: Rahul, Manjesh Kumar Hanawal, Sameer G. Kulkarni, Tirumaleswar Reddy K

papers.title: Optimizing HQC with Enhanced Parallel Binary Polynomial Multiplication on GPUs
papers.abstract: Graphics processing units (GPUs) are widely employed as accelerators in modern servers to handle key-establishment requests in bulk. Such deployments require the GPU implementation to sustain high throughput while keeping each request within its latency bound. In this work, we present a high-performance, end-to-end GPU implementation of Hamming Quasi-Cyclic (HQC), a code-based key encapsulation mechanism (KEM). We propose two novel techniques to accelerate the dominant cost of HQC, which is binary polynomial multiplication over Galois Field GF(2). The first is a parallelization of the Frobenius additive fast Fourier transform (FAFFT), and the second is a mapping of the cyclic product, viewed as a Toeplitz matrix–vector product, onto one-bit integer (INT1) tensor cores. We further explore the design space of these multipliers, measuring them directly on the GPU to derive the best combination for the architecture. We further propose a GPU-resident computation strategy that keeps the entire KEM on the GPU, thereby reducing costly memory traffic. Beyond multiplication, we introduce warp-level parallelization strategies to accelerate the remaining stages, hashing, Reed–Muller/Reed–Solomon (RM/RS) coding, and fixed-weight sampling, which become the performance bottleneck once multiplication is optimized. By varying the mapping of KEM instances to GPU threads, we derive five variants spanning the trade-off between throughput and latency and organize them into a thread-to-KEM mapping taxonomy. On an RTX 4090, the Coarse-Grained (CG) variant maximizes batch throughput. Our multiplier reaches 3,828k polymul/s for standalone multiplication, about 2.9× the latest GPU HQC implementation HIGH, and for the full KEM the CG variant achieves 1.56×, 1.55×, and 2.03× higher end-to-end throughput than HIGH for keygen, encaps, and decaps. For single-shot latency the tensor-core-based BMMAw variant achieves a latency as low as 254 µs. The proposed warp-parallel FGmw variant still attains a latency of 354 µs, demonstrating that our approach remains effective on GPU architectures lacking INT1 tensor-core support. All five variants are further evaluated on an RTX 3090 and an embedded Jetson AGX Orin to confirm cross-platform portability.
papers.authors: DongCheon Kim, JunHyeok Choi, Wai Kong Lee, Seog Chung Seo

papers.title: Fundamental Limits of Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation with User Dropouts in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Secure aggregation enables a server to compute the sum of users' gradients or model updates without revealing individual values. With user dropouts, correlated random keys protect local gradients while allowing recovery of the desired gradient sum. We consider three phases: key distribution, masked-gradient upload, and mask elimination. Users establish correlated keys, upload masked gradients, and provide additional messages to eliminate residual aggregate masks. Existing information-theoretic schemes typically design mask-elimination communication for a prescribed dropout threshold and evaluate its cost under worst-case dropouts across the masked-gradient upload and mask-elimination phases. Such designs cannot adjust communication to actual dropout scenarios. Moreover, the randomness and communication costs of establishing correlated keys remain largely unexplored. To address these limitations, we formulate an adaptive secure aggregation framework under the T-colluding security constraint and construct a single scheme that supports all feasible dropout scenarios by adapting its communication to the actual number of dropouts. We establish converse bounds on four resources: key randomness, key-distribution communication, masked-gradient communication, and mask-elimination communication. The latter two bounds are characterized for each realized dropout set in the masked-gradient upload phase. The proposed scheme achieves the optimal masked-gradient communication rate for every feasible dropout scenario and the optimal mask-elimination communication rate in almost all feasible regimes. Its key rate and key-distribution communication rate are each optimal or within a factor of two of their respective information-theoretic optima. These results characterize the fundamental randomness and communication costs of secure aggregation with user dropouts.
papers.authors: Jinbao Zhu, Kai Wan, Giuseppe Caire

papers.title: PRICE: Privacy-Preserving Image Classification in Mobile Edge-Cloud Computing with Homomorphic Encryption
papers.abstract: Cloud-assisted image classification enables many mobile AI applications, but transmitting raw images to the cloud raises significant privacy concerns. Homomorphic encryption (HE) allows computation over encrypted data; however, existing end-to-end HE-based inference pipelines incur prohibitive latency and computational overhead, limiting their feasibility for latency-sensitive mobile systems. This paper addresses how to enable efficient encrypted image classification in mobile edge-cloud environments without sacrificing accuracy. We propose PRICE, a three-tier edge-cloud architecture that partitions deep neural network inference between a trusted edge and an untrusted cloud. The edge performs lightweight feature extraction in plaintext, while only compact embeddings are encrypted using the Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) scheme and offloaded to the cloud for encrypted final-layer inference. This design avoids homomorphic evaluation of deep backbone layers, significantly reducing computation depth, ciphertext size, and end-to-end latency. To further improve efficiency, we develop RowHyDiag, a row-packed hybrid diagonal encoding with hoisted-rotation-aware encrypted matrix-vector computation, which minimizes rotation operations and improves slot utilization. Extensive experiments on real devices across five datasets demonstrate that, under the evaluated 128-bit-security configurations, RowHyDiag achieves up to 31.8$\times$ faster cloud inference, 85.3$\times$ fewer rotations, and 83.0$\times$ lower setup payload than the conventional Halevi-Shoup diagonal method. RowHyDiag also outperforms the PEGASUS linear-transformation baseline, providing 1.1-4.5$\times$ faster cloud inference and 1.2-3.4$\times$ lower setup payload. The results show that PRICE enables deployment-ready, low-latency encrypted inference for mobile edge-cloud systems under a trusted-edge threat model.
papers.authors: Duc-Huy Nguyen, Bui Duc Manh, Chi-Hieu Nguyen, Dinh Thai Hoang, Diep N. Nguyen, Van-Dinh Nguyen, Quoc-Viet Pham

papers.title: SemVideoSte: Agentic AI for Cross-Modal Semantic Video Steganography Communication
papers.abstract: We propose an agentic artificial intelligence (AI)-driven cross-modal semantic video steganography communication (SemVideoSte) scheme for secure cross-modal information transmission. Agentic AI interprets the service context to determine a semantically matched public prompt and coordinates video generation, message embedding, semantic transmission, and message recovery process. A multi-mask mechanism combines variational autoencoder (VAE) reconstruction robustness, semantic transmission robustness, and latent separability to select reliable embedding positions. Meanwhile, a private digital token controls the random seed and guidance offset to construct positive and negative terminal latent states, enabling coverless message embedding during the final diffusion sampling step. Simulation results on open-source datasets demonstrate that SemVideoSte achieves high embedding capacity, reliable message recovery, and strong semantic consistency under different channel conditions. In addition, eavesdroppers without the correct digital token cannot reliably recover the secret message, and the generated stego videos effectively resist the steganalysis detection. We further establish a prototype testbed to verify the practical feasibility of SemVideoSte.
papers.authors: Rui Meng, Song Gao, Tingting Zhu, Zixun Tang, Jinke Ren, Xiaodong Xu, Pei Xiao, Shuguang Cui, Ping Zhang

papers.title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
papers.abstract: Phone scams impose substantial and growing costs on individuals and financial systems worldwide, yet existing countermeasures impose no resource cost on perpetrators. Strategic scam-baiting, in which automated agents engage scammers to deplete their operational capacity, offers a proactive alternative but requires dynamic strategy adaptation that static systems cannot provide. We introduce a game-theoretic framework enabling LLMs to learn effective counter-strategies through in-context experience without fine-tuning. The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .
papers.authors: Nardine Basta, Robin Carpentier, Benjamin Zi Hao Zhao, Dali Kaafar

papers.title: BrushOff: Stroke-Based Re-rendering as a Watermark Removal Attack on Painting
papers.abstract: Invisible watermarks are used to mark who owns a painting. We show that a simple attack removes the most robust one we test. The attack redraws the watermarked painting with brush strokes, using a pretrained stroke-based renderer. We call this attack BrushOff. It needs no training, no knowledge of the watermark, and no generative model. We test four watermarks on 500 paintings from five styles. VINE, a recent watermark built to survive image editing, survives all 14 conventional distortions we test, with at least 97.8% detection. Repainting lowers its detection to 1.8%, while the output keeps a no-reference quality score close to that of the clean paintings. Diffusion regeneration can also remove VINE, but at the same removal level it moves the image twice as far from the painting in DreamSim distance, and it changes what the painting shows. Because the renderer draws a countable number of strokes, we can control the attack strength step by step. Finally, we test what kind of signal survives. A simple probe that stores bits in the relative brightness of neighboring regions survives repainting, while a probe that uses absolute brightness does not. The same probe fails under diffusion regeneration, while VINE fails under repainting. Robustness to these two attacks is therefore a separate property, and benchmarks should test both.
papers.authors: Hao Chen, Junnan Xu

papers.title: Quantum State Search with Classical Interactive Advice
papers.abstract: We study whether a quantum verifier can find a hidden quantum state by exchanging classical messages with an unbounded prover who knows the state. The verifier has access to a reflection oracle about the target. For a Haar-random $n$-qubit target, we prove that achieving constant average fidelity with the target requires $(q+1)^2(B+1)=\Omega(2^n)$, where $q$ is the number of verifier queries and $B$ is the total prover-to-verifier communication. The bound allows arbitrary classical interaction and unrestricted computation between queries. Our proof extends the lower bound of Aaronson and Kuperberg (ToC'07) from a single classical proof to an arbitrary classical interaction. As a result, we obtain a quantum-oracle separation of QMA from QCIP. In particular, we give a unitary oracle $\mathcal{U}$ such that there exists a language $L\in\mathrm{QMA}^{\mathcal{U}}$ but $L\notin\mathrm{QCIP}^{\mathcal{U}}$. Our separation holds even for UniqueQMA, the restriction of QMA to verification with a unique quantum witness, which is known to be strictly weaker than QMA in the quantum black-box setting. We further give an oracle construction for a notion known as QMA--QCIP[2] gap problem. This gives average case hardness for a QMA language under classical access to a QCIP[2] decision oracle and is used in establishing negative results on witness encryption and quantum indistinguishability obfuscation.
papers.authors: Mohammed Barhoush

papers.title: Analysis of an AI based code distinguisher
papers.abstract: Recently, DeepDistinguisher demonstrated the capability of transformer-like architectures to accurately distinguish Goppa codes from linear codes randomly generated, outperforming traditional distinguishers in certain settings. The purpose of our research is to examine the working mechanism of the mentioned machine learning algorithm. In particular, we explore the performance of the distinguisher using saliency maps and attention visualization techniques. We first identify a low-weight-row artifact present in the random instances used during training and show that the model partially relies on this feature. After removing this artifact, the distinguisher still achieves significant accuracy, suggesting the use of more structural properties. Inspired by the constraints induced by the minimum distance of Goppa codes, we proposed a rule based on pairwise XOR operation between the rows of the generator matrix. Our experiments have shown that the predictions made by DeepDistinguisher and XOR-based rule are highly correlated especially for high-rate codes. Furthermore, when evaluated on random matrices satisfying both the minimum distance and XOR constraints, the neural distinguisher loses most of its predictive power. This suggests that transformer-based architectures exploit general combinatorial properties of a code rather than some hidden underlying algebraic structure.
papers.authors: Quentin Lavit, Julien Seinturier, Pascal Véron

papers.title: Exact Compilation and Resource Laws for Hidden Integer Feedback
papers.abstract: Hidden randomized rounding couples the privacy loss of successive integer releases. We study a rational-feedback mechanism under predictable signed-unit participation and full observation of every physical output. A preparation's lifetime connects three results. First, preserving complete carries until an observed echo synchronizes the worlds gives exact finite-law point compilation, with support-width exponent $3C-2$ at every fixed budget $C\ge2$. Second, releasing commitments earlier gives a monotone hierarchy whose exact endpoint, strict gaps and numerical brackets quantify calibration loss. At one fixed discrete Gaussian, a loss allowance of 0.09 requires all four commitments. Third, legal regeneration yields an unrestricted KL rate with a square-root testing remainder and a complete asymptotic frontier under joint physical-time and participation constraints. At fixed rational parameters, finite-window occupation programs approximate that frontier to error $2^{-b}$ in polynomial bit time in $b$. Verified countable-transcript semantics and independently checked finite certificates support these analyses. A matched static workload illustrates the resulting design tradeoff: a structured finite integer matrix improves error and fresh randomness, while the scalar feedback instance retains fewer noise-state and source-table bits.
papers.authors: Ganxuan Yang, Siqi Wen, Shuyan Yu, Jidong Yuan

papers.title: Blame-aware Recomposition for Secure Compilation Proofs of Low-Level Compartment Isolation
papers.abstract: The security guarantees of existing formally verified compilers for compartmentalized programs in unsafe languages like C stop at a rather high level, assuming a built-in protection mechanism and a block-based memory model. Verifying a concrete, low-level enforcement mechanism for compartment isolation is still a major challenge for current proof techniques. In particular, Abate et al.'s proof technique fails because one of their proof steps, recomposition, essentially requires hiding all information about the code of each compartment, which is not practically achievable at a low level. We propose an extension of their proof technique to a low-level setting where compartments can fully observe each other's code. To do so, we introduce an overlay semantics that allows us to characterize these observations as a form of undefined behaviour, and we use a novel variant of recomposition that we call blame-aware recomposition, which essentially allows recomposing executions as needed in the original high-level proof technique, even if the low-level context observes the code, because this context is ultimately going to be discarded. We apply this new proof to a compartment isolation mechanism that uses a programmable tag-based reference monitor.
papers.authors: Basile Schlosser, Jérémy Thibault, Catalin Hritcu

papers.title: From if to Oops: Turning a conditional into a key-recovery oracle
papers.abstract: Deterministic variants of CSIDH remove randomness from the group action, either through implementation techniques or, as in Houben's deterministic CSIDH and OSIDH-LD, by design. Since earlier fault attacks on CSIDH mostly target random point sampling, determinism seems to close that avenue. We show that it opens another: every secret-dependent step occurs at a fixed, public point of every execution, so an attacker can fault the same step repeatedly. Our attack forces the mask that selects which of two lanes computes the next isogeny to zero, for example by skipping one instruction. Whether the output changes reveals whether a secret exponent reaches a chosen threshold, and a binary search over these thresholds recovers the full key with one fault per execution: at most 297 oracle queries for OSIDH-LD and 222 for deterministic CSIDH with CSIDH-512-sized keys. We recover full OSIDH-LD keys in a software fault simulation of the reference implementation, and show on a ChipWhisperer-Lite that the targeted instruction is skipped with probability at least $0.94$ at an isolated fault position. Finally, we argue that fault resistance requires giving up determinism, and propose countermeasures relying on randomization.
papers.authors: Gustavo Banegas, Nia Dimitrova, Monika Trimoska

papers.title: Many Repairs, One Direction: Steering Code Models Toward Safer Cryptographic API Use
papers.abstract: Cryptographic API misuse in large language model-generated code can compromise software security. While many existing approaches improve code security by modifying model parameters or inputs, how representation changes associated with different cryptographic API repairs can support a shared intervention for safer code generation remains underexplored. To investigate this, we construct 48,000 matched program pairs across four programming languages and ten cryptographic API misuse categories. Each pair changes a specified API decision while preserving the programming task. Subtracting the misuse program's internal representation from its secure counterpart's gives a repair vector. Across five models, comparisons of mean repair vectors reveal stronger organization by misuse category than by language. These category-specific patterns also support a shared intervention. We introduce CrypSteer, which extracts a shared direction by normalizing repair differences and selecting a principal component aligned with repairs across misuse categories. With model weights fixed, adding one shared direction per model to its internal activations during generation improves aggregate target security rates by 5.28--15.00 percentage points over unsteered generation across languages and misuse categories. These findings connect the shared structure of cryptographic repair representations to a reusable intervention for safer code generation.
papers.authors: Tianhe Lu, Sakuna Harinda Jayasundara, Eric Spero, Ewan Tempero, Robert Biddle, Giovanni Russello

papers.title: Proof-of-Machine-Learning-Inference: Mining Knowledge, Not Hashes
papers.abstract: Bitcoin-style Proof-of-Work (PoW) secures permissionless blockchains but spends substantial computation on hash puzzles which have no utility other than extending the chain. At the same time, we have seen that the rise of generative AI has created significant demand for computational resources that are unfortunately available only to a few players. We propose a solution that solves both problems at the same time. In particular, we present Proof-of-ML-Inference (PoML), a consensus protocol in which miners perform user-requested machine-learning inference as part of their consensus algorithm. We identify exactly what computational assumptions are needed for ML inference to safely replace hash work, formalize those assumptions, and give evidence that LLMs and diffusion models satisfy them. We then formally analyse the security of our protocol by reducing the security of our protocol to the security of the Bitcoin Backbone model. Finally, we empirically evaluate block-time stability, showing that, in a simulated environment, PoML maintains a block production rate close to its calibrated block-time target.
papers.authors: Wan Ki Wong, Michele Ciampi, Rik Sarkar

papers.title: Connection Escrow: Holding AI-Agent Pod Egress in the Kernel Until an Isolated Verifier Rules
papers.abstract: AI agents in containers act by opening network connections, and the text that drives them can be hostile. Controls placed between the agent and its tools are bypassed by a child process or a direct socket, and their approval is not tied to the connection the kernel later opens. We present connection escrow: every outbound TCP connection from a supervised pod is parked inside the kernel's connect() path, before any packet exists, by a 98-instruction eBPF program on the pod's cgroup. A node interceptor attributes the held socket to its kernel socket cookie, process, executable digest, cgroup and pod identity, parks the first bytes the agent writes, and asks a verifier in a separate container with its own key. The connection is released only on a signed verdict naming that one socket cookie and destination, unexpired and unused; no verdict by the deadline resets it, and a late approval is refused. The agent is unmodified. A 36-check adversarial suite with real cgroups passes on the eBPF hold point (33 of the checks also apply, and pass, on an iptables hold point): refused connections never reach the destination; forged, rebound, replayed, expired and late verdicts are refused; the agent's attempt to reach the verifier is itself escrowed; child-process and renamed-binary bypasses fail; UDP is pinned to the resolver. On a Kubernetes cluster, unmodified pods are held per connection and attributed to their SPIFFE identity, a raw socket that bypasses a sidecar proxy is held, and 600 connections from six pods are gated. The hold adds 4.5 ms median per released connection, of which 24 us is policy. Finally, we gate on request content without terminating TLS: an eBPF uprobe reads the plaintext at the agent's TLS-library boundary (shared OpenSSL, static OpenSSL, Go crypto/tls), a model scores it, and the connection is held on that verdict while TLS stays end-to-end and the enforcer holds no key.
papers.authors: Ashok Subbabhatta Gopalakrishna

papers.title: Concrete LDVR Attacks with Fewer Signers
papers.abstract: We improve the concrete parameters of the attacks on the low-dimensional vector representation (LDVR) problem by Rodríguez García and Tessaro (ePrint 2026/2126), whose attack on canonical evaluation points uses $5{,}020$ signers. By combining their Chinese remainder theorem construction with a generalized birthday search over many challenges, we obtain a concrete attack with $488$ signers and $173$ corruptions over the Curve25519 scalar field. In $64$ batches of $2^{25}$ challenges, the search finds solutions for six distinct challenges. We compare the counts measured at each stage of the search with predictions from an explicit heuristic model. For adversarially chosen evaluation points, we build on the binary attacks of Rodríguez García and Tessaro and give a construction that attains the optimal LDVR success probability for every oracle query budget when $2\le n\le253$ and $t_c=t$ in the uniform oracle model. At $228$ signers and $114$ corruptions, our implementation finds a successful subset using SHA-512 challenges after a cumulative total of $360.13$ million queries across two runs, taking $168.60$ seconds in total. We also give an explicit set of $256$ evaluation points for which an efficient subset search attack using $128$ corruptions succeeds with probability at least $51.92\%$ per uniform challenge. For both canonical and adversarially chosen evaluation points, we analyze the query complexity and report measured and estimated running times.
papers.authors: Renas Bacho

papers.title: Fortress: Fork Resistant Transparency logs Relying on Social graph Structure
papers.abstract: Transparency systems -- such as Key Transparency (KT), Certificate Transparency, and binary transparency -- require that all honest participants see the same view of an untrusted server's directory, or, failing that, that the misbehaviour is publicly detected. Every existing design closes this gap with an external trust anchor: a publicly available bulletin board (BB), a blockchain, or an out-of-band (OOB) gossip network among auditors. We observe that transparency systems already have a built-in resource that has so far been overlooked: the social graph induced by the users themselves. We ask whether it can replace the bulletin board or the external gossip channel entirely, and answer in the affirmative (if occasional out-of-band interactions are allowed). We formalise a new primitive, Social-Graph based Forking-Resilient Transparency (sg-FORT), which captures the security guarantees of a BB-free transparency system and we construct Fortress Fork Resistant Transparency logs Relying on Social graph Structure, to our knowledge the first such protocol. In every epoch either all users output the same post, or at least one honest user produces a publicly verifiable Proof of Misbehaviour. Our guarantees hold against an arbitrary malicious server, including a snapshot adversary that may compromise a user and learn its secret state, as long as the server does not compromise close users. In honest executions, OOB interactions occur only when a user resets their secrets, so the total OOB cost approaches the natural lower bound of one call per reset -- dramatically below the full-gossip alternative. We prove security under standard cryptographic assumptions on signatures and dictionary commitment. Under simplifying assumptions (synchronous epochs, always-online users), we view this as a first feasibility result that opens up the design space of social-graph-based transparency systems.
papers.authors: Anastasiia Kucherenko, Melissa Chase, Esha Ghosh

papers.title: Q-MALDetect: Quantum Image-Based Malware Detection and Adversarial Robustness Analysis
papers.abstract: Quantum machine-learning (QML) models are increasingly considered for security applications, yet their adversarial robustness in malware analysis remains insufficiently understood. This paper presents Q-MALDetect, a hybrid convolutional and variational-quantum detector for byte-image representations of x86-64 Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) binaries, and evaluates it under feature-space and a range of Grad-CAM-guided, executable-aware evasion attacks. The model achieves 97.2% training accuracy, but its robustness deteriorates as attack strength increases, with the strongest evaluated feature-space attack reaching a 78.7% attack success rate (ASR). Among executable-aware attacks, Grad-CAM-guided no-operation (NOP) insertion produces the highest conditional ASR of 32.9%. Dynamic adversarial training is the most effective evaluated defense, reducing feature-space ASR to as low as 5.0%, executable-aware ASR to 7.7%, and the sequential-attack ASR to 34.0%. In contrast, convolutional-autoencoder preprocessing increases executable-aware ASR to 39.7%, coinciding with a rise in Grad-CAM attribution mass within the mutable .text region from 35.2% to 45.7%. Ablation results reveal no monotonic relationship between qubit count and robustness, while the encoding interface modifies the learned attack surface without neutralizing the strongest attack. These findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of attacks and defenses depends strongly on the perturbation constraints and evaluation conditions. Reliable deployment of QML malware detectors therefore requires assessment against both feature-space and executable-aware attacks rather than reliance on clean accuracy or generic denoising alone.
papers.authors: Walid El Maouaki, Mohammad Izen, Nouhaila Innan, Alberto Marchisio, Muhammad Shafique

papers.title: LeakBench: Auditing Reward Hacking through Prediction-Time Leakage in Clinical Modeling Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous clinical-modeling agents can optimize predictive performance while violating conditions that make a model usable. We introduce LeakBench, an executable, guideline-derived audit suite that tests agent decisions for prediction-time leakage, calibration, site-level evaluation, support awareness, and decision-curve net benefit. LeakBench combines a synthetic task with known failure structure and two real-data settings: MIMIC-IV (430k admissions) and governed multi-hospital inpatient record front-page (MHFP) data. Our primary analysis uses reward hacking descriptively, without attributing intent: an agent selects prediction-time-invalid inputs because they improve its validation reward. A deterministic optimizer and every evaluated unconstrained local-model configuration select a fatal leaking feature. In fully logged September 2026 A/B runs, DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6-astra each leak in 10/10 unconstrained runs and 0/10 runs with an explicit admission-time constraint. This contrast is version-sensitive: a blinded Claude/Fable-5.1 chat run does not leak in either condition, while explicit-constraint violations appear only in a historical August 2026 slice lacking raw trajectories. Replacing AUROC with AUPRC does not remove leakage selection. Renaming or disguising the leaking inputs changes neither selection nor provenance-based detection; a name-based filter fails. A deterministic provenance verifier-in-loop removes the leak, making the LLM repair loop defense-in-depth. Specific verifier feedback clears fatal leakage in a hosted agent, and a three-seed ablation finds principle-only feedback clears decision-level defects, though these mitigation results are limited. LeakBench treats trustworthy clinical prediction as a property of an agent's modeling process, not merely its score; it is an audit testbed with known-failure controls, not yet an expert-validated benchmark.
papers.authors: Xiaoyuan Bao, Jingsi Jiang, Jiao Shan, Yulong Cao, Haoyu Wang, Zida Liu, Jun Gao

papers.title: SPLASH: Contrastive Audit Pressure for Detecting and Localizing Security Hallucinations in Generated Code
papers.abstract: Code generated by large language models often passes every functional test while remaining insecure. These security hallucinations are common, written with high confidence, and repeated across samples, so neither the generator's own uncertainty nor static analyzers reliably catch them. We introduce SPLASH, which is guided by a new measure called audit pressure. It contrasts teacher-forced log-probabilities for the generated program under a security review and a style review. Aggregated to statements and programs, and grounded in a probabilistic model of competing edits, audit pressure allows SPLASH to choose the secure program among a model's candidate programs and locate the vulnerable statement, with no model training, CWE-specific rules, or internal access to the generating model. On 63,684 programs generated by 12 models for 899 tasks, SPLASH picks secure code in 74% of cases, places the vulnerable statement first in 58% of insecure programs, and chooses better than a frontier LLM judge.
papers.authors: Mirza Masfiqur Rahman, MD Ajwad Akil, Imtiaz Karim, Ashish Kundu, Ramana Kompella, Elisa Bertino

papers.title: IISFA: Ineffective Instruction-Skip Fault Attacks on Bitslice Implementations
papers.abstract: Redundancy countermeasures prevent differential fault analysis by withholding faulty ciphertexts. Ineffective fault analysis and statistical ineffective fault attacks exploit executions in which an injected fault leaves the result unchanged, using constraints on intermediate values or statistical bias to recover keys. In this paper, we present an Ineffective Instruction-Skip Fault Attack (IISFA) on bitsliced implementations protected by redundancy. A bitsliced instruction processes $m$ S-boxes simultaneously. Skipping it leaves the group unchanged exactly when all $m$ S-box inputs belong to its ineffective set, which we compute from the implementation. Each ciphertext output by the device therefore restricts all $m$ $n$-bit subkeys to candidates whose S-box inputs belong to that set. The ineffective probability specifies how often a uniformly random S-box input makes the skip ineffective, and its $m$-th power gives the ciphertext output probability for independent inputs. We determine which key candidates remain indistinguishable under a single target instruction. We give key-recovery procedures for both known and chosen plaintexts and combine different target instructions across queries, with one instruction skipped per execution. We calculate expected injection counts or enclosing intervals for the known- and chosen-plaintext procedures from the ineffective sets and use them to reduce the search for efficient target sequences. We evaluate five bitsliced implementations of GIFT, SKINNY and PIPO on an 8-bit AVR microcontroller under a redundancy countermeasure using clock glitches. All measured key-recovery campaigns succeed in every trial.
papers.authors: Hanbeom Shin, Dongwoo Kang, Donggeun Kwon, Seokhie Hong, HeeSeok Kim

papers.title: Adaptive Cyber-Defense for Evolving Attacker Capabilities using Reinforcement Learning and Behavior Trees
papers.abstract: Autonomous cyber-defense agents trained using reinforcement learning (RL) are increasingly adopted for defending enterprise computer networks. However, existing approaches may become brittle as attacker capabilities evolve and enable new attack strategies. In this work, we study the problem of adapting defender policies learned in CAGE Challenge Scenario 2 (CC2), a benchmark enterprise network defense scenario, to an extended network scenario with new attacker capabilities represented by new attacker actions. Effective attack strategies that leverage new actions are initially unknown, and therefore attacker policies must be learned before defender adaptation can occur. To address this challenge, we develop adversarial RL (ARL) with behavior trees (ARLBT), which uses reward behavior trees (RBTs) to define progression-based reward functions and condition attacker policies on RBT execution. The proposed RBT incorporates the new attacker actions into structured attack strategies while leveraging parallel execution to generate rewards across multiple network nodes simultaneously. We evaluate ARLBT for learning attacker policies against two baseline defender policies across network scenarios with different sets of new attacker actions and compare against multiple attacker baselines. The results demonstrate that ARLBT improves attacker success compared to ARL using the original CC2 reward function and that conditioning policies on RBT execution can improve sample efficiency. We further show that defender policies can be adapted against the learned attackers, improving robustness to attacks that leverage new attacker actions.
papers.authors: Nicholas Potteiger, Ankita Samaddar, Xenofon Koutsoukos

papers.title: Spectrum of Liability: Forensically Sound Acquisition of Wireless Evidence for the Reconstruction of Maritime Cyber-Physical Incidents
papers.abstract: Modern maritime navigation depends on mandatory wireless inputs, most notably GNSS and AIS, whose reception can be spoofed or jammed. When groundings or collisions occur, liability and safety investigations often turn on whether RF interference corrupted bridge instruments, yet the artifacts typically available (VDR outputs, IBS logs, screenshots, decoded messages) are downstream, lossy, and easy to contest in adversarial proceedings. We introduce a forensically sound acquisition methodology that preserves upstream wireless evidence together with the minimal contemporaneous context needed to interpret it. Our system records coherent, multichannel IQ across relevant bands while simultaneously collecting time-aligned receiver and instrument-state metadata (e.g., decoded AIS/GNSS outputs and NMEA sentences), enabling later re-decoding and physical-layer reanalysis tied to what the onboard stack indicated at the time. To make the record independently auditable, we package samples and metadata into a single append-only forensic envelope that cryptographically binds per-stream hash chains with trusted-time anchors and periodic checkpoints, allowing third parties to detect tampering (modification, truncation, splicing, cross-case substitution) and to verify the claimed recording window. A prototype implementation shows the approach is practical: integrity mechanisms add negligible storage overhead and modest compute cost at operationally relevant multiband capture rates.
papers.authors: Giacomo Longo, Alessandro Cantelli-Forti, Alessio Merlo, Enrico Russo

papers.title: SEAL: Towards Persistent Tool Poisoning Attack against LLM Agents via Prefix-Eliciting Trigger
papers.abstract: Tool poisoning has emerged as a critical security threat to LLM agents, where adversaries embed malicious instructions in tool descriptions or external resources that enter the agent's context, allowing adversaries to manipulate agent's tool selection process. However, existing tool poisoning attacks primarily rely on an idealized assumption that the attacks task effect within a single interaction round. We show that their effectiveness degrades sharply in realistic multi-round agentic settings. We further reveal that this degradation stems from the fact that agents do not consistently surface attack-relevant signals in their reasoning as the planning context evolves, thereby weakening the attack's influence across rounds. To investigate whether tool poisoning remains a practical threat in such realistic settings, we propose SEAL, a two-stage method for persistent tool poisoning. Specifically, SEAL first performs Prefix-Eliciting Trigger Optimization (PETO) to optimize context-specific triggers that elicit attack-relevant reasoning prefixes, improving effectiveness within individual contexts. It then applies Local-to-Universal Trigger Aggregation (L2U) to combine these local triggers into a single universal trigger, improving generalization across different contexts and execution rounds. Extensive experiments across seven representative multi-round scenarios and different models demonstrate the attack effectiveness of SEAL, its transferability across target models, and its resistance to potential defenses.
papers.authors: Nanjun Zhou, Yiming Li, Yukun Chen, Ting Qiao, Enhao Huang, Zhan Qin

papers.title: Equivalent Non-linear Shift Register Transformations and Espresso
papers.abstract: The stream cipher Espresso was designed by E. Dubrova and M. Hell as a hardware-efficient candidate for 5G security. It has two components - a 256-bit binary non-linear feedback shift register (NFSR), with 14 feedback taps, and a 20-variable non-linear output function. However, the security of Espresso with regard to several standard cryptanalytic attacks are estimated using an alternate NFSR, which has only two feedback taps. The above analysis is based on the claim that this alternate NFSR is obtained using a transformation algorithm which preserves the output sequence of the original NFSR. This issue has become all the more significant in the light of recent results on hardware performance evaluations, which assume that the stated equivalence holds. This article presents the first successful attempt in settling the above question of Espresso NFSR equivalence. We arrive at our main result by a careful analysis of existing transformation methods relevant to the question. In doing so, we first identify and correct a critical flaw in the proof of a foundational result of E. Dubrova. Next, in the context of Espresso equivalence, we analyze and unify the transformation framework of Dubrova and the one proposed by Yao and Parampalli. Based on our analysis, we have succeeded in transforming the LFSR in an Espresso-equivalent design reported by Yao and Parampalli to the Espresso alternate NFSR. Further, we have obtained a corresponding non-linear output function which achieves output-equivalence with the LFSR design, and hence, with Espresso.
papers.authors: Anirban Ghatak, Kaushik Sarkar, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Ambrish Awasthi, Indivar Gupta

papers.title: BitPCE: Batched Multi-Dimensional PolicyResolution with GPU Bitmap Algebra
papers.abstract: Policy controllers must determine which workloads match rules spanning several label dimensions. Hash sets, compressed bitmaps, and GPU set-processing primitives address the underlying set operations. However, intermediate results, repeated scope evaluations, dependent policy updates, and host transfers can dominate the cost of a heterogeneous batch. We study this problem as batched intersection-of-unions (IoU). Our design exploits independent scope--word tasks, reusable endpoint expressions, and policy dependencies. The challenges are preserving wildcard, empty-group, and exclusion semantics, recognizing equal scopes, and retaining unchanged recipients affected by source edits. BitPCE addresses them with register-resident GPU evaluation, canonical scope compilation, and dependency-complete candidate selection under a stated rendering contract. IP-only changes reuse cached memberships. We establish correctness and word-work bounds. On a four-vCPU A10G host, resident GPU execution is 3.46--36.60$\times$ faster than the best tested native CPU path, including CRoaring, and 1.14--2.22$\times$ faster than an adapted operand-parallel GPU reduction. Gains narrow at the host-output boundary: on an eight-vCPU host, including upload and compact identifier output, resolution takes 16.3 ms versus 19.3 ms for CPU at 100K objects and 500 scopes. Sparse labels and small batches can favor CPU execution. Scope reuse, candidate selection, and incremental transfers are measured as components; complete update-to-enforcement latency remains unevaluated.
papers.authors: Shengwei Wang

papers.title: Registered ABE via Predicate Encodings, Revisited
papers.abstract: Predicate encodings, proposed by Wee (TCC'14), are a simple framework that abstracts a variety of attribute-based encryption (ABE) schemes. Zhu et al. showed how to apply predicate encodings to registered ABE (Reg-ABE) using the same definition as in vanilla ABE (Asiacrypt'23). We provide a new definition of predicate encodings that is more suitable for registered ABE and allows us to obtain more efficient Reg-ABE schemes than those by Zhu et al. for predicates captured by predicate encodings. Notably, we obtain \begin{itemize} \item the first Reg-ABE scheme for (non-)zero inner product with $ O(\log L) $-size ciphertexts, \item the first Reg-ABE scheme for conjunctions/disjunctions with $ O(\log L) $-size ciphertexts, \item the first registered broadcast encryption scheme with $ O(\log L) $-size ciphertexts, \end{itemize} under the standard $ k $-Lin assumption, where $ L $ denotes the maximum number of users. Prior to our work, Reg-ABE schemes for (non-)zero inner product, conjunctions, and disjunctions require $ O(\ell\log L) $-size ciphertexts where $ \ell $ is the vector length or the policy size, and registered broadcast encryption schemes rely on the generic group model.
papers.authors: Junichi Tomida

papers.title: Accountable partial understanding: securing the epistemic attack surface of agentic systems
papers.abstract: Attackers profit from what defenders do not understand. Software security has treated the gap between system behavior and human comprehension as a condition to narrow through analysis and assurance, booking the remainder as accepted risk. Agentic AI systems change that gap: when software reads, writes, explains, and authorizes security-relevant behavior, partial understanding moves faster, grows more opaque, and couples to delegated authority. This paper characterizes the resulting epistemic attack surface and presents a taxonomy of four interacting attack categories, which target the interpretation of intent, the production and consumption of evidence, the scope of delegated authority, and the comprehension of human supervisors. It then defines accountable partial understanding (APU) and specifies six necessary conditions: bounded scope with explicit assumptions, inspectable evidence, assigned responsibility, visible residual unknowns, actionability, and temporal maintenance. It explains why delegating interpretation to software agents differs from distributing knowledge among people and distinguishes APU from risk acceptance, explainable AI, assurance cases, formal verification, and human-in-the-loop oversight. From the conditions, the paper derives five design principles: bounded delegation, decoupled evidence, assumption tracking with invalidation, role-specific accountability views, and intervention-preserving design with residual unknown registers. It introduces two measurable probe dimensions, evidence linkage and invalidation latency, for testing whether accountability mechanisms hold under change and adversarial pressure. Three running examples (an AI coding agent, an autonomous cyber-defense agent, and an AI-mediated insulin delivery update) ground the analysis. Security without full understanding is already here; the task is to make it accountable.
papers.authors: Josiah Dykstra

papers.title: Differential privacy with adjustable preservation of multivariate relationships
papers.abstract: This paper derives an exact attenuation formula for multivariate cross-moments under differential privacy achieved through randomized response. From a proposed alternative formulation of randomization matrices compliant with differential privacy guarantees we show that, under attribute-level randomization and where the randomization of the whole distribution is characterized by Kronecker products, any cross-moment of the anonymized dataset involving distinct attributes is equal to the original cross-moment multiplied by attenuation parameters, themselves determined by the part of the overall privacy budget allocated to each attribute. This characterization enables explicit and transparent controls of multivariate relationships preservations in differential privacy through privacy budget allocation. A simple numerical illustration demonstrates that identical total budgets can yield substantially different covariance-preservation profiles. The results also make the multiplicative loss of higher-order interactions explicit and thus can support mechanism design guided by analytical priorities.
papers.authors: Nicolas Ruiz

papers.title: Signature Knowledge Shielding: Protecting Antivirus Detection Knowledge through Robust Embedding Matching
papers.abstract: Antivirus (AV) signatures encode valuable detection knowledge accumulated through expert analysis, yet repeated black-box queries can expose this knowledge for unauthorized reuse and targeted evasion. We propose Signature Knowledge Shielding (SKS), a design paradigm that protects existing AV rules, termed Protected Signatures (PS), through auxiliary Shielding Signatures (SS). SKS uses AV-supervised importance ranking to discover candidate byte blocks, filters and selects them through negative-sample calibration, and combines SS matches with original AV verdicts through logical OR. SS matching introduces additional positive responses and verdict changes during probing, making detection feedback less directly attributable to PS and increasing the difficulty of localizing signature-related content, while preserving original positive verdicts. Within SKS, we integrate five individually tuned non-learning matching methods and further propose Robust Embedding Matching (REM), a lightweight learned matcher trained with random context and byte perturbations. REM provides stronger and more consistent protection against content modifications and scanning-alignment changes. We develop and open-source a ClamAV-based prototype and evaluate it against five probing methods. With an observed additional test false-positive rate below 0.1%, REM raises the mean query count of state-of-the-art probing to as much as 282.57 times the unprotected baseline, while introducing only 0.67% GPU scanning overhead. These results demonstrate that SKS can substantially increase signature-extraction costs with limited impact on detection utility and scanning efficiency.
papers.authors: Jieshuai Yang, Zhi Wang, Yan Jia, Zhenhua Wu, Jianfei Tang, Chenbin Su, Jingwei Ye, Jianwen Tian, Wanpeng Li

papers.title: PhantomTac: Hijacking Robotic Tactile Systems with Deploy-and-forget Tags
papers.abstract: Tactile perception is crucial for precise robotic manipulation, providing an important foundation for dexterous, closed-loop force control. Among various tactile sensing techniques, magnetic tactile sensors stand out thanks to their fine-grained, three-dimensional force perception capability and strong robustness against visual occlusion. In this study, we discover a physical loophole called PhantomTac in magnetic tactile sensors. The attacker can alter the magnetic field, thus spoofing the force interpreted by magnetic tactile sensors. The attacker can stealthily deploy such an attack by simply attaching a thin (the thickness is around 0.5 mm), battery-free magnetic tag to the surface of an object. Hence, the attack tag can be easily concealed by a barcode sticker. Such an attack scheme is "deploy-and-forget" -- the attacker can deploy the tag and leave. When a robotic hand is picking up an object, it may severely damage the object. Specifically, spoofing the normal force can crush the object, whereas spoofing the shear force can lead to a loose grip, thus dropping the object. Compared with directly sabotaging the robotic hand, PhantomTac is much more concealed as the attacker does not need access to the device. We performed extensive reverse-engineering efforts to characterize the sensing mechanism of commercial-off-the-shelf tactile sensors and proposed a practical tag design. End-to-end evaluations conducted on real robots and robotic arms demonstrate that our attack can bypass existing anti-interference mechanisms and effectively hijack their closed-loop control processes, achieving an attack success rate exceeding 95% when the grasping-position offset is bounded within 8 mm. Finally, based on the limitations of existing anti-magnetic interference mechanisms, we propose a multimodal-consistency defense mechanism to mitigate such physical-layer security threats.
papers.authors: Binbin Zhang, Yifeng Zhang, Xiaomeng Chen, Dongyao Chen

papers.title: Blind-DLPA: An End-to-End Framework for Profiled Blind Side-Channel Analysis
papers.abstract: Conventional profiled side-channel analysis generally assumes that the plaintexts or ciphertexts associated with target traces are available during key recovery. We consider a profiled blind setting in which the attacker can obtain labeled traces from a profiling device using known inputs and keys, but observes only leakage traces from the target device. Under this setting, we propose Blind-DLPA, an end-to-end multi-task framework for {profiled blind side-channel analysis (profiled BSCA) that processes complete preprocessed trace windows} and jointly estimates the soft Hamming-weight posteriors of an input variable and a key-dependent intermediate variable. These posteriors are combined with pre-computed theoretical joint distributions to rank the key hypotheses, avoiding both manual {point of interest} (PoI) selection and a parameter-sensitive Gaussian label-error model. Evaluations on unprotected AES and Kyber demonstrate successful key recovery, while experiments on protected AES implementations show robustness to desynchronization and Boolean masking. To the best of our knowledge, Blind-DLPA provides the first reported profiled blind key recovery on the ASCAD dataset, reaching a guessing entropy of zero with 39 attack traces. Complementing these results, we revisit the Ascon Hamming-weight joint-distribution model adopted in prior work and identify previously overlooked collisions between key-dependent theoretical distributions that prevent unique key recovery under this model.
papers.authors: Pei Cao, Chi Zhang, Dawu Gu

papers.title: NIOCIS: Typed-Decision Next-Hop Routing with Node-Conditioned Option Spaces for Tool-Use Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-use agents pay per decision: at each hop a language model re-reads the state and thinks for seconds, though its actions are finite and decisions recur. We present NIOCIS, a routing layer that folds execution logs into a loop-collapsed action graph (forward transitions plus recovery back-edges) answering one typed question: which declared option at a state, plus stop, does the fleet take next? A small model reads a calibrated distribution over them in one pass, emitting no text. On 1,615 production security-operations episodes we measure what the layer replaces, returns and is bounded by. Replaces: the typed encoder matches the logged next hop on 32.2% of the 3,875 held-out decisions (34.9% within the declared options) in 10 ms of encoder time (19.5 ms for the typed-choice form), against 2.2 s per LLM hop; two feature readouts reach 32.8% and 32.3%, an ordering the paired test does not resolve, so the typed layer is chosen for cost, not a separated lead. Tuning: jpt-4b reaches 9.9% zero-shot and 31.9% fine-tuned, a gap an exact paired test does not resolve (p=0.68), at 244 ms. Returns little: the realised hop falls outside the declared options for 7.9% of decisions and outside the model's top twenty for 9.3%; the most confident 15% holds 91.9% accuracy. Bounded: a cross-trace leave-one-out test puts the released state's ceiling at 25.6--44.9% as the state key grows more specific, i.e. repeated states disagree more often than they agree; the option-space ablation attributes the gain to per-node candidate restriction (+3.5 points over a flat catalog) rather than graph traversal (zero within its interval); a gated self-evolution loop lifts every arm above its anchor yet ends below full supervision; a confidence-gated cascade loses agreement when the escalation arm is the zero-shot stand-in; and agreement past a third of the fleet needs a state carrying the plan and the observation.
papers.authors: Jin Han, Mingfeng Xin, Feng Liang, Jingtao Yu

papers.title: A Key-Recovery Attack on the GTLN Knapsack Cryptosystem via Continued Fractions
papers.abstract: We present a continued-fraction key-recovery attack on the knapsack-based public-key cryptosystem proposed by Gómez-Torrecillas, Lobillo, and Navarro (GTLN). The key observation is that ratios of public-key differences closely approximate rational numbers with small denominators, enabling their exact recovery by continued fractions. Divisibility relations in the recovered fractions yield multiples of two private-key integers through greatest common divisor computations. Once these two integers are identified by a bounded cofactor search, all remaining private-key integers except the modulus and the shift are uniquely determined. Further greatest common divisor computations, cofactor enumeration, and modular inversion then recover the secret modulus and shift. The above process of key recovery uses only public keys. For fixed cofactor bounds, the algorithm runs in polynomial time in the public-key bit length, while a heuristic analysis predicts a high probability of recovering the original key. In experiments with prime-based key generation, our Python implementation recovered the complete private key in all 2,400 trials across the 24 recommended parameter sets, with each attack taking less than 0.05 seconds.
papers.authors: Shiyi zhou, Yingpu Deng, Shi Ying

papers.title: Towards Architectural-Level Safety Control: Relocating Hazardous Knowledge into Removable Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.abstract: Large language models acquire broad knowledge from web-scale corpora during pretraining, including knowledge that could be hazardous if misused. Removing such knowledge from the model itself without degrading general capability is desirable but difficult, as it is deeply entangled with general capability within the same parameters. Existing safety alignment and unlearning methods typically adjust these shared parameters, tending to suppress the expression of hazardous knowledge rather than remove it. As a result, the knowledge remains in the model and is readily recoverable by subsequent fine-tuning. To address this limitation, we propose REX (Relocating into Removable EXperts), a knowledge relocation method that separates hazardous knowledge from general capability at the architectural level. Exploiting the modular structure of Mixture-of-Experts models, REX expands the model with a set of new, physically removable experts designated to hold hazardous knowledge. Through expert expansion, selective gradient masking and routing differentiation, it relocates hazardous knowledge out of the original experts and concentrates it in the new ones. Excising these new experts yields a model suitable for public release. This removal holds consistently across Intern-S2, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B; on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, for instance, excision lowers WMDP-Bio accuracy by 48.4 points while MMLU changes by less than 3 points. The excised model matches the strongest of nine unlearning baselines in removing hazardous knowledge, and it is the only one that preserves this removal under subsequent fine-tuning. After 250M tokens of standard fine-tuning on Qwen3.5, the best baseline rebounds on WMDP-Bio from 44.1% to 78.3%, whereas REX rises only from 32.4% to 42.8%.
papers.authors: Cheng Jin, Zhongtian Ma, Xiao Wang, Han Qi, Xiaoyu Wen, Xiang Wang, Youbang Sun, Xia Hu, Bowen Zhou, Chaochao Lu, Qiaosheng Zhang

papers.title: SAT and Neural Network Filters for Misinjections in Fault Attacks
papers.abstract: A misinjection, an injection that misses the fault form an attack assumes, can make an elimination fault attack discard the correct key. They occur when the attacker has not determined the timing of the device, and a random-delay countermeasure wider than the S-box layer can force them even on one who has. This paper presents a SAT filter that removes misinjections without the secret key, one injection at a time. It models the differential propagation from the injected round to the end of the cipher in SAT and rejects an injection when the model has no solution for the assumed fault and the observed ciphertext difference. The paper also presents a neural network filter, which passes an injection when the score of a network trained for the same decision is at least 0.5, and a combined filter, which passes it only when the SAT model of the injection also has a solution. We measure the filters on faults injected by clock glitching into GIFT-64, GIFT-128 and BAKSHEESH on a microcontroller, in three settings, a non-profiling attacker without and with a random-delay countermeasure and a profiling attacker with it. The SAT filter rejected none of the 14669 intended faults and, for the non-profiling attacker without the random-delay countermeasure, at least 0.940 of the misinjections at the full-diffusion round, over at least 385 each. For the same attacker it raises the success probability of ToFA on BAKSHEESH, which recovers the master key, from 5.2% to 61.2%, and the combined filter raises it to 96.2%, each over 2000 trials.
papers.authors: Hanbeom Shin, Dongwoo Kang, Donggeun Kwon, Seokhie Hong, HeeSeok Kim

papers.title: Formalization of Rényi Differential Privacy in Isabelle/HOL (Draft version)
papers.abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is a gold-standard definition of privacy designed to evaluate the privacy guarantee of databases. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) is an important variant of DP that gives tight evaluations of machine learning algorithms. These formulations are easy to understand, but evaluating privacy for actual databases is complicated. Even a small change in the database can break its privacy, and evaluations of DP and RDP themselves are complicated. In particular, RDP evaluations in recent studies have become much harder. Therefore, formal verification of them has been studied for over a decade. In this paper, we propose an Isabelle/HOL library for formalizing Rényi differential privacy in a general setting. We first formalize RDP for continuous distributions. As a technical basis, we formalize several properties of convex functions and $f$-divergences for nonnegative convex functions. We formalize basic properties of RDP, conversion laws from RDP to DP, the moment accountants in DP, and the Gaussian mechanism and its RDP. Finally, we discuss the stochastic gradient descent mechanism with Gaussian noise and formalize a rough evaluation of its RDP and DP.
papers.authors: Tetsuya Sato

papers.title: On Pearl Blockchain's Proof of Useful Work: Systematization and Flexibility
papers.abstract: We revisit the proof-of-useful-work (PoUW) scheme in Pearl blockchain's white paper (Pearl Research Team), giving a systematic sensitivity characterization as an alternative to its Jackpot policy, along with efficient algorithm for verifying the sensitivity condition. Beyond its independent interest, our characterization yields a more flexible PoUW scheme that eenables miner autonomy: each miner can independently choose its noise magnitude to tailor the trade-off between computational accuracy and mining efficiency to its own needs.
papers.authors: Youlong Ding

papers.title: Locate, Then Reason: End-to-End Patch Presence Testing in Stripped Binaries
papers.abstract: Binary patch presence testing (PPT) determines whether a security fix is present in a stripped binary. Prior systems often assume that patch-relevant code is known or successfully matched. Function-level matching is brittle to compilation changes, inlining, finite model context, and missing usage context; moreover, similarity suppresses the patch-sized distinction needed for the verdict. We present PatchAlign, an end-to-end binary PPT workflow, which performs large-scale localization that maximizes recall economically, then the final verdict reasons for patch-specific evidence. PatchAlign uses instruction-aligned retrieval and caller-callee context to accurately locate patch-relevant binary code pieces, then screens the shortlist and compares target binary code with vulnerable and patched references using an LLM. Our experiments indicate that PatchAlign can precisely localize patch-relevant code and determine patch status without a target-location oracle.
papers.authors: Huaijin Wang, Tongda Wang, Zhibo Liu, Yue Zhang, Shuai Wang, Pengfei Hu, Jianzhong Liu, Fangtian Zhong, Shaohua Wang

papers.title: Don't Judge an Agent by Its Messages: Private-State Leakage under Passive Monitoring of Agent Communication
papers.abstract: An AI agent can reproduce the distribution of its messages and of the receiver's task outcomes while disclosing private information that the task never required. We ask what a passive audit can certify when the auditor knows the authorised sender and the exact observable law but has no trusted pairing of messages with the private states behind them. For a single round, compatible mutual-information leakage forms a sharp interval, and fixing the entire task-relevant message law, with every declared task utility, can still leave a full private bit undetermined; total leakage is determined if and only if, in every task state, the remaining private state or the authorised message is a deterministic function of that state. For a sender, such as an LLM, that selects among its own responses, we prove that in a balanced case its change to the message law within each task state equals $(1-2^{-k})$ times the honest messages' dependence on the attribute, which also sets, up to a constant, how many messages a monitor needs. With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on a synthetic routing task, selection among 16 responses lets a public decoder recover a private bit in all 8,192 held-out rounds at 98.60\% routing accuracy (honest sender 98.90\%). A monitor that knows the selection rule reaches AUC 0.645 on single messages, close to the ceiling of 0.671 that honest messages predict, and 0.972 over 16, while generic monitors stay near chance. A law-preserving sender built from the same samples recovers the bit in 97.7\% of rounds, and every monitor without the true bit stays near chance against it. A canonical task interface preserves every receiver decision and bounds the remaining information about a balanced attribute by twice the routing-error rate, even for a receiver that shares a key with the sender. These results distinguish what passive auditing can certify from what restricting communication can enforce.
papers.authors: Daksh Pandey, Sayon Duttagupta, Xinhai Zou, Amit Singh Bhati

papers.title: Hierarchical Rule Auditing with Exact Ternary GPU Correlation
papers.abstract: Auditing firewall logs against requirements mapped to controls and frameworks must retain overlapping obligations, preserve uncertainty from missing attributes and count distinct affected records. Direct, bitmap and relational methods can express this audit; a correlation implementation must preserve distinctions that ordinary match counts and rule-hit totals discard. We present an exact ternary correlation algorithm that compiles categorical conjunctions into one bounded-integer matrix product. A dominating false-predicate penalty separates known mismatches from missing evidence, while per-record hierarchy unions prevent duplicate counting. We prove their composition and handle high-cardinality endpoints through exact address classes and versioned labels. Evaluation compares eight CPU/GPU implementations, includes public traffic and 133 published source-address ACLs with generated observations, and measures hierarchy and policy-rebuild costs. On an NVIDIA L4, matched fused execution reduces latency by 8.8 to 11.2 percent relative to two-product correlation across five tested shapes. At 100,000 records and 1,024 requirements, it takes 12.28 ms versus 13.82 ms for two products and 12.29 ms for GPU bitmaps. Bitmaps remain faster in most regimes, with hierarchy operations and reductions dominating the measured fused-correlation stage intervals.
papers.authors: shengwei wang

papers.title: Same Data, Different Bytes: Serialization-Invariant Integrity Checks for Agent-Published Datasets
papers.abstract: Agent networks require reliable ways for requesting agents to verify where data is located, how it can be accessed, and whether the data received matches what the data owner made available. Checksum mismatches can reflect either altered content or serialization differences that preserve data equivalence under specified rules. Data identification mechanisms for agents, such as DataFacts, describe where data can be accessed and provide checksums for checking received data against published references. We propose a serialization-invariant identification method that assigns the same identifier to data representations equivalent under explicit rules. We use DataFacts as a case study, retaining its existing checksum alongside the proposed identifier. In a controlled agent study, we compare the proposed configuration with ordinary-tool and checksum baselines across equivalent re-encodings, altered content, and unavailable references. The study includes three model tiers from each of two providers. For equivalent re-encodings, the proposed configuration increased expected-outcome rates by 80.4 percentage points over the ordinary-tool baseline and by 70.2 percentage points over the checksum baseline. The proposed configuration also increased evidence-supported rejection of altered content by 3.5 percentage points over the checksum baseline. We contribute a serialization-invariant identification method with explicit equivalence rules, an integration approach illustrated through DataFacts, and an empirical evaluation against ordinary-tool and checksum baselines.
papers.authors: Jin Gao, Maura Clark

papers.title: Consistency Is the Attack Surface: Detecting Coordinated Retrieval Poisoning with Embedding Geometry
papers.abstract: Consistency-based defenses for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) rest on an assumption that a sparse adversary breaks: a poisoning campaign may modify a negligible fraction of the corpus, yet retrieval concentrates its passages into the reader's context. Across four Natural Questions retrieval seeds, at least one injection reaches the top-5 in 94.1% of targeted query--seed rows, and all three form a retrieved majority in 52.9%. Under our short-answer protocol, RobustRAG and ReliabilityRAG reach exposure-conditional attack success 0.512, against 0.576 for undefended RAG, while lowering clean accuracy from 0.328 to 0.216. Coordination, however, leaves a fingerprint: a dense, query-anchored component in the evidence embedding geometry. CoordGuard audits this structure from robustly normalized query-weighted affinities, without poison labels, correct answers, or reader gradients. Its always-filter mode suppresses the selected component whenever one forms; a benign-calibrated gate suppresses it only at unusually high scores and traces a robustness--utility frontier. Pooling four retrieval seeds, e5 always-filtering reduces $\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{exp}}$ to 0.167 overall and 0.138 on parametrically unknown queries, at a 13.6-point clean cost, while a Contriever gate retains clean accuracy 0.315 at $\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{exp}}=0.331$. The reduction transfers across two readers, three tasks, and multiple retriever--auditor pairs, and count-matched controls attribute it to component-targeted removal rather than deletion volume. These findings recast poison detection from judging truth to auditing the structure of retrieved evidence.
papers.authors: Zeyan Li, Qirong Guo, Jianfeng Xu

papers.title: Temporal Dynamics and Security Assessment of SRT Protocol: A 96-Day Longitudinal Analysis of Production Streaming Infrastructure
papers.abstract: This study presents a 96-day longitudinal analysis of Secure Reliable Transport (SRT) protocol behavior in a production streaming environment between Iraq and Turkey, examining 262,672 transport metric samples and 5,033,104 system resource measurements collected between October 2025 and January 2026. The research addresses temporal patterns, system-resource relationships, attack vulnerability, and anomaly detection. Results reveal significant temporal variation: Negative Acknowledgment exhibits 7.6-fold hourly variation and 11.5-fold daily variation (p < 0.001), though with small effect sizes (eta^2 < 0.04), indicating that temporal period explains less than 4 percent of total variance. Central Processing Unit (CPU) utilization emerges as the strongest system-level correlate of transport variation (r = 0.617 with NAK rate). Controlled User Datagram Protocol (UDP) flood experiments at 500 packets per second cause CPU increases of 176 to 806 percent, while SRT transport metrics change by only plus or minus 13 percent demonstrating protocol resilience through the Automatic Repeat Request mechanism. An unexpected anomaly reaching 97.7 percent CPU enabled signature-based differentiation between attack types. A Z-score anomaly detection method outperforms fixed thresholds, detecting all 7 security events. This study contributes the longest temporal characterization of SRT metrics reported to date, the first system-SRT correlation analysis, and the first controlled security assessment of SRT infrastructure. These findings provide actionable guidance for capacity planning, security hardening, and multi-metric monitoring of production SRT deployments.
papers.authors: Ahmed F. K. Koysha, Ferdi Sönmez

papers.title: Secure Agentic Coding through Counterexample-Grounded Feedback
papers.abstract: As coding models and agent harnesses become more capable, reliable security verification is becoming a central bottleneck.
